I collect pressed flowers in my history scroll. When the instructor opens it, petals fall out. It's very pretty.
I have a jar of marbles. Twenty-seven. One is cracked inside and when you hold it up, it looks like lightning.
I've collected every kind of leaf in the Academy yard. There are nine. I thought there would be more.
I collect drawings of the Hokage. Every kid in my class draws them different. One has a moustache.
I keep the shells from the sunflower seeds I eat. It's a big pile. I don't know why. I just started.
I collect the little paper fortunes from the shrine. Even the bad ones. Especially the bad ones. They're funnier.
My collection of practice shuriken that missed is very big. The ones that hit go back in the box.
Our instructor can catch a piece of chalk without even looking. Somebody threw one once. Once.
When the instructor's happy, they tap the desk twice. When they're cross, three times. Count the taps.
Our instructor makes the best paper cranes. If you get top marks, you get a crane on your desk.
The instructor yawned in the middle of the lesson today. I didn't know instructors could get tired.
Our instructor has a tea mug with a chip in it. Nobody's allowed to touch the mug.
The instructor says "eyes on me" so many times a day. I counted. Thirty-four times on Second Day.
Our instructor can do all twelve hand signs in one breath. I tried and ran out of breath at the Snake.
When it's somebody's birthday, the instructor lets them ring the end-of-day bell. My birthday's coming up. I'm going to ring it so hard.
Our instructor writes on the board with both hands sometimes. It's very strange and very impressive.
The instructor knows everybody's sandals. If you leave yours in the yard, they're back on your desk in the morning.
I saw our instructor eating at Ichiraku after school. It was so strange, like seeing a fish walk.
The instructor gave me extra homework because I finished early. I've learned to finish at the exact right time.
I saw a squad come back through the gate all muddy and tired, and the youngest one was still smiling. I want to be that one.
A Genin let me hold their kunai pouch for a second while they tied their sandal. It was so heavy. Full of real kunai.
Two Genin were racing over the roofs on our street. Our cat watched them the whole time like it was a contest.
The new Genin wear their headbands everywhere. On their forehead, on their arm, round their neck. I'd wear mine everywhere too.
I saw a Genin trip over a bucket at the market. They pretended it was a training exercise. I believed them for a whole minute.
A Chunin asked me directions to the bathhouse. A real Chunin! I gave very good directions.
When I see a Jonin on the street, I stand very straight in case they need a new squad member right away.
A Genin threw a shuriken at a falling leaf and pinned it to a tree. I keep looking at that tree.
My mum's a ninja and I don't know what she does. She just says "work". Work must be very exciting.
My parents sell vegetables, so I know every vegetable in the village. Ask me about any radish.
My dad's a ninja who came back from a long mission with a beard. I didn't recognise him for a second.
My mum is a nurse. She says she's not a ninja, but she's the bravest person I know.
My dad's a carpenter and he made my desk at home. It's got a secret drawer. It's not secret anymore. I just told you.
My parents both work at the market, so I know all the stallholders. They give me free stuff on my birthday.
My mum's a Chunin and she makes me do push-ups before dinner. Ten push-ups, then rice.
My dad is a cook at a tea house and brings home the cakes that broke. Broken cakes taste exactly the same. Better, even.
My parents aren't ninja and they worry about me going to the Academy. I tell them I'm fine. I tell them every day.
My mum works at the gate. She knows every traveller who comes in. She says she knows everyone, which means me too, so I behave.
I learned to whistle today! Well, it's half a whistle. Mostly air. But some whistle.
I can wiggle my ears. Nobody else in class can. It's my secret skill. It's not a secret now.
I'm learning to juggle with three rice balls. I've dropped about forty rice balls. The ants are very happy.
I tied my sandal laces together by accident and fell over in front of everyone. I said it was a new taijutsu.
I sneezed so hard in class that my practice headband flew off. It landed on the instructor's desk. I went to get it very quietly.
I learned the word for every colour in the dango stall. Pink, white, green and a new one: brownish.
I tried to stay awake all night to see the sunrise. I fell asleep at the window. I saw the sunrise from my dreams.
I can hold my breath for a count of forty. Underwater it's thirty. Under a blanket it's forever.
I practise my signature in case I'm famous one day. I've got a really good one with a swirl.
I found a coin in my old sandal. It's been there since last winter. That's a winter coin. It's worth more.
I got hiccups in the middle of the test and the whole class laughed. The instructor gave me water. I got hiccups again.
I learned to do a cartwheel! Well, a half-cartwheel. Then I sit down. It counts.
I lost my front tooth today! It came out in a rice cracker. I'm keeping the tooth. Not the cracker.
I can tie seven kinds of knot. The instructor only taught us three. The other four I made up.
I spun round twenty times and then tried to walk straight. I walked into the woodshed. Science.
I want to visit every shop in the village before I graduate. I've done eighteen. The pawn shop is scary.
The bathhouse has a cold milk box. You drink the milk after your bath, hands on your hips. That's the rule.
I found a shortcut from the Academy to Ichiraku through the alley behind the tailor. It saves a whole minute. A ramen minute.
There's a bench by the river where you can see the ferry, the herons and the Hokage Rock all at once. It's the best bench.
The furniture shop has a giant bed on display. I lay on it once until the shopkeeper coughed.
I watched the smith hit a glowing bar until it turned into a kunai. Sparks went everywhere. One landed on my sleeve. I'm fine.
The flower shop smells like a garden that's also a cake. I don't know how.
There's a tiny shrine at the end of our street with a stone frog. I give it a pebble every morning for luck.
The tea house garden has a pond with a bamboo pipe that clonks when it fills up. I can wait for the clonk forever.
The scroll shop has a scroll as long as the whole room, rolled up in a glass case. I want to know what's on it.
My best friend and I have a secret handshake. It's eleven moves long. We get it wrong every time and laugh.
I got into a fight with my best friend over the last rice cracker. Then we split it. Then we were friends again.
There's a kid in my class who can do the Clone perfectly and never shows off. I want to be friends with them.
My friend and I are going to be on the same squad. We've decided. We just have to tell the Hokage.
I wrote my friend a letter even though they live two doors down. I gave it to the courier. It took a day.
I don't have a best friend yet. I have a lot of medium friends. That's good too.
My friend can burp the whole name of the village. I'm learning. I've got to the first part.
Me and my friend made a pact to graduate on the same day. We spat on our hands. Then we washed them.
My friend lent me their favourite marble for the whole week. That's how you know someone trusts you.
I did my homework at Ichiraku. The broth got on page three. Now page three smells delicious.
The workshop smells like sawdust and glue. I made a little box today. It doesn't close, but it's a box.
Today we practised walking without making a sound. The floor in the hall creaks in seven places. I know all seven now.
The instructor tested our memory with twenty objects on a tray. I remembered the kunai, the cup and the frog. There was no frog.
We practised escaping from a rope tied round our wrists. I got out! Then I couldn't get the rope off my foot.
We learned how to read tracks in the yard. Mine were the easiest because I'd been stomping.
Today was first aid. I bandaged my partner's arm, and then their other arm, and then I got carried away.
We had to climb the rope in the hall. I got halfway and then just held on and looked at the ceiling.
In survival class we learned which mushrooms you can eat. The answer is mostly don't.
We learned how to light a fire with flint. My spark went straight into my own sleeve. The instructor was very calm.
We practised hiding in the yard. I was a bush for an hour. A very good bush.
For homework we had to watch the stars and write down what we saw. I wrote stars. Lots of stars.
My cat brings me presents. Leaves, a sock, once a whole fish from the market. I had to give the fish back.
I've been asking for a ninken for so long my parents bought me a toy one. I'm still asking.
I taught my neighbour's dog to sit when I do the Rat sign. Now every time I practise, it sits.
My little brother got a goldfish and named it Hokage. Now we have to say "feed the Hokage" every morning.
There's a stray dog that waits at the Academy gate every afternoon. Somebody always has a bit of lunch left over.
My grandma's cat sits on my homework every evening. I think it's helping. It's not helping.
They say if you go to the training grounds at midnight you can hear the old swords clashing. I think it's just the Gekko practising.
Somebody said the furniture shop's big wardrobe goes to another room inside. I opened it. It's a wardrobe.
My friend's cousin swears there's a ninja who lives in the tallest tree in the village and never comes down.
I heard the bath house keeper once boiled an egg in the big tub. Now I check the tub for eggs every time.
There's a rumour that the dango stall man can juggle twelve sticks without dropping one. I've seen four. That's still good.
Everyone says the library has a scroll that teaches you a jutsu just by reading it. I've read twelve scrolls. Nothing yet.
Some days I want to be a ninja and some days I want to run Ichiraku. Some days both at once.
I asked a grown-up what the hardest part of being a ninja is, and they said waking up early. I'm already a ninja, then.
I want to go on a mission to the sea and bring back a shell for everyone in my class.
When I'm a Genin, I'll protect the old grandma on our lane first. Then the rest of the village.
I'm going to be the ninja who can talk to animals. I've started with the crow. It just stares.
When I'm grown up I'll buy a house with a round water tank on the roof and swim in it every summer.
In my dreams I can run up the Hokage Rock without stopping. When I wake up my legs are tired, like I really did it.
If I could have one jutsu, I'd make it stop the rain just over my head. Everyone else gets wet but not me.
I'm hungry. I'm always hungry. My mum says I have a hole in my stomach. I think it's a ninja stomach.
I'm bored. Being bored is the worst. Do you want to do something? Anything? Something with dango?
I'm so tired from running laps that I could sleep standing up like the gate guards.
I'm having the best day. I got a gold star, found a ryo and the dango stall gave me an extra. Nothing can ruin it.
Today was a bad day. I dropped my lunch and got the Ram wrong. But I'm here now, and you're nice, so it's a bit better.
I'm in a good mood because tomorrow is a day with no lessons. I'm going to sleep until the sun is right in my eyes.
I can't sit still today. My legs want to run. My hands want to throw. My mouth wants dango.
My head's full of hand signs and sums. If I shake it, I can hear them rattle.
Grown-ups always say "when you're older". I'm older than I was yesterday. When is older?
I asked my grandpa what the village was like when he was a kid. He said smaller and with more mud.
Why do grown-ups drink tea when they could drink juice? I'll never understand grown-ups.
My mum says I'll understand when I'm a parent. I'm never going to be a parent. I'm going to be a Hokage.
Grown-ups talk about the weather all the time. Rain, sun, wind. Don't they have anything exciting to talk about?
I want to stay up as late as grown-ups do. What do they even do at night? I bet it's sitting.
The best seat on the ferry is right at the front where the water splashes your toes.
I made a boat out of a leaf and a twig and sailed it in the gutter. It went round the corner and I never saw it again. Brave boat.
I like walking along the top of the low wall by the market. You have to balance. The shopkeepers shout, but nicely.
There's a puddle outside the tailor's that's been there for a month. It has tadpoles now. I check on them every day.
I counted every step from my house to the Hokage Residence. Seven hundred and twelve. Seven hundred and nine if you jump the gutter.
The best place to watch the main street is from the bench outside the noodle shop. You see everybody, and you can smell ramen.
I climbed onto the roof of the woodshed and could see three clan gates from there. And a cat. The cat saw me too.
The cobbles on the main street have a crack shaped like a snake. Every kid in the village steps over it for luck.
I drew a map of my perfect village. It has a dango river and a ramen mountain and the Academy is just one room for napping.
I tried to stay as still as the training post for an hour. I made it to a count of eighty. The post wins.
I can do a really good impression of the instructor. "Eyes on me!" See? I'm not doing it in class, though.
I'm going to teach my little sister all the hand signs before she starts the Academy. She'll be the best in her class because of me.
I practise bowing to my reflection in the river. The river bows back. It's very polite.
I keep a diary. Today I wrote "dango good, test bad, frog in pond". That's the whole day, really.
I wish I could talk to the Hokage just for a minute. I'd ask what they eat for breakfast. That's the most important question.
I'm going to make the whole class laugh at the graduation party. I've been saving a joke for a year. It's a really good one.
When I can't decide something, I flip a ryo. Then I do the opposite. It works every time.
I talk to the moon before bed sometimes. Just to say goodnight. The moon doesn't mind.
I'm going to remember everything about being a kid so I can tell my own students one day. Even the boring bits.
I tried to sneak a dango into class in my sleeve. The sleeve was sticky all day. Worth it.
My sandals are too small, but they're my lucky ones, so I'm wearing them until my toes give up.
The Academy gate squeaks when you open it slowly. If you open it fast, it squeaks shorter. I've tested both.
I wrapped my practice kunai in a cloth like a real ninja's. It looks very serious now. It's still blunt.
I traded a shiny button for a hawk feather from the courier loft. Best trade of my whole life.
I've decided my favourite number is twelve, because of the hand signs. My second favourite is three, because of dango.
I saw a shooting star over the wall last night. I wished so hard I forgot what I wished for.
When I grow up, I'm going to give every Academy kid a free dango on their first day. That's my promise.
No compound, no crest, no elders telling me how to bow. Just a headband and a name my grandmother sold rice under.
My family were farmers for six generations. I'm the first to throw a kunai, and they still don't know which end is sharp.
Nobody expects anything of a clanless Genin. That's the best head start there is.
I used to envy the clan kids their techniques. Then I watched one of them get lectured at the Hyuga gate for twenty minutes over a bow.
My jutsu are the ones anybody can learn. I just learned them harder.
I've got no clan day, so I made my own. Every year on the day I graduated, I buy myself the most expensive bowl at Ichiraku.
Sometimes I walk past the Senju hall and wonder what it's like to have a tree older than your family's memory. Then I go home to my landlady's cat.
My mother runs a laundry by the river. She irons my flak vest every week and tells the customers I'm in the guard, which is close enough.
A clan teaches you who you are. Being clanless, you have to work it out yourself, and I think I got a good answer.
When I made Chunin, the whole apartment block threw a party on the landing. Nobody had a crest; everybody had a pot of something.
The clan kids have someone to teach them their family's way. Mine was the library, an old Jonin and a lot of bruises.
My squad was an Inuzuka, a Hyuga and me. I was the one who kept the maps, carried the rice and got us home.
Most of the Leaf's shinobi are clanless. The clans are famous, but it's ordinary families who fill the Mission Desk queue every morning.
Clanless shinobi live in the apartment blocks near the Residence. You can tell which flats are ours by the laundry: all headbands and no crests.
The great clans have their quarters. We have the noodle shops, the bath house and the bench outside the Mission Desk, and I'd say we got the better deal.
A clanless Genin can learn a lesser technique from a friendly clan, if they earn it. I'm working on the Nara. They're hard to impress, and very slow to say so.
Clan days, the clanless shinobi cover the gate and the patrols so the clans can celebrate. Then they cover ours on New Year. It evens out.
There's a bar near the barracks where the clanless Jonin drink. No crests on the walls, just a board with every name that's ever made Jonin from an ordinary family.
I'll admit it, I'm proud of it. Every rank I have, I got without anyone's grandfather putting in a word.
Some evenings I'd like to go home to a big table and twenty cousins. Then I remember my flat is quiet, and I make tea, and it's fine.
People ask me which clan I'm from all the time. I tell them the Leaf, and it's never once been wrong.
You're one of us, {player}: no crest, no compound, no rules about how deep to bow. Make your own name; it's the only kind we get.
Clanless and in the Academy? Good. Learn from all of them. The clans only teach their own, but we can watch everyone.
Don't let the clan kids make you feel small. Half the Hokage's guard grew up in an apartment block, same as you.
The old Jonin in the flat below mine has stopped coming to the bench outside the Mission Desk. It's not like them. Someone should knock.
A clanless Genin from my block keeps getting turned down for squad trials. I'd like someone with a clan to vouch for the kid once.
Our family's only heirloom is a bent kettle that went through three wars and a flood. We still use it. The tea tastes of history and rust.
I joke that my family's secret technique is getting up early. It's not a joke. It's why I made Chunin.
My grandfather says clans are like big trees. Fine to sit under, but you'll never see the sky.
We're not shinobi in this family. We bake. Every Genin squad that ever came back from a mission has eaten one of our buns.
I've lived next door to a shinobi family for twenty years. You stop jumping when someone lands on your roof at night. Mostly.
My daughter wanted to go to the Academy. We talked her round to the tea house instead. Some days I wonder if we did right.
My son made Genin last spring. Nobody in our family had so much as touched a kunai. I polish his headband when he isn't looking.
The village needs its shinobi, but it runs on its grocers, its cooks and its bath keepers. I'm proud of my apron.
Civilians don't get clan days, but we've got Market Day, and nobody's ever had to bow to a cabbage.
Our street is all civilian families: a cobbler, a laundress, two cooks and me. We share one garden and the arguments that come with it.
I was a little afraid of shinobi as a child. Then a Chunin carried my grandmother home from the market in the rain, and I wasn't anymore.
My grandfather says the Leaf was a farming village before it was a shinobi one. He likes to remind the Jonin of that at the bath house.
I can't do a single hand sign, but I can carry four trays of tea up three flights without spilling. We all have our training.
About half the Leaf is ordinary people: shopkeepers, farmers, carpenters and children who'll never throw a shuriken in their lives.
Civilian families live on the market street, the residential streets and down by the river. The shinobi are everywhere else, and on the roofs.
The Academy takes anyone with the will to try. Most civilian children try for a year, and most come home and help in the family shop.
Civilians pay the same ryo as anyone at Ichiraku. Shinobi just order more.
When the village is quiet, nobody notices the shopkeepers. When the shops shut for a festival, everybody notices.
We have our own customs: the first loaf of the year goes to the shrine, the first fish to the oldest neighbour, the first tea to whoever came furthest.
The civilian families of the riverside have a rowing race every summer. No jutsu allowed. The shinobi bet on it anyway.
Every civilian street has a shinobi family on it somewhere. They keep us safe; we keep them fed. That's the bargain, and it's a good one.
Shinobi land on my roof to cut across the street. I leave a sign saying "please walk on the left tiles". The good ones do.
My neighbour is a Jonin. We swap pickles and gossip over the fence, and I've never once asked what the job's like.
Sometimes I'm glad I'll never be called to the gate in the middle of the night. Sometimes I'm a little envious. Both are true.
The cobbler on our street has gone quiet since the shop next door closed. I keep meaning to bring round some soup; maybe you could come too.
Our street's well bucket keeps going missing, and turns up on a different roof every week. We suspect a Genin. We'd like it back.
My family has kept the same stall for a hundred years. Hokage come and go; the turnip price is eternal.
I grew up thinking the Hokage Rock was where the Hokage slept. My mother let me think so until I was nine.
Our family's training is the abacus. My little sister can add faster than a Chunin can throw, and she reminds them often.
We civilians remember the shinobi who were kind to us as children. You'd be surprised how long that kindness lasts.
Civilian children who leave the Academy still keep their practice headbands. Half the shopkeepers on the market street have one in a drawer.
When the gate bell rings for a squad coming home, the whole riverside steps out to look. We don't know them all, but we wave anyway.
A civilian wedding at the shrine has no clan crests and no rules about bows. Just a lot of family and far too much sweet rice.
Clanless families pass down a headband instead of a crest. Mine has three names scratched inside it, and room for a fourth.
Our house is the one by the gate barracks with the target wall out front. The wall has more holes than wall by now.
Every Shiranui learns senbon before chopsticks. My little brother eats noodles by spearing them one at a time.
We serve in the Hokage's guard, mostly. It's quiet work: a lot of standing and a little of being very fast.
Clan day is a throwing contest by the barracks. The guard comes to watch, and the Hagane bet on the outcome.
Yes, we keep a senbon in our mouths. No, it isn't sharp at that end. Everybody asks.
The Namiashi and we share the guard rotation, and we'll never agree on who's better at it. Keeps both houses sharp.
I smile easy and worry hard. Somebody in the guard has to look calm, and it may as well be me.
I can hit a falling leaf with a senbon at twenty paces. Parties, you'd think I'd be popular. Mostly people back away.
I nap standing up. Fourteen years of guard duty will do that.
My father taught me one thing about guarding: the dull hour is the dangerous one.
Somebody keeps moving the targets on our wall a hand's width to the left every night. My aim's fine; my patience isn't.
Our house is near the police station, with bars on the windows. The bars are for the neighbours' peace of mind, not ours.
Morino work as interrogators. People cross the street when we pass in our greatcoats. Then they come to us for advice on their landlords.
At home we're gentle. My grandmother grows violets on the windowsill behind the bars and talks to them every morning.
The police and we disagree over who holds a prisoner and for how long. We argue over it at tea. The tea is very polite.
Clan day is a long dinner with no questions at the table. That's the rule: one night a year, nobody asks anybody anything.
Every Morino coat has the same deep inner pocket. Children fill it with sweets before they're old enough to fill it with notes.
I can tell when someone's lying by how they hold a cup. It ruins dinner parties.
The village thinks we're frightening. I think honesty is frightening, and we just don't look away from it.
I keep canaries. Three of them. They sing whenever I come home, and it's the best part of my day.
I've never raised my voice in an interview. Quiet is far more effective. It works on my children too.
A woman from the river district keeps coming to our gate asking for news of her brother. We've no word, but she should hear that from someone kind.
Ask any shopkeeper on the Academy streets who taught them to write, and nine times in ten the answer is an Umino.
Our houses are on the Academy streets, so close you can hear the morning roll call from our kitchens.
Clan day is teachers' day. Former pupils leave notes on our doorsteps, and some of them are very rude about our handwriting.
We tie our hair back with a brush cord, every one of us. It started as a joke and became a family mark.
There's always a pile of marking on an Umino table. We eat around it.
Umino don't take holidays in exam week. We don't take holidays much at all, if I'm honest.
I can hear a pencil stop moving from across a classroom. It means the child is either stuck or about to throw it.
I keep a box of every note a pupil has ever given me. The box is three boxes now.
I'm stretched thin. Everyone's children are my children for four hours a day, and then they're mine again in my dreams.
One of the pupils has stopped coming to class. The family hasn't said why, and the child's desk is very tidy now.
Our shop is on the market street, the one with the pink awning. You can't miss it, and believe me, plenty of people have tried.
The Haruno sold dry goods for four generations, and then the children started becoming ninja. The shop survives anyway.
Every Haruno works the counter at least one Market Day a month, ninja or not. Even the Chunin.
Our garden is small and very neat. The cherry tree in it was planted the year the shop first opened.
We buy shelves and crates from the Kinoshita yard every season. They complain about our prices; we complain about their splinters.
The anniversary sale is our clan day, more or less. The whole family wears pink aprons and the street eats free sweets.
I can count change faster than most shinobi can throw a kunai. Different skill, same reflexes.
I love the shop and I love the field, and I've never been able to choose. So I do both, badly, and happily.
I keep the books in a pink ledger. It's not a family rule; I just think numbers deserve a nice home.
Bargaining is a conversation. The best customers are the ones who haggle back and leave smiling.
Haruno prices are fair and we'll tell you so twice. Rice crackers two ryo, tea tins ten, and the cushions are on sale this week.
Our dojo near the training grounds is small, but the floor is polished like water. That's on purpose.
They call us wave-foot. Every Namiashi learns to cross the river stepping stones without a splash before they can hold a sword.
We serve in the Hokage's guard beside the Shiranui and the Gekko. Three families, three styles, and one long argument.
The Gekko say they move like moonlight. We say moonlight doesn't move at all, it just sits there looking pale.
Clan day is a footwork contest on the river stones. Whoever splashes first serves dinner.
Barefoot in the dojo, sandals on the street, and never shoes. Shoes make you forget where the ground is.
I can't walk across a room without counting my steps. It's a family habit, and it makes me very punctual.
I fell in the river eleven times before I crossed it dry. My grandfather made me count every one out loud.
I'm quiet, I know. Swordsmen of my family speak with their feet.
I envy the Gekko their moon platform. I'd never tell them. Please don't.
Somebody has shifted one of the river stones our children train on. Just a little, just enough to make the youngest slip.
Hagane guard the gate and run the messages. If anything happens in the Leaf, we've heard about it by lunch.
Every Hagane name means some kind of metal. My cousins are Iron, Copper and a very unlucky one named after tin.
Our family shop is the metalworker's beside the forge on the market street. Hinges, locks, gate fittings, the solid stuff.
The gate's boring for weeks and then it isn't for an hour. A Hagane learns to be ready for that hour.
The Tobari take the wall at night and we take it by day. We leave each other notes in the gate booth, mostly about the kettle.
A bandaged nose is practically our family crest. Doors, maces, the odd cart. We bump into things at speed.
I can't keep a secret, so nobody tells me any. It's very freeing.
I carry a mace because my grandmother did. It's heavy, ugly and I wouldn't trade it for any blade in the Leaf.
My favourite sound is the gate bell at dawn. Means everyone made it through the night.
I know every carter by the sound of their wheels. That one squeaks, that one wobbles, that one owes me a peach.
A message on the relay came back with the seal broken. Nobody on the route admits to dropping it, and I've asked everybody twice.
Our yard on the carpenters' lane raised half the houses in the Leaf and rebuilt the other half after storms.
Every piece of furniture in the furniture shop comes from our benches. If it wobbles, it isn't ours.
The yard opens with the sound of six planes on cedar at dawn. The neighbours set their clocks by it.
Clan day is a roof-raising. We pick a house that needs a new roof and the whole family puts one on in a day.
The Haruno buy our crates and shelves every season. We grumble about their bargaining; they grumble about splinters.
A Kinoshita child's first piece is a stool. Mine still stands in the yard, and nobody's allowed to sit on it.
I can tell what wood a beam is by tapping it with a knuckle. My knuckles are mostly scar.
I hate nails. A joint that needs a nail is a joint that wasn't cut right.
I build furniture for other people's homes and my own flat is three crates and a cushion. Isn't that always the way?
I like the smell of sawdust better than flowers. My spouse buys me cedar shavings for birthdays.
A cheap crew from outside the lane is underbidding us on every roof. Their joints won't last a winter, and someone will get hurt.
Our stone houses are at the quarry edge of the village. Stone stays cool in summer and stubborn in winter, like us.
The shrine up the slope is ours. The shimenawa ropes over its gate are renewed every year, and the knots are older than the Leaf.
The spider on our cloth is a guardian, not a threat. Visitors flinch at it; children of the family pat it for luck.
We live in the Leaf and we keep our own counsel. That isn't coldness. A mountain doesn't explain itself either.
Offerings at our shrine are simple: rice, salt and a stone from the quarry. Choose the stone carefully.
Clan day is the rope renewal. Every member twists one strand, so the rope has all of us in it.
I can split a slab along its grain with one tap. It's the only party trick I have, and I'm proud of it.
I came down from the shrine to live in the village when I was twelve. It still feels too loud, and I still like it.
I don't talk about the shrine. That isn't secrecy; it's just that some things lose something when you describe them.
The quarry dust gets into everything. My tea tastes of stone and I've grown to like it.
Somebody left the wrong offering at the shrine gate: a coin and a scrap of cloth. The elders are uneasy, and they don't say why lightly.
Our houses are beside the hospital herb gardens. The drying racks run along every fence, and the whole street smells like tea.
Lily of the valley is our flower. It's beautiful and every part of it is poison. People find that a little too fitting.
Suzuran can drink what would make you very ill. We were raised on bitter brews, which explains our faces.
The hospital buys our salves and the Yamanaka buy our cuttings. Then they undercut us at the market. We sigh and carry on.
Clan day, we brew the year's first tonic and everyone in the family takes one cup. Nobody enjoys it.
A Suzuran apprentice spends a year naming plants before touching a pestle. The poisonous ones are named twice.
I've tasted every plant in the garden, including the ones on the second shelf. My grandmother says that's why I'm so calm.
I'm a healer who knows ten ways to stop a heart. The two go together more than people like to think.
I love the drying room at night. Everything smells of summer, even in the snow.
I've never been ill a day in my life. I take no credit; I've just been mildly poisoned for thirty years.
The hospital's run short on fever root, and the clan's patch by the river was dug up. Not picked. Dug, roots and all.
Our houses are on the dark lanes behind the wall, shuttered and padded. You can shout in our parlour and the street won't hear.
Tobari keep the night watch and the lanterns. If a lamp's lit on the wall after dark, one of us lit it.
We walk softly. Every Tobari child learns to cross a floor of dry leaves without a sound before they learn to run.
The Hagane take the day and we take the night. Their kettle is never where we left it.
Clan day is the lantern-keepers' round. Every lantern in the village is cleaned, trimmed and relit by one of us in a single night.
We wear mufflers all year round. Partly for the cold, mostly for the quiet.
I sleep in the afternoons with a pillow over my head. The village is very loud when you're used to the night.
Nobody thanks the night watch. That's fine. The thanks is waking up and finding the village still there.
I can hear a moth land. It's not a technique, just years of listening.
I've seen more sunrises than anyone I know, and I've never once been awake for a breakfast.
Three lanterns along the north wall keep going out before midnight. The wicks are trimmed, the oil's full, and still.
Our family keeps its senbon in bamboo cases, one per member, hung by the door. Count the cases and you know who's home.
The gate barracks cook feeds us for free on festival nights. We guard the door; it's a fair trade.
The bars on our windows were put up by a great-grandfather nobody remembers liking. We've kept them; the violets climb them nicely.
A Morino greatcoat is passed down, not bought. Mine has three generations of mending in the lining.
Every Umino house has a slate by the door. Visitors write their name; we correct the spelling. We can't help it.
The family meets for dinner on the last day of term. Twelve teachers at one table, and nobody is allowed to mention a pupil.
The shop bell is the one my great-grandmother hung on the first day. It's cracked, and we'd never replace it.
Haruno children grow up stacking crates. That's why so many of us made Genin; our arms were ready before our jutsu.
The dojo floor is oiled every new moon. The whole family slides about in socks for a day afterwards, pretending it's training.
Our swords are short and light. A Namiashi blade follows the feet, never the other way round.
Clan day, every Hagane hammers one nail into the beam over the shop door. The beam's more iron than wood by now.
We swap gate gossip at dinner like other families swap recipes. My grandfather keeps score of who heard it first.
The yard keeps a plank from every house we've built, labelled and stacked in the loft. The loft is groaning.
Kinoshita apprentices sweep the shavings for a year before they touch a saw. The yard is very clean and the apprentices are very bored.
Our houses have no wood in the walls at all. A fire can't touch us, and a draught can't find a way in.
The quarry bell rings at noon so the cutters stop for rice. The family eats on the same flat stone it always has.
Our kitchen and our workroom share a wall, and the jars are labelled very clearly. Visitors still check before they take a biscuit.
Suzuran gardens are planted by the moon. Roots at new moon, leaves at full, and seeds whenever the old folks stop arguing.
Our breakfast is at sunset. Guests who come at dawn find the family yawning over bowls of soup.
The lantern-keepers' oil is stored in our cellar. The whole lane smells faintly of it, and nobody here notices anymore.
No clan? Half the guard's clanless, {player}, and they throw as well as any of us. Come try the target wall.
I asked about you, out of habit. Clanless, the Hokage's apartment, top marks for turning up on time. That's a cleaner file than most.
Plenty of my best pupils had no clan to lean on. They leaned on each other, and on their instructors. You can lean on us too.
If nobody at home checks your homework, bring it to an Umino door. Somebody's always marking anyway.
We're hardly a great clan ourselves, {player}. Shopkeepers with ninja children. You'd fit right in at our counter.
You walk light for someone nobody taught. No family footwork, just your own. I'd like to see what the river stones make of it.
Clanless kid in the Hokage's blocks, top of the gate gossip for a week. Don't worry, it was all nice. Mostly.
On your own in a flat with nothing in it? Come by the yard. We always have an offcut stool going spare.
A child without a clan, alone in a loud village. We came down from the mountain the same way. It gets easier.
Living alone, are you eating properly? I can tell from here you're not. Take this tea home; it isn't poison, I promise.
I've seen your window lit late from the wall. Alone in the blocks, I'd guess. Sleep, {player}. The watch has the night.
The tree in our hall was a sapling when the village was founded. We water it before we feed ourselves, every morning.
Every Senju child plants a sapling on their first clan day. Mine is by the east wall, crooked and stubborn, a lot like me.
Guests at the hall are given tea under the tree. Nobody refuses, and nobody has ever been allowed to sit with their back to it.
The founders' shrine is swept twice a day. Most mornings the cousins argue over whose turn it is, which is half the point.
Our quarter sits right under the Rock, beside the Residence. Living that close to the faces, you learn to stand up straight.
The hall roof leaks wherever the branches grew through it. We put bowls under the drips and call it the tree's music.
The Uzumaki memorial stands just over our wall. Our elders leave a cup of tea there on the first morning of every month.
We were a great clan once and we're a small one now. The tree doesn't seem to mind, so we try not to either.
I like pruning best. You have to know what to cut and what to leave, and the tree tells you if you got it wrong.
My grandmother can name every Senju who ever sat under that tree. It takes her most of an afternoon.
I'm not as strong as the stories about my family. I've made my peace with being good at gardening instead.
Living in a founding family means everyone expects you to be wise. Mostly I just remember to water things.
A dry week is coming, the elders say, and the tree drinks more than the well gives. We'll need extra hands with buckets.
Our hall is mostly a memorial now. The spiral is on every beam, and every name on the wall is read aloud once a year.
The seals on the memorial are repainted each spring. One wrong stroke and you start the whole panel again.
There are so few of us that clan day is one long table. We set out bowls for the ones who aren't here and fill them anyway.
The sealing-mask hall is the loudest quiet room in the village. All those faces on the wall, and you can feel them watching.
The Senju have looked after us since before I was born. We repay them with noise and seals, which seems to suit them.
We live long, my family. My great-aunt still climbs the memorial ladder at ninety, and complains when anyone holds it.
Brushes for sealing are made from the tips of a weasel's tail. I've got one that belonged to someone I never met.
I practise seal strokes on the back of rice paper every night. My hand is steady now; it used to look like a spider walked through ink.
I'm loud, I know. When there's only a handful of you, you have to be loud enough for everyone who's missing.
I learned all the names on the wall before I learned my letters. My grandfather made a song out of them.
Some days the memorial feels heavy. Then I repaint a seal and it feels like keeping a promise instead.
The ladder by the memorial has a cracked rung, and nobody here is a carpenter. I'd rather ask before somebody falls.
The fan is on every wall in our quarter. My grandmother stitches it into the hem of every cloth she owns, dishcloths too.
Most of the Military Police are Uchiha. The station is in the far corner of the quarter, and the lanterns there never go out.
At sixteen we take the police oath in front of the whole clan. I've seen grown Jonin cry at it and swear it was the smoke.
Our quarter is on the edge of the village. People say it's so we keep watch on the wall. People say a lot of things.
Guests in an Uchiha house don't ask about eyes. That's the first rule, and nearly the only one we explain.
The police festival parade goes through the main street every summer. The children wear paper fans and march out of step.
The Morino think they should hold every prisoner. We think prisoners should be held by people who caught them. Old argument.
Our grilled rice crackers are the best in the Leaf. That's not pride; it's just true, and I'll fight anyone who says otherwise.
I joined the police because my family expected it. I stayed because I'm good at it, and that surprised me.
We have a reputation for taking offence. I take offence at that, so I suppose it's earned.
I'd like to see the main street without someone stepping aside for me. Just once. It's the uniform, mostly.
I practise fire jutsu at the lake at dawn. My little cousin counts how long the fireball lasts and never gets the number right.
A market stall keeps reporting thefts to the station and then refusing to say what was taken. I'd like to know what we're guarding.
A bow in the Hyuga estate has a depth for every person: elder, guest, cousin, main house, branch. You learn them before you can read.
Tea in the main hall is taken in silence. The first person to speak sets the topic, so nobody speaks lightly.
Sparring is how we talk. Two cousins who quarrel will be on the dojo floor before dinner, and friends by dessert.
The koi in our pond are older than some of the servants. The eldest is white with one gold spot and it sulks if you're late with the food.
The estate is two houses under one roof line, main and branch. Visitors notice; we pretend they don't.
We're a short walk from the Residence. Hyuga have carried messages along that road for longer than anyone remembers.
The gardeners rake the gravel in straight lines every morning. A crooked line means someone ran across it, and everyone knows who.
I've held a bow at exactly the right depth for an hour while an elder spoke. My back remembers it better than my head.
In the branch house we're taught that duty is a kind of freedom. Some days I'm sure of it. Some days I spar very hard.
My favourite place in the estate is the edge of the pond at dawn, before anyone asks me to be correct.
I can tell how angry my father is by how quietly he sets down his cup. Today it barely made a sound.
One of the young branch-house cousins has been training alone at night, far past the curfew. I'd like someone to check on them without making it a matter.
Every porch in our quarter has a shogi board. Nobody finishes a game in one sitting; we leave them set up for weeks.
The deer forest is behind the house, and the deer are counted every year by hand. You'd be amazed how badly deer stand in line.
People call us lazy. We call it thinking lying down. The clouds help.
The memorial for the three clans stands near the forest's edge. The Yamanaka bring flowers, the Akimichi bring snacks, we bring the shade.
Our alliance with the Akimichi and the Yamanaka is older than the village. We still split the bill three ways at the barbecue house.
Antlers the deer drop in spring are gathered by the children. What happens to them after that is family business.
The forest paths look the same to visitors, but every Nara knows them by the shadows at noon.
I once spent a whole summer afternoon watching one cloud. My mother asked what I'd done all day. I said, a lot.
I lose at shogi to my grandfather every time. I've started to suspect it's on purpose, so I'll keep coming back.
Strategy is just being too lazy to make the same mistake twice.
The deer trust me more than people do. I don't take it personally; deer are better judges of character.
A few of the deer have been limping near the forest's north edge. It's probably a fallen fence. Probably.
Our kitchen hall feeds forty on an ordinary night. On clan day, nobody's counting.
We always set one more place than we need. Someone always turns up to fill it.
Never refuse the third helping in an Akimichi house. The first two are hospitality; the third is a promise.
The storehouse behind the hall has rice from three harvests. A clan that eats this well plans for the lean years.
The barbecue house down the street is ours. Every Akimichi child learns to turn meat before they learn to throw a kunai.
Strength is like food: it's meant to be shared. That's the first thing my grandfather taught me, at a table, naturally.
We live right by the market street. The fishmongers know us by name and the grocer saves us the big sacks.
The three-clan alliance meets for barbecue once a month. The Nara never pay on time and the Yamanaka always bring flowers we can't eat.
I can cook for fifty, but I've never cooked for one. I wouldn't know how to make a pot that small.
Some of my family want to be shinobi, some want to be chefs. I want both, and I'm told that's greedy. Fine.
Comment on an Akimichi's size and you'll learn a lot about yourself very quickly. I'm just warning you.
My favourite sound is a full table going quiet because the food's arrived.
The barbecue house has had a quiet season. Some of the elders want to change the menu, and some would rather close it than change a thing.
The flower shop is the front of our compound, right on the main street. Most of the village thinks that's all we are.
A bouquet always says something. Get the flowers wrong and you've said something you didn't mean.
The greenhouse behind the shop grows what the market can't: orchids, winter roses and a moonflower that blooms once a year.
The quiet hall at the back is where we train. It's called quiet for a reason; even the birds seem to land softly there.
Many of the village's sensors are Yamanaka. We hear things in a crowd that others miss, and we learn early not to repeat them.
The Suzuran sell herbs on the same street. We send each other customers at the hospital and steal them at the market.
At clan day we make a garland of one flower from every member's garden. It's longer every year, and that's the point.
I can read a room the way other people read a menu. It's not a technique, just years behind a shop counter.
My favourite flower is the one nobody buys. The plain ones are honest, and I like honest.
I tried to give up the shop for the field once. I lasted a month before I missed the smell of the cold room.
Some days I'd like to be a little less perceptive. You notice too much about people at the counter.
Someone keeps ordering a bouquet with a message no flower should send, and asking us to leave it unsigned. I'd like to know who it's for.
Every Inuzuka has a ninken. You don't pick the dog; the dog picks you, and a dog's choice is final.
Our compound is right by the main gate, which suits us. The dogs need the outer fields and so do we.
On clan day the pups are brought out and the children sit in a circle. The pups wander until one sits down in a lap. That's that.
The clinic sees half the dogs in the village, not just ours. There's always one barking, and it's usually the healthy one.
Dinner in our house is loud. Dinner in the kennels is louder. Nobody minds either.
The Aburame think we're too noisy. We think they're too quiet. Every year we race them in the outer fields to settle it.
The run behind the kennels is the size of a training ground, and the fence still has holes the dogs pretend aren't theirs.
My partner's been with me since I was six. I can't remember a morning I woke up without a cold nose in my ear.
I'd go hungry before my dog did. Anybody in the clan would. That's the whole of the rule.
People say I smell like a kennel. I say they smell like soap and shame, and the dogs agree with me.
I've never been able to whisper. Grew up shouting over forty dogs, so the dogs got the volume and so did I.
A young ninken has gone missing near the wall. Its partner's frantic, and the scent trail stops dead at a stream.
Every guest in a Sarutobi house is offered a seat by the hearth. Even in summer, even if the guest is only delivering a letter.
The monkey on our gate has been repainted so many times its face has softened. My uncle swears it used to look fierce.
The fire-training yard behind the house is black to the ankle. Nothing grows there, and we like it like that.
We have a long staff tradition. The old staves hang in the hall by height, and the tallest is taller than the doorway.
At New Year our family leads the lantern walk through the village. A thousand lanterns and every one lit from the same flame.
The Shimura disagree with us about everything at council, and I mean everything. Once it was the colour of the new curtains.
Our house is near the Residence. When I was small, I thought the Hokage was just a neighbour who worked very late.
I've given more of my life to this village than to my own garden, and my garden is a mess. I'd choose the same again.
My grandfather taught me to light a pipe, a lantern and a fireball in the same week. My mother has never forgiven him.
I talk too much about the village. Tell me if I start a speech; my cousins time them.
I'm tired a lot. A Sarutobi is supposed to burn bright, and nobody mentions how much fuel that takes.
We need a hundred more lanterns for the walk this year, and the paper merchant's sold out. Somebody has to find another supplier.
Visitors to the insect gardens stand still and let the kikaichu taste their chakra. It takes about a minute. Nobody has ever enjoyed that minute.
The first rule of the Aburame house: never swat. The second is to remember the first.
Our hive walls hum all night. Guests can't sleep; family can't sleep without it.
Insect night is in early summer. We open the garden gates and the fireflies come up off the grass all at once. The whole street goes quiet.
The house is dark timber at the edge of the woods. The insects prefer shade, and so, frankly, do we.
The Inuzuka's dogs dig in our garden beds. We document every incident, with drawings. The file is very thick.
Every Aburame wears lenses outdoors. People think it's to hide. It's because pollen is a nightmare.
People find me cold. I'm not. I simply see no reason to say a thing twice when once was accurate.
I keep a notebook of every beetle in the village. There are one hundred and twelve kinds. I've named the rarest ones after the weather.
My favourite hour is dusk in the garden. The day insects go to bed and the night ones wake, and for a moment nobody is working.
I laughed once, at the Academy. It surprised everyone so much I've been careful ever since.
A rare beetle is hatching in the east garden this week, and the dogs next door won't stay out. I'd value a polite fence.
The house is mostly empty. The ninken come and go as they please; they've lived here longer than I have.
Everyone in the village knows this lane. Very few knock on the door. I've stopped minding.
The yard has kennels for six. Two of them are in use, and the other four still get fresh straw every week.
There's a memorial stone I visit quietly. That's a custom in this family, and there's nothing more to it than that.
The roof leaks over the old study. I've put a bucket there so long the bucket has a name.
I'm the only one in the family who still lives here. Some evenings I set two cups out of habit.
I read too much. When the house is this quiet, a book is the only voice that doesn't echo.
The dogs decide who's worth greeting. They've been right about everyone so far, including me, which was humbling.
I'm not good at visits. If I come to your door and stand there for a while, it means I'm trying.
I keep the house the way it was. Not because I'm sad, mostly. It's easier than deciding what to change.
The old ninken sleeps on the porch every afternoon in the same patch of sun. I think it's waiting for something. I don't ask.
The lane's landlord keeps asking whether the house is for sale. It isn't. I could use someone to say so more loudly than I do.
Our house is on the old artists' lane. Every room is half studio, and the screens are painted on both sides.
A portrait is a promise in this family. You don't paint someone unless you mean to keep them in your life.
A painted eye is never finished in public. We cover the easel when the last stroke goes on.
The light in the north studio is the best in the village. We fight over it, politely, in turns.
Our genjutsu and our painting grew from the same root. Nobody outside the family quite believes that until they see a screen move.
The Yuhi have their grove and we have our studio. Two schools of illusion, and we compliment each other's work in the most cutting way possible.
We hold an exhibition every autumn. Half the village comes for the art and half comes to see whether the paintings blink.
I paint the same pear every morning before I'm allowed to paint anything else. Thirty years, and the pear is still the hardest subject.
Ink gets under my nails and never comes out. I've accepted being permanently grey at the fingertips.
I can't look at a wall without wanting to paint it. My landlord has asked me to stop asking.
Some days I'm not sure whether I'm seeing what's there or what I'd rather paint. That's the family gift, and the family worry.
One of the smaller screens from the hall has gone missing. The house won't say much about it, but everyone is rather quiet today.
A sealed letter is never opened by its carrier. In this house that rule is older than the house itself.
Silence is a courtesy here. If I don't speak, I'm not ignoring you. I'm being polite.
The house is close to the Rock. The shadow of the faces reaches our roof by mid-afternoon.
Shimura sit on the council and always have. We disagree with the Sarutobi on every point, and we keep the minutes of each disagreement.
We eat at the same time every evening, in the same order, at the same table. Visitors find it severe. We find it restful.
Our garden is gravel and three stones. Anything more would be decoration.
I was taught to say exactly what I mean, once. Most people use three times the words for half the meaning.
I have one indulgence: a sweet bean cake after a long council day. Don't tell anyone.
People think our family is cold. We are not cold. We are simply not wasteful with warmth.
I run the same route along the wall every morning before light. I've done it for twenty years, and I intend to do it for twenty more.
I respect the Sarutobi, though I would never say so at council. Their hearth is warm. Their arguments are not good.
A council letter went astray between the Residence and our gate last week. It was found, still sealed. Someone wanted it found.
Our house sits in a grove of old trees. We train among them, and the trees have long since learned not to believe their eyes.
Grove viewing is in spring, when the roses climb the oldest trunks. Guests come for the flowers and stay for the tea.
Tea in our grove may not be tea. Guests are told so before they drink. It's only polite.
Roses, thorns and crimson. Every Yuhi house has the same three things on its gate.
The Kurama paint their illusions; we grow ours. They say ours are untidy. We say theirs are flat.
The oldest tree in the grove has a split down the middle. Children of the family sit in the split on their first clan day.
The thorns on our hedge are left long on purpose. The gardeners wear thick gloves and grumble beautifully.
I prune roses at dawn because nobody can see me get pricked. I always get pricked.
My grandmother could make a guest believe the teacup was empty for a whole afternoon. I'm still working on a minute.
I like the grove best in the rain, when the illusions and the mist get mixed up and nobody can tell which is which.
I've been told I have a cold stare. I've practised it in the mirror, so I'm glad it works.
One of the old trees in the grove is losing its leaves out of season. The elders blame the Kurama's studio water. The Kurama blame the weather.
Our dojo is by the training grounds, and the moon-viewing platform is on its roof. On a clear night you can see half the village from there.
Kenjutsu duels are held under the full moon. The moon is the judge; the clan is only the audience.
A blade in this family is named and never lent. Lend your sword and you might as well lend your hand.
We're a quiet family. Most people only notice us when we come off the night shift, pale and polite.
The Namiashi think they move like water. We move like moonlight. We've argued about which is faster for a hundred years.
The dojo floor has a crescent worn into it where the first form ends. Every Gekko child has stood in that crescent.
Moon viewing in autumn is our clan day. Rice dumplings on the platform, and the duels after.
I sleep poorly. Most of my family do. We tell ourselves it's the moon, and that's a fine story.
I practise the first kata three hundred times before breakfast. It's dull, which is the point.
My blade is called Still Water. I named it at twelve, and I've regretted how serious that sounds ever since.
I cough in the cold. I always have. A swordsman learns to make even a cough sound polite.
A named blade in the family was lent, against custom, and hasn't come back. Nobody will say who lent it. Everybody knows.
No clan of your own? The founders started this village so that wouldn't matter. Come and have tea under the tree sometime.
The tree in our hall shelters whoever sits under it, {player}. It has never once asked anybody for a family name.
We know a little about being a family of few, {player}. You'll always be welcome to sit with us at the long table.
A clanless child living alone in the blocks? Come to the memorial in spring and help us paint. We could use the noise.
No crest at all? Hm. Then whatever you become, nobody will be able to say it was handed to you. I almost envy that.
You stare at the fan on our gate like it might bite. It won't, {player}. Most of us only bite at the police station.
You bowed at our gate like a startled crane. No clan to teach you, I suppose. Watch the gardener; a gardener's bow is the safest to copy.
The elders asked who you were, and I said no one's. They found that very interesting. You may get invited to tea, which is terrifying.
No family telling you how to think? Lucky. Half my life is cousins explaining a strategy I already figured out.
Clanless, living alone, and still turning up to the Academy every morning. That takes more effort than most Nara spend in a year.
You live alone in the blocks? Then who's feeding you? Never mind, I know the answer. Come to the kitchen hall on clan day.
We set one more place than we need, remember. Most nights lately, I've been thinking of it as your place, {player}.
No clan flower to call your own? Pick one. Go on, any flower in the shop. A person should have something that's theirs.
The quiet ones without a family name often see the most. I'd wager you notice more of this street than you let on.
No clan? No pack, then. That's no good. Come round the kennels; the pups don't care whose kid you are.
The dogs keep sniffing round you, {player}. They do that with people who need a pack. Take the hint.
The Will of Fire doesn't care who your family is. Every child of the Leaf carries it. That includes you, {player}.
There's a seat by our hearth for anyone in the village, and especially for the ones who don't have a hearth of their own.
You have no clan's chakra pattern. The kikaichu found you very interesting for that reason. So do I, objectively speaking.
A clanless student asks better questions about insects than our own children. I find that both encouraging and slightly embarrassing.
An empty house and a flat on your own. We have that in common, more or less. Stop by if the quiet gets loud.
The old ninken took a liking to you. They don't do that for clans; they do it for people.
A face with no family resemblance to anyone is a gift to a painter. You'd be a fascinating portrait, {player}.
Clanless? Then nobody has told you what colours you're supposed to like. Lucky. Most of us were raised arguing about blue.
No clan behind you. Then your conduct will be your only name. Keep it clean.
The clanless serve the village without asking what it owes their family. I respect that more than I say.
No family grove to train in? The old trees don't check lineage. Come to the grove viewing in spring and see what they make of you.
I was curious what a clanless orphan would make of our tea. You spotted it wasn't tea faster than my cousins do. Interesting.
You've no family blade to inherit, so the blade you carry one day will be named by you alone. That's a rare thing in this family's eyes.
Clanless and up at dawn for practice? I passed you on my way home. A swordsman notices who keeps hours like that.
The broth goes on at four in the morning: pork bones, kelp and a lot of patience. By the lunch rush it has had eight hours, and you can taste every one.
Noodles get cut fresh twice a day. Come at three and you get the second batch, which between us is the better one.
Running a noodle counter is nine parts washing up and one part cooking. Nobody mentions that when you pick up the ladle.
Everyone thinks the secret is the broth. It's the soy base underneath, and that pot never leaves my sight.
You can spot a Jonin at the counter: they eat fast, say nothing and always take the stool facing the door.
Rain is the best thing that can happen to a ramen shop. Nobody wants cold rice when the street turns into a river.
I burned my first hundred pots of broth. The hundred-and-first I served, and the customer came back the next day. That was enough.
The third stool wobbles and I won't fix it. The regular who sits there says it keeps a person humble.
I've fed three generations of Genin at this counter. They come back as Jonin and still order the same bowl.
A plain bowl is six ryo, miso seven, and the special is whatever I was brave enough to try this morning.
Ramen puts a little chakra back in you. Ask any Genin who comes in straight off the training ground.
I take part-time help at the counter: scallions, bowls, the mop. Seventy ryo a shift, if nothing gets broken.
Extra pork is two ryo, and I've seen customers argue over it like it was a border treaty.
The boat that brings the pink swirl fish cake has been late three days running. If it misses tomorrow, the bowls go out bare.
Somebody leaves exact change on the end stool before we open, every morning, with the shutter still locked. I would love to know how.
A good kitchen in the Leaf runs on rice. Two pots on the go from dawn, and if the second one burns, the whole lunch rush burns with it.
Shinobi eat at odd hours. I keep a pot of miso warm until midnight for whoever comes back late from the gate.
The tea houses buy my pickles by the jar. Plum, radish and ginger, salted for a month in the cellar.
Onigiri are a cook's handshake. Square ones say the cook was in a hurry; round ones say they cared.
Mackerel on Market Day, tofu the rest of the week, and eel only when the river is generous.
I learned to cook in my grandmother's kitchen by being told I was wrong every day for six years. She was right every time.
I wanted to be a shinobi once. Now I feed them, which I think is the better half of the deal.
I taste everything twice. Once for salt and once to be sure I wasn't fooling myself the first time.
A bento is eight ryo: rice, an egg roll, pickles, and fish if the boats came in.
A full meal steadies the legs. Eat before a long night and you won't stagger home half as badly.
If you have a cooking pot at home, buy the rice dry from the grocer. It works out at about a third of the price of mine.
My big iron pan went missing from the back step. Iron that heavy doesn't wander off on its own.
Someone keeps ordering a bento for a name nobody here knows, and paying in advance. The box always gets collected.
The cabbages come in through the main gate before sunrise. If the cart's late, the whole market eats less salad.
Rice sells by the scoop, miso by the cup, and soy by the bottle you bring yourself. Forget the bottle and you pay for one.
Shinobi buy the strangest lists: twenty eggs, a sack of flour and eighty sheets of plain paper. I've stopped asking.
Spring is bamboo shoots, summer is cucumbers, autumn is chestnuts and winter is whatever kept in the cellar.
Half my shop is on shelves and half is in the storeroom behind, sorted by the date it came in. Oldest sells first.
I can tell a good melon by knocking on it. My father could tell by looking. I'm still working on that.
Ten years behind this counter and I've never once taken a day off on Market Day. It feels like skipping my own birthday.
I keep a slate of who owes me what. Most of the names on it are Academy children who'll pay me back as Genin.
An onigiri is three ryo and a bag of rice is twelve. If you cook for yourself, the rice goes further.
I need someone to stock shelves on busy mornings. Forty ryo a shift, fifty if you can carry a sack of rice up the stairs.
Dried fish keeps for a mission. Fresh fish keeps until noon. Buy accordingly.
Every third night a sack of chestnuts goes missing from the storeroom, and the window is far too small for a thief.
The farmer who grows my radishes hasn't come in for a week. The gate guards say the cart never passed.
River fish in the morning, sea fish twice a week on the coastal cart, and the eel are only for those who order a day ahead.
Ice is the dearest thing on this stall. A water-style Genin earns good pocket money keeping my boxes cold in summer.
You learn to read a fish by its eye. Clear and it swam this morning; cloudy and it's been travelling.
The stall smells of the river no matter how often I scrub it. My family says I smell of it too.
Mackerel goes salted for the Akimichi, filleted for the tea houses and whole for anyone who knows what they're doing.
My hands haven't been warm since I was twelve. Twenty years of cold water and colder fish.
I was the slowest gutter in my family. Now I'm the fastest on the street, because I was too stubborn to stay slow.
The old neighbour upstairs buys one sardine a day for a cat, and pays in exact coins. I always slip in a second.
Sardines are a ryo apiece, trout four, and eel I won't quote until I see what the river gives me.
Fish grilled with salt is about the best thing a tired shinobi can eat. Cheaper than ramen, too.
I'll trade you a fillet for an hour of carrying boxes. Fish now, or forty ryo at closing.
The drying racks behind the stall were picked clean two nights running. Whatever took the fish left the nets tied neatly.
The coastal cart is two days late, and the driver has never once been late in eleven years.
The fields outside the wall feed half the village. Every cabbage you eat came past the gate guards first.
We plant rice in spring with the whole family in the paddy, knee-deep, singing badly to keep time.
Shinobi trample the edges of the east field cutting across to the training grounds. We put up a fence; they jump it.
A farmer's day starts before the shrine bell and ends when the light goes. The village sleeps on our schedule, not the other way round.
The best fertilizer is the bath house's old straw. The bath keeper gives it free if we cart it ourselves.
I've never been past the far hills and never wanted to. Everything I need grows on four fields.
I name the scarecrows after Hokage. Out of respect, mind you. The crows have never shown them any.
My grandfather planted the persimmon tree by the gate road. I eat the first one every autumn standing under it.
Pulling weeds pays forty ryo a morning, and you get to take home whatever's bruised.
I sell straight from the cart on Market Day. A cabbage is two ryo; the grocer sells the same one for three.
Something has been digging up the sweet potatoes on the far field, neat rows of holes, and not a footprint anywhere.
The gate wants new paperwork for every cart now. My cabbages wait in the sun while the stamp goes round.
The irrigation ditch by the old mill keeps silting up overnight. Someone's damming it upstream, or something is.
A good Leaf house is joined, not nailed. Cut the joints true and the beams hold each other up for a hundred years.
Cedar for the frames, cypress for the baths, and pine for anything a shinobi is likely to break.
Half our work is repair. Training accidents, a stray paper bomb, a Genin who missed the roof they were jumping to.
Tatami frames are cut to one size across the whole village. Your room is measured in mats, not in feet.
The carpenters' lane wakes up to the sound of planes on cedar. You can find the yard with your eyes shut.
I keep my first chisel on a nail above the bench. It's blunt, chipped and worth more to me than the rest of the rack.
I count the rings of every board before I cut it. Feels rude not to know how old something is before you saw it in half.
I can't sit on a chair without checking the joints. My family has learned to stop asking why I'm on the floor.
A low table runs about sixty ryo. A full set for a flat is a week's work for a Genin, but it lasts a lifetime.
Furniture sells back at half what you paid, so buy the piece you actually want the first time.
Bring your own planks and cloth to a workbench and you can build simple pieces yourself. Just don't ask me to fix them after.
A whole stack of seasoned cedar vanished from the yard overnight. Too heavy for one person to carry, and nobody heard a cart.
The landlady on the corner wants the roof fixed before the rains, and pays in pickles. I'll need a pair of hands.
Mission clothes come back to me in three states: torn, scorched or something I'd rather not ask about.
Every Genin squad orders new outfits within a month of graduating. Then they ruin them within a month of that.
Shinobi cloth is double-stitched at the knees and elbows. Civilians ask why; shinobi never do.
Festival week is my busiest. Everyone wants a yukata, and nobody remembers to order it until three days before.
The dye vats out the back run indigo, rust and dark green. Somehow every clan wants a shade that's just slightly different.
I can guess a person's measurements across a crowded street. It makes me terrible company at festivals.
My mother sewed for the old Hokage's household. She said a hem tells you whether the wearer runs or walks.
I've stuck myself with a needle so many times my thumb has a callus shaped like a thimble.
Rank outfits are issued, but a variant of your own runs a hundred ryo for the simple cut and up to six hundred for the fine one.
A patch is five ryo, a new sleeve twenty, and a whole new jacket if you've been setting yourself on fire again.
Someone ordered a full mourning set, paid in advance, and never came to collect it. The name on the slip isn't anyone in the village.
My bolt of good festival silk is gone. The shutter was locked, and the only thing out of place is a single loose thread on the step.
A kunai is three things: the point, the balance and the ring. Get the ring wrong and you can't hang it on a finger to throw.
The forge never goes fully cold. I bank the coals at night and wake them at dawn with the bellows.
Shuriken are punched from sheet steel, then filed by hand. The filing is where a cheap star and a good one part ways.
Most of my steel comes from the quarry road and the rest from what Genin drag back from bandit camps.
A tempered blade is the colour of straw at the edge and blue at the spine. Too far either way and it's a paperweight.
I lost the tip of a finger to my first anvil. The anvil's still here and so am I, so I call it even.
I don't like making swords. A kunai builds a fence or saves a life; a sword only has the one use.
My apprentice years were spent pumping bellows until my arms shook. I'd do it all again.
Kunai run five ryo for practice grade and up to forty for proper steel. Shuriken are cheaper, but you lose more of them.
Work a few shifts at the forge, eighty ryo each, and I'll start teaching you what the anvil is for.
Steel is ten ryo a bar from the rack, if you've got a forge at home and the nerve to use it.
A blade you forge yourself can come out better than my shop stock, if your hammer is honest.
Someone is buying up all the senbon wire in the market. A whole spool at a time, from every stall.
Every flower in the shop means something. Hand someone yellow chrysanthemums by mistake and you'll spend the evening explaining.
The cut flowers come in before dawn and go into cold water within the hour, or they sulk all day.
Hospital visitors buy small bunches, nothing with a strong smell. The nurses have rules about that.
Funerals take white, graduations take something bright, and apologies take whatever the shop has most of.
Camellias drop their heads whole. Some families won't have them in the house, and I never argue.
I talk to the plants in the greenhouse. They don't answer, which makes them better listeners than most customers.
My favourite is the plain white bellflower. It never sells, so I keep one on the counter for myself.
I could never be a medic. I cried for an hour when the hydrangeas froze.
A single stem is three ryo, a small bunch twelve, and a proper arrangement starts at thirty.
I take on help for watering and wrapping. Fifty ryo a shift and you go home smelling far better than a ramen cook.
A potted plant brightens a flat for years. It counts as furniture, and it's the only furniture that grows.
A bouquet of red spider lilies turns up on the step every week, unsigned. We don't even sell them.
Lessons run nine till noon on weekdays. The afternoons are for marking, and the evenings are for wondering where the afternoon went.
The first term is hand signs until the children dream of them. Rat, Ox, Tiger, over and over, until their fingers stop arguing.
Every class has one child who can't sit still, one who won't speak and one who will be Hokage. Usually they're the same child.
The target posts in the yard have been replaced six times this year. The children are getting better, which is the problem.
History is the lesson they groan at, and it's the one that matters most once they're out past the wall.
I keep every graduation photograph on the staff room wall. I can name every face, even the ones who didn't make it to Chunin.
I failed the Academy exam my first year. I tell every class that, and it's the only lesson they never forget.
Some nights I correct papers by lantern light until the ink runs out. My spouse says I'm married to the red brush.
Someone keeps leaving perfect answers to tomorrow's test on the blackboard before dawn. In chalk, in my own handwriting.
One of my pupils has stopped coming to afternoon practice. The family says the child leaves every day at noon.
A Clone that falls over is still a Clone. I mark the effort first and the jutsu second.
The swing by the old tree out front has outlasted four instructors. We'd riot if anyone took it down.
Parents ask me whether their child will make Genin. I tell them honestly: the child decides that, not me.
A medic's chakra has to be thinner than thread. Push too hard and you heal the wound and bruise everything around it.
Mission season fills the third floor. Sprains, burns, a kunai in the shoulder, and one Genin a week who tried to catch a paper bomb.
Every medic learns anatomy from scrolls first, then fish, then each other. In that order, thankfully.
We revive anyone brought in knocked out, no questions asked and no bill sent. The village pays for that, and it's worth it.
A field kit holds bandages, a needle, a splint and a soldier pill. Most of the job is the bandages.
I fainted at the sight of blood in my first week. My instructor made me hold the bowl for a month. I don't faint anymore.
I count the patients I've sent home, not the ones I couldn't. It's the only way to sleep after a night shift.
My hands shake when I'm not working. As soon as there's a wound in front of me, they go perfectly still.
Soldier pills are sixty ryo at the hospital stall. They refill chakra in a hurry, and taste like a punishment.
Fall in the field and you wake up here in the morning, patched and rested. No bill, but your thrown kit stays wherever you dropped it.
The herb room's stock of numbing salve keeps running out a week early. Somebody is either very clumsy or very careful.
A patient on the third floor won't say what happened to their hands. I'd like to know before they leave.
The medics get the glory; the nurses get the sheets. Forty beds, changed every morning before the medics have had their tea.
Visiting hours are ten to six. Shinobi come in through the window at midnight anyway, and I've stopped shouting about it.
Every bed on the second floor has a bell. The one by the window has been rung more than all the others together.
Genin are the worst patients. They try to leave the moment they can stand, and half of them can't.
The hospital kitchen makes rice porridge for everyone, no matter what's wrong with them. It works more often than you'd think.
I'm not a shinobi and never will be. But I've held the hand of more Jonin than most Jonin have met.
I knit between rounds. The children's ward has a scarf on every bed, and none of them match.
My worst habit is checking everyone's pulse when I shake their hand. My friends have learned to wave instead.
The night shift is short two nurses this week. Someone who can stay awake until dawn would be a real help, and the tea's free.
An old patient keeps asking for the same visitor by a name none of us recognise. I'd like to find them before the week is out.
The children's ward has lost its picture book, the one with the frog Hokage. It's the only thing that gets them to sleep.
Flowers go on the sill, not the bedside table. Too many patients have knocked a vase onto a fresh bandage.
The worst noise in this building is a quiet ward. I'd take a room full of complaining Genin over silence any day.
A patrol walks the same streets in a different order every night. Predictable is the one thing a guard must never be.
Most of my shifts are lost children, lost purses and lost tempers outside the bath house at closing.
The guard house keeps a lantern burning on every corner it watches. Count them from the Rock and you can see our route.
Fights on Market Day are always over the same three things: the last eel, the best stall and whose dog it was.
We relieve the watch at six and at six. Twelve hours on the cobbles and you learn which stones wobble.
I joined the guard because I wasn't fast enough for the field. Turns out walking slowly and watching closely is its own skill.
I know every cat on my route by sight. They're better informants than the people.
I've never drawn my blade in the street. I mean to keep it that way until I retire.
Lanterns on the east lane keep going out at the same hour every night. Not blown out: someone turns the wick right down.
