A shopkeeper on the market street swears the shutters were locked from the inside after a theft. I'm still turning that one over.
Someone's been chalking little arrows on the walls along my route. They don't point anywhere I can see.
Every traveller signs the book: name, village, purpose and how long. We fill one book a month and the archive keeps them all.
Carts come in at dawn, squads go out at eight, merchants arrive at noon. You could set a clock by the gate.
The booth has two chairs, one cushion and a kettle that's older than both of us.
The painted characters on the doors get touched up every spring. Climbing up there is the most exciting thing that happens all season.
A squad leaving on a mission salutes the booth. A squad coming back usually just waves, if they can lift an arm.
Nine years at this gate. I've seen everyone leave, and nearly everyone come back. The nearly is the part I think about.
People think gate duty is boring. It is. That's how you know it's working.
We play shogi between carts. The board's been on the counter so long the pieces have worn smooth.
Past the gate is the outer road and the training fields. Beyond the far hills you need a mission scroll and a stamped pass.
Squads leave from here, but the paperwork starts at the Mission Desk. Get it stamped there first or you'll be turned round.
A farmer's cart has been stuck at the booth all morning over a missing stamp. The cabbages are not getting any fresher.
Three travellers this month signed the book in the same handwriting under different names. Probably nothing. Probably.
I buy cloth from the coastal towns, sell it here, buy tea here and sell it there. The road between is where the money goes.
The Leaf is the safest market on the road, which means it's also the one where everyone haggles hardest.
Market Day draws carts from three valleys. I've done more business by noon on a Market Day than in the rest of the week.
A merchant's caravan hires Genin to guard it. Cheap, eager and they mostly know which end of a kunai goes forward.
I've crossed the far hills forty times. The only thing I've never got used to is coming home and finding the village bigger.
My ledger is older than I am. My grandmother started it, and I still write in her columns.
I can't sleep in a bed that doesn't move. Too many nights on a cart.
Everything has a price, and in the Leaf it's usually in ryo notes. Coins are for the road, where nobody trusts paper.
The pawn shop gives half what a thing's worth. I give sixty percent, if you can wait until my cart's back.
Prices go up three days before a festival and fall the morning after. Buy your lanterns in the quiet weeks.
Hiring a squad of Genin for a D-rank costs less than you'd think. Getting them to stop chasing the client's cat is extra.
A crate of mine came in with the seals intact and half the tea missing. Nobody on my side opened it, and I'd swear to that.
My usual supplier in the river town hasn't answered three letters. Either they're ill, or they've found a better buyer.
The Academy library has four thousand scrolls and one rule: nothing leaves the room still rolled the wrong way.
Children borrow the jutsu scrolls and bring them back with fingerprints on the hand sign pages. That's how I know they read them.
Overdue books get a reminder slip, then a visit, then a note to the instructor. The note usually works.
A library is the quietest place in a loud village. Even the Inuzuka children whisper in here.
I read every scroll before it goes on the shelf. I've read some of them four times. The cookery ones mostly.
I wanted to be a scholar in the capital. Then I found out the Leaf's library needed someone, and I never left.
I can't stand a bent corner. It's not personal. It's just wrong.
The beginners' scrolls on chakra control are on the lowest shelf by the window. Start there, not with the fire jutsu.
The workshop is through the door at the end of the library. Mind the shavings; nobody sweeps them up.
Eleven scrolls are overdue, scattered across the whole village. If someone could fetch them back, I'd stop dreaming about them.
Somebody returns a scroll to the wrong shelf every night. Always the same one, always one shelf to the left.
Green tea for the morning, roasted tea after dinner and barley tea in summer. Serve them in the wrong order and the regulars notice.
The water comes from the shrine spring, carried up in the morning. Tap water makes good tea; spring water makes better.
A tea house is the village's parlour. Half of the Leaf's marriages, quarrels and business deals started on these cushions.
Whisk the matcha until the foam is like a calm pond. If you can see the bottom of the bowl, start again.
The ceremony room upstairs has one rule: shinobi leave their pouches at the door. Even the Jonin.
I've poured tea for two Hokage in this room. Both of them asked for a second cup, and both of them forgot to pay.
I spent three years learning to fold a cloth. People laugh, until they see what a badly folded cloth does to a ceremony.
My mother ran this house and her mother before. I'll be the first to run it without a cat on the counter. I miss the cat.
A pot of green tea is four ryo. Drink it in the evening and you'll stay sharp an hour longer than you should.
Dango with tea is the classic pairing. My dango aren't the best on the street, but they're the best with tea.
I need someone to sweep the garden path and change the hanging scroll. Fifty ryo a shift, and all the tea you want.
The tea house across the corner dropped its prices again. One more week of this and one of us closes.
The boilers go on at three in the afternoon and the first bathers arrive at four. By six the steam's so thick you can't see the mural.
Wash first, then soak. I've watched Jonin shrink like children when I catch them skipping the stools.
The mural on the big wall is the Hokage Rock at sunrise. It's been repainted twice, and the second time someone gave the third face a moustache.
Training ground regulars come in caked in mud at sundown. I keep a separate tub for them, and I'm not ashamed.
Everyone in the village passes through here sooner or later. A bath house hears more news than the Residence.
I've never once had a bath in my own bath house. By closing, the last thing I want is more hot water.
I keep a list of who sings in the tubs. It's longer than you'd expect, and it includes a council member.
My grandfather built the boiler. I talk to it every morning, and it starts more willingly when I do.
A soak is three ryo, a towel one more, and the milk in the cold box is two. It's the best seven ryo in the Leaf.
A long soak after a hard day eases the legs. You won't wake up stiff, and you'll sleep like a stone.
The lost and found basket is full again: a comb, a single sandal and a wooden charm. Somebody must miss them.
The boiler's been coughing all week. If it gives out before the festival, the whole village goes unwashed.
Everything on these shelves has a story. Most of them start with somebody needing ryo in a hurry.
Bandit camp loot comes through my door every week. I don't ask where it came from, because I already know.
The back room is for things people promised to come back for. Some of them have waited longer than I have.
I'm the only shop in the Leaf where a rusty sword and a silver hairpin sit side by side, and I like it that way.
I keep a ledger of every pledge, every name and every date. Some days I read it the way other people read novels.
I hate selling a pledge that wasn't collected. I give it a month longer than the law says, every time.
A child once pawned a marble to buy a parent's birthday present. I still have the marble. The child is a Chunin now.
I pay half the value, in notes, on the spot. If you want the full price, go and haggle in the market.
Salvage from a bandit camp is the only loot worth bringing in. Leaves and rocks I can find on my own.
Buy back a pledged piece within the month and you pay what I paid plus a tenth. After that, it's on the shelf.
Somebody pawned a forehead protector with a village mark I've never seen. They left before I could ask a single question.
A family heirloom came in that I'm almost sure was reported stolen. I'd rather return it than sell it.
Ninken come in with thorns in their pads, ticks in their ears and, once a month, a kunai in somewhere awkward.
The clinic sees more dogs than anything else, but I've stitched a cat, two hawks and a very offended tortoise.
A ninken's nose is a weapon. I treat it like one: no smoke, no perfume and no spicy food within reach.
Every pup in the clan gets checked at six weeks, weighed at twelve and paired with a partner at the clan day.
Village cats are the hardest patients. A ninken will hold still for a stitch. A cat considers it a challenge.
I was bitten twenty-three times in my first year. I stopped counting after that, which is a kind of progress.
I wanted to be a medic, but people complain too much. Dogs just look at you, and you know.
My own dog is fourteen and grey round the muzzle. It still meets me at the gate every evening.
Adopting a pup is free; feeding it isn't. Budget a few ryo a day for meat, more once it starts growing.
A check-up is five ryo, a stitched paw fifteen. Pets are knocked out, never killed, but they still need mending afterwards.
Three ninken came in this week with the same scratch on the same leg. Something near the wall has thorns we don't know.
A stray cat keeps bringing kittens to the clinic step, one a day, as if it's lending them to us.
The shrine bell rings at dawn and dusk, and once more at midnight on New Year. The rest of the year, the crows do the ringing.
Wish plaques go on the wall by the gate. I read them all, though I'm only supposed to burn them at year's end.
Shinobi come here the night before a long mission. They don't pray, mostly. They just stand under the tree for a while.
The rope over the main hall is renewed every autumn. It takes eight people and an argument to tie the knots.
Weddings in spring, the dead in autumn and children's blessings on the first warm day. The shrine keeps the village's calendar.
I sweep the steps every morning. All two hundred of them. It's the only part of the job I'm sure I'm doing right.
I was a Genin once, for a year. I found I preferred keeping lanterns lit to blowing things up.
The fox statues by the gate wear the knitted caps I make them each winter. Somebody steals one every year, and I knit another.
A wish plaque is five ryo and a charm for safe travel ten. The money goes on lamp oil and rope.
Fortunes are two ryo. Bad ones get tied to the branch outside and left behind for the wind to take.
Somebody has been granting the small wishes on the plaques before I can read them. A lost doll found, a fence mended. I'd like to thank them.
The old stone lantern on the lower steps has a crack running through it, and it grows a little every week.
Half my work is shop signs. The other half is fixing shop signs after Genin practise their throws on them.
The best light in the village is on the old artists' lane at four in the afternoon. Every painter in the Leaf knows it.
I grind my own colours: red from cinnabar, blue from the river stones and black from the soot of the tea house chimney.
The Hokage Rock is the hardest thing to paint. The faces change every hour with the light, and they never sit still.
Lanterns for the festival are painted in the last week before it. The lane smells of glue and paper for days.
I paint the same view of the river every morning. Two hundred paintings so far, and none of them are right.
My first commission was a ramen shop's menu. I misspelled miso, and they kept it up for four years out of spite.
I can't stand a crooked frame in anyone's house. I've straightened pictures at funerals.
A small scroll painting is forty ryo and a poster for your wall twenty. Furniture's fine, but a wall wants something to look at.
I'll paint a nameplate for your door for ten ryo. Be sure of the spelling first.
My best brush went missing from the studio, and a painting of a heron turned up on the bath house wall the same night. Not bad, either.
A courier knows every shortcut in the village: the alley behind the tea house, the steps under the bridge, and which roofs hold.
Letters inside the village go by foot, letters outside by hawk, and the urgent ones by a Genin with very fast legs.
The Residence sends a sealed bundle to the clan seats every morning. A sealed letter is never opened by its carrier.
Rain is bad, snow is worse and Market Day is a nightmare. You can't run a parcel through that crowd.
I've delivered to every door in the Leaf. Some I've knocked on so often the dogs stopped barking at me.
I can't walk anywhere slowly anymore. My family says I go to the bath house like there's a fire.
My first delivery was a cake. I ran so fast the cake didn't arrive as a cake.
I keep a map of the village in my head that's better than the one at the Residence. Nobody believes me until they're lost.
Inside the wall, a letter is a ryo and a parcel three. Past the gate, the hawk charges more than I do.
I need runners on festival days. Sixty ryo a shift, and you get to see every corner of the village before lunch.
A parcel came in addressed to a house that's been empty for ten years. Somebody has to know who sent it.
A letter on my round has gone missing twice, the same letter, sent again. I'd like to know where it keeps ending up.
Three colours on a stick: pink for spring, white for winter and green for summer. Autumn is the stick, I suppose.
The rice flour gets kneaded by hand until it's as soft as an earlobe. That's the old test and nobody has found a better one.
Grilled dango with sweet soy go on the brazier out front. The smell brings in more customers than any sign.
Cherry blossom season sells more dango in a week than the whole of winter. We work through the night for it.
A dango stick has to be bamboo, split thin. Pine splinters and cedar tastes, and both are bad for business.
I ate dango for breakfast every day of my childhood. My teeth have opinions about that now.
I tried to invent a fourth colour once. Purple. The customers called it bruised dango and I gave up within a week.
I never sell the last stick of the day. That one is mine, and it's always the best one.
Three ryo a stick, eight for three. A stick or two speeds your chakra back up, so the training ground crowd buys them by the dozen.
Sweet soy or bean paste, take your pick. The soy ones keep better in a pouch, if you're taking them on a mission.
Someone has been buying exactly forty sticks every morning for a week and carrying them toward the Hokage Rock.
The grills here burn charcoal, never wood. Wood smoke tastes of the forest; charcoal tastes of nothing, so the meat can talk.
A squad celebrating a mission orders three plates of beef, two of pork and whatever the loudest member can't finish.
Every table has its own grill, and every table has one person who insists on doing all the turning.
The marinade is soy, pear, garlic and something the clan won't let me write down.
After the Chunin Exams, the whole house is booked for a week. Winners and losers both eat here, just at different tables.
I stopped smelling smoke years ago. My clothes haven't, and my family hangs them on the porch at night.
I can tell when beef is done by the sound. A good sizzle says turn me. A loud one says too late.
Some cooks get burns on their hands. I get them on my forearms, from leaning over to steal a bite.
A plate of beef is twelve ryo, pork ten, and the vegetables are free for anyone who actually eats them.
Barbecue before a spar puts power in your fists. Not much, but enough for the taijutsu crowd to swear by it.
The charcoal merchant hasn't come in two weeks. If the stock runs out, we're cooking on the shrine's candles.
The ferry crosses where the river is too wide for stepping stones and too slow for anything else. Fifteen crossings on a good day.
Shinobi can walk across the water, so they think the ferry is for old people. Then their chakra runs out halfway.
The river is three different rivers: brown in spring, green in summer and grey all winter.
I pole the boat, I don't row it. A pole knows the bottom; an oar only knows the surface.
The river people mend nets on the far bank in the mornings. If you want to know anything, ask there, not in the market.
I've poled this ferry for thirty-one years. My father did it for forty. I don't think I'll beat him.
I talk to the herons. They don't trust me yet, but they're closer than they used to be.
I've never learned to swim. Nobody believes it, and I'm too old to start now.
A crossing is one ryo. Carts are five, and dogs are free if they sit still.
They're building a new bridge downstream. When it opens, nobody will need the ferry. I'd like one good season first.
Somebody keeps untying the boat at night and bringing it back before dawn, tied to the wrong post.
The herb gardens by the hospital grow eighty plants, and seven of them could kill you. We label those twice.
Drying racks need shade and wind, never sun. Sun cooks the leaves and leaves you with expensive hay.
Medics buy salves, cooks buy spices, and the Academy buys everything that smells strong enough to wake a class.
Half of a good herbalist's work is knowing which plant looks almost exactly like the one you want.
Pick yarrow at dawn, mugwort at noon and moonflower only after dark. Plants have schedules too.
I taste a little of every new batch. My tongue can name a bitter root from across the room.
I can't walk past a weed without checking what it is. It makes my walks very slow.
My grandmother said a garden tells you about the gardener. Mine says I never have enough time.
A burn salve is ten ryo and a sleep tea four. I only sell the strong mixes to medics.
Weeding the gardens pays forty ryo a morning, and you'll learn three plants that save lives.
The hospital is short on fever root, and the patch by the river that usually supplies it has been dug up.
A whole tray of drying moonflower vanished overnight. It's useless to anyone who doesn't know how to brew it.
Forty dogs, forty bowls, forty names. Feeding time is the loudest ten minutes in the whole village.
A ninken pup sleeps in a pile with its littermates until it chooses a partner. After that, it sleeps at its partner's feet.
The run behind the kennels is the length of three training grounds. The dogs still find a way to dig under the fence.
Every kennel has a slate with the dog's name, age, partner and favourite food. The food column causes the most arguments.
The old ninken get the sunny kennels. They've earned the warm floor more than any of us.
I've been bitten, chased, licked and sat on, sometimes all by the same dog before breakfast.
I keep a jar of dried fish in my pocket. My family complains, but every dog in the village knows my name.
When a dog retires, it comes home with me. I've got six now, and a very small flat.
A pup is yours to adopt at the clinic. Just know it'll want feeding, walking and the best spot on your bed.
I pay forty ryo a shift for kennel help: brushing, bowls and the bit we don't talk about.
One of the young ninken slips its kennel every night and comes back at dawn smelling of the river.
The tongs are the cook's, the grill is the guest's. Reach for my tongs and you'll be eating your beef raw.
Lunch is quiet, the dinner rush is a battle, and the last table always wants one more plate just as the coals die.
A squad's first meal after graduating is on the house. It's the oldest custom on this street, and the best advertising.
The brazier takes an hour to come up to heat, so I light it before I've even had my tea.
Children count their pocket money at my counter one coin at a time. I never hurry them; they're my future regulars.
Regulars at the tea house next door order from me through the window. We've passed sticks across that gap for twenty years.
On festival nights I sell dango from a tray round my neck. My shoulders remember it for a week.
Fog on the river at dawn is so thick I steer by the sound of the bank. The frogs tell me where the shallows are.
The boat's had three new hulls and four new poles, but the bench is the one my father carved. That makes it the same boat.
Market Day mornings, the ferry carries more vegetables than people. The cabbages are better company.
Anglers on the far bank wave me over just to ask what's biting. I always tell them trout, and I'm usually right.
The night shift's worst enemy isn't thieves. It's the bakery on the corner at four, when the first loaves come out.
A guard learns the village by its sounds. The tea house shutters at ten, the bath house boiler at eleven, the last dog at midnight.
My boots get resoled every season. I wear through the left one first, and nobody can tell me why.
Bath day for the kennels is a war. The dogs win every time, and I go home wetter than they do.
A ninken that won't eat is the first sign of trouble. I check every bowl at sundown, all forty of them.
The pups learn their names in a week, their partner's scent in a day and the sound of the treat jar in an hour.
Festival masks are the best-paid work of the year. Fox, cat and crane sell out; nobody ever wants the frog.
I carry a stub of charcoal and a folded sheet in my sleeve. You never know when a cloud will do something worth keeping.
A painter's apprentice spends a year mixing colours before touching a brush. I spent two, because I kept eating the persimmon black.
Ink for a scroll has to dry in the shade. In the sun it cracks, and the crack runs right through the Hokage's nose.
Steam rooms are for the old regulars at dawn. They've had the same seats for forty years, and they'll tell you so.
The pails are cypress, the stools are cypress, and the whole place smells like a forest after rain. I'll fight anyone who brings in plastic buckets.
Closing is midnight. I scrub the tiles till one, and I've never once been too tired to enjoy the quiet.
The hawk loft is on the roof of the Residence. The birds go out at dawn and come home by dusk, and a late hawk is a worry.
I've worn out more sandals than any shinobi in the Leaf. The cobbler on the main street gives me a regular's price.
Every courier has a route they hate. Mine is the steps up to the shrine, all two hundred of them, with a parcel of lamp oil.
A Genin bought a single sunflower every day for a week and wouldn't say who for. I wrapped each one a little nicer.
The greenhouse has to be warm in winter, cool in summer and damp all year. It's more demanding than any customer.
Market Day I set out buckets on the street. By noon the lilies are gone and only the stubborn carnations are left.
The kettle in the booth goes on before the first cart and doesn't go off until the last squad's home.
Travellers always ask how far to the Hokage Rock. I point up. They look up. That's usually the best part of my day.
Foreign merchants try to tip us. Rules say no, so we point them to the dango stall instead. The dango maker loves us.
Mint spreads like gossip. Plant it anywhere but a pot and it'll be in your neighbour's garden by summer.
Every jar on my shelf is labelled in two hands: mine, and the hand of whoever taught me. The second hand is fading.
The bees from the Aburame gardens visit my lavender. We've never spoken about it, but I think they approve.
The reading tables are oak and older than the Academy itself. Every one is carved with initials I pretend not to see.
I keep a pot of tea behind the desk and a blanket for anyone who falls asleep over the history scrolls.
Spring is the busiest season here. The final-year pupils remember the exam exists and descend on the jutsu shelves.
A medic's first lesson is to heal a fish without killing it. My first fish didn't survive. Neither did my second.
The night rotation is quiet until it isn't. Two in the morning is when a squad comes in from the road.
We keep a shelf of fresh clothes by the ward door, because nobody should leave a hospital in what they arrived in.
The bell over the door is a bandit's bell I bought for three ryo. It's the only honest thing a bandit ever gave anyone.
Rainy days, people come in to sell. Sunny days, they come in to buy back. I could predict the weather by my ledger.
I polish every blade that comes in, even the ones nobody will buy. A thing deserves to be looked after while it waits.
The big cedar behind the hall is older than the village. We don't tie anything to it; it has seen enough.
Children dare each other to ring the bell at night. I pretend to sleep through it. It's cheaper than buying a lock.
New Year's Eve, the queue for the bell reaches the bottom step. I hand out hot sweet sake to everyone old enough.
Pockets inside the sleeve are a shinobi favourite. Civilians want them too now, for snacks, mostly.
The fitting room curtain is the oldest thing in the shop. Everyone in the Leaf has stood behind it at least once.
Chunin vests are made elsewhere, but they all come here to have the straps let out after a winter of good dinners.
The hanging scroll changes with the season. Plum blossom in spring, a waterfall in summer, a single persimmon in autumn.
Guests sit on the cushion facing the garden. Hosts sit facing the guests. Nobody sits facing the door, not even Jonin.
The best tea in the house is the one I pour for myself at closing, when the cushions are empty and the garden is dark.
Hawks from the courier loft come here for their claws. They hate me, and I can't blame them.
The waiting room is half dogs, half children holding dogs, and one cat glaring at all of them from the top shelf.
The clinic's own dog sleeps under my desk and growls at anyone who comes in with a needle.
Screens are the hardest piece to make well. Paper that sags tells everyone your frame was off by a hair.
The kitchen fire goes out at nine, but the rice for tomorrow soaks overnight. Every good day starts the evening before.
Harvest week the whole field shuts its gate at dawn and opens it at dusk. Anyone who helps eats dinner with the family.
The gutting knife is sharpened every morning on the same stone. The stone has a dip in it now, the shape of my wrist.
Shinobi families buy rice in big sacks and forget to come back for the change. I keep an envelope for each of them.
Caravans leave in the cool before dawn and stop at noon. The road teaches you patience whether you want it or not.
Nurses carry three things everywhere: a watch, a pencil and a sweet for whichever child is crying the loudest.
Shinobi bring blades back nicked and ask for them sharpened by morning. Morning, always. Nobody ever asks for next week.
Graduation day, the instructors tie each headband by hand. Mine shake every year, and I've done it for twelve.
The lanterns over the counter go on at dusk, and that's when the regulars start coming in from the training grounds.
Restless! I climbed the watchtower just to look at the hills past the wall. One day I'll walk to the far ridge.
I traded a merchant from the east road a jar of pickles for a map. Half the map is wrong. I love it.
I've been sleeping on the roof this week. The sky's bigger up there. My back disagrees.
A trader told me about a village where the houses float on a lake. I've been dreaming of boats all morning.
I keep a pack by my door, ready to go. Spare socks, rope, dried fish. I've never needed it. One day.
I walked the whole length of the wall this morning. It's further than you'd think, and the view never gets old.
My grandfather crossed three countries with a cart and a goat. I've only crossed the river. I've some catching up to do.
I've been learning to read the clouds. The fisherfolk say a mackerel sky means rain by tomorrow. We'll see.
I ate a fruit today I've never seen before. Spiky outside, sweet inside. The merchant said it comes from the south coast.
I found a path behind the shrine that goes up into the trees. I followed it for an hour and found... more trees. Wonderful.
My dream is to see the sea. Real salt water, waves bigger than the Hokage Rock. That's what they say, anyway.
I've been collecting stones from every place I've been. The jar's half full. Most are from the riverbank, if I'm honest.
A courier stopped at the tea house today, dusty to the knees. I bought the tea just to hear where the road had been.
I tried to cook a dish I heard about from a traveller. Fish wrapped in leaves, buried in coals. The fish didn't survive.
Every time the main gate opens I stop and watch. Carts, couriers, squads. I like guessing where they're headed.
I swam across the river and back before breakfast. The cold makes you feel like you could do anything.
I spent the morning drawing a map of the village from memory. Got the Rock right. Everything else wandered.
They say there's a hot spring three days north. I'm saving up the time off. I've already packed a towel.
I bought new sandals for walking. Broke them in by walking to the farms and back. Twice. Blisters, but happy.
My wife and I are planning a trip to the border villages. She wants the markets. I want the mountains. We'll do both.
I climbed the tallest tree in the training grounds. Saw smoke from the farms, a hawk below me, and my own house. Tiny.
I keep asking couriers to bring back a postcard of something. One brought me a drawing of a cow. Best gift I've had.
The fishermen took me out on their boat at dawn. I caught nothing and fell in. Best morning in months.
I've been learning words in the trade dialect from the merchants. So far I can say "too expensive" and "where is the toilet".
I keep the window open at night so I can hear the wind from the forest. It always sounds like it's got somewhere to be.
There's a cave above the quarry I've been meaning to explore. Bats, probably. Maybe something better.
I'm a courier's apprentice now. Only inside the walls so far, but I run every route like it's a mountain pass.
I sell maps at the market. Most people buy them to frame. I buy them back when they move. Maps should travel.
My last mission took me past a waterfall taller than the Rock. I'd do a hundred D-ranks to see that again.
I always volunteer for the escort missions on the east road. Every inn has its own pickles. I'm keeping score.
Coming home over the hills after a mission, that first sight of the faces on the Rock. Nothing beats it.
I slept under the stars for five nights on my last mission. Back in a bed, I can't sleep. Too soft, too quiet.
Travellers come in through the main gate and sign the guard's book. I've read it. People come from very far away.
The east road has a waystation with a stone lantern. Squads leave a pebble on it when they come home safe.
Merchants from the south bring salt and dried squid in autumn. The whole market street smells of the sea for a week.
The Leaf sits in a bowl of hills, and every road in starts with a climb. That's why couriers have such good calves.
My compass rolled off the bridge and into the reeds. It was my grandfather's. Points north and slightly to the left.
A traveller left a sealed letter at the tea house for "whoever is going east". Nobody's going east. It's just sitting there.
I've been trying to find the old trail to the lookout rock. The map says it's behind the Nara forest. I can't find the start.
I lost my walking stick at the river crossing. It had a carved hawk on top. I'd hate for it to wash away.
Good! Better if I were somewhere new, but good.
Every day's an adventure if you walk a different street.
I learned to tie six knots from a ferryman today. A traveller should know at least six. I know four, properly.
My boots are drying by the stove after a walk through the marsh by the farms. Worth every soggy step.
I asked the gate guard what's the furthest anyone's come from. A dancer from beyond the desert. I've been dreaming of sand.
Fascinating! I took apart my clock to see how it works. Now I know. It doesn't, any more.
I spent the morning figuring out why the bathhouse water stays hot. There's a whole furnace under there! Did you know?
Why do cats always sit on the one paper you're reading? I watched mine for an hour. I have theories. No answers.
I asked the fishmonger how far fish swim in a day. The fishmonger asked me to leave. Still, I'd like to know.
I've been timing how long the bread takes to rise in different rooms. The kitchen wins. I'm testing the attic tomorrow.
Did you know ants walk in a line because they follow a smell? I put a lemon peel across one line. Total chaos.
A traveller at the gate had shoes with metal on the bottom. Metal! For ice, apparently. Where do they have that much ice?
I've been trying to work out how the Hokage faces were carved. Ladders? Ropes? Earth jutsu? Nobody gives a straight answer.
My daughter asked how rain gets into the clouds. I said "it climbs." I need a better answer by dinnertime.
I spent an hour watching the potter. Did you know the wheel has to spin a certain speed or the bowl flops? Wonderful.
I read a whole scroll about bees. They dance to show each other where flowers are! I tried it. My neighbour stared.
I can't stop wondering what the Aburame feed their insects. Is it rude to ask? I asked. It was a bit rude.
I've started a list of every bird I hear in the morning. Seven so far. One of them sounds like a squeaky door.
I peeked into the scroll shop's back room. Shelves to the ceiling! The owner shooed me out, but I saw a map.
Have you ever wondered why ramen broth goes cloudy? It's the bones! I asked at Ichiraku. Got a lecture and a free egg.
I'm learning how lanterns are folded. There's a trick at the corners. I've ruined twelve sheets. Thirteen's lucky.
I measured how deep the river is under the second bridge. Deeper than my rope. I need a longer rope.
Someone told me the tea house has a secret menu. I've been ordering random things to find it. I've found indigestion.
I've been asking old residents what the village looked like when they were young. Everyone remembers a different Leaf.
I heard snow is just tiny ice flowers. I caught some on a black cloth last winter. They really are! Every one different.
I took a compass to the training grounds and it pointed slightly off near the big rock. Iron in the stone? Has to be.
I spent the evening wondering why we say "good morning" but not "good noon". Language is so odd.
I asked a medic how bones heal. Very long answer. I understood a third. I want the rest, though.
I've been comparing the dango shops. Shape, sweetness, chew. My notes are very serious. My teeth are very sore.
My son found a beetle with a blue shell. We spent the whole afternoon looking it up. Still not sure what it is.
I tried to find where the river starts. Followed it upstream until the wall. What's beyond? I'm dying to know.
I've been listening to the bells at the shrine. Each one rings a slightly different note. Who tuned them?
I spent an hour asking the carpenter how joints fit without nails. I think I owe the carpenter a lunch now.
I sell paper at the market. You'd never guess how many kinds there are. Seal paper, letter paper, lantern paper, all different.
I've been watching the shinobi train from my window. How do they stick to walls? Chakra in the feet, they say. But how?
I've been testing how much chakra it takes to walk on water versus up a wall. Water's harder. Why? It moves, I suppose.
On my last mission, I found a plant that glows faintly at dusk. I pressed one. The library has no record. Exciting!
I keep asking my sensei why hand signs work. The answer is always "practice". That's not an answer. That's homework.
Every clan in the Leaf has its own crest, and the old ones are carved above their gates. I've drawn every one.
The Leaf's water comes down from the hills in clay pipes. Some of them are older than the Academy. Imagine that.
The bathhouse, the bakery and the forge all share a chimney flue under the market street. That's why it's so warm there.
I heard there's a fish in the river as big as a dog. The fisherfolk say it steals bait. I want to see it so badly.
Someone's leaving little stacks of stones at the crossroads every morning. Seven stones each time. What does it mean?
I lent my magnifying glass to someone at the Academy and never got it back. Brass handle. I need it for my beetles.
There's a locked shed behind the potter's. Nobody uses it. There's light under the door sometimes. Now I can't stop wondering.
Good! Wait, why do people ask that? Do you really want to know? I'm curious.
Interesting, as always! Something's always going on.
I've been wondering why the dango shop's bell sounds sweeter than the tea house's. Same size. Different metal?
A medic let me look at a leaf under a glass lens. It's full of tiny rooms! Like a village!
Why do the Hyuga koi all swim the same way round the pond? I watched for an hour. Clockwise. Always.
Amazing! I ran around the wall twice before breakfast! My legs are jelly! I'm going again tonight!
I burned the rice. Then the fish. Then the tea. I've decided cooking is my enemy, and I will defeat it!
I argued with the fishmonger for twenty minutes about the price of eel. I lost. I'm going back tomorrow. With a plan!
My brother said I couldn't lift the big rock by the river. I lifted it! Then I dropped it on my foot. Still counts!
I yelled at a cloud today. It was blocking the sun on my laundry! It moved. Coincidence? I don't think so!
I'm going to win the festival eating contest this year! I've been stretching my stomach with rice all week!
Somebody cut in line at the bathhouse, so I gave them a speech about fairness. The whole line clapped!
My wife says I wake up like a kettle boiling over. I don't see what's wrong with that. Mornings are great!
I chopped enough firewood for the whole winter! In one day! My arms are on fire! Worth it!
I lost a race to a dog. A small dog. We're racing again tomorrow, and this time I'm wearing proper sandals.
I tried to be patient today. I lasted until breakfast. Patience is overrated!
My shogi opponent at the tea house took an hour to make one move. One hour! I nearly flipped the board. Nearly.
I'm painting my house bright red! The neighbours will hate it! I love it!
I finally finished the shelf I started last spring! It's crooked! It's perfect! It's mine!
My kids challenged me to a snowball fight. I lost to three people under ten. I demand a rematch!
I sang at the tea house last night. Loudly. I was asked to sing more quietly. I don't have a quiet setting!
I swam the river in one breath! Almost one breath. Two breaths. It was a big river!
I'm learning the drums for the festival. My neighbours are learning to sleep through drums.
Nothing makes me madder than soggy tempura. Nothing! I sent it back twice. The third one was perfect. We're friends now.
My sister borrowed my best sandals and broke the strap! I'm furious! And I forgave her already. That's how it is.
I climbed to the top of the Hokage Rock and shouted good morning to the whole village. Some of them shouted back!
I can't sit still. I tried meditating with my cousin. I lasted forty seconds. That's a record!
I made the spiciest curry in the Leaf! My eyes are still watering. My tongue's on holiday.
I got so excited about the first snow I ran outside in my sleeping robe. The neighbours saw. I don't care!
I'm going to beat the old man at the dango stand at arm wrestling one day. Twelve losses so far. Thirteen's my number!
I sell grilled squid on the market street! I shout the loudest! I sell the most! Coincidence? No!
I'm not a shinobi, but I'll race any Genin to the bridge! Most of them win. Not all! Two didn't!
I finished my D-rank in an hour! Then asked for another! The Desk ran out! I'm going to train instead!
My sensei says I charge in too fast. I say the enemy's too slow! We've agreed to disagree loudly.
I've been practising a fire jutsu all week. I singed my eyebrows. They'll grow back! The jutsu won't wait!
My rival beat me in the sparring ring today. I'm not angry! I'm fired up! Tomorrow it's my turn!
Every Leaf Festival the shinobi hold a roof race across the market street! The crowd goes wild! I've never won! Yet!
The barbecue house has a wall of fame for the biggest appetites! There's a gap on it with my name invisibly written!
The training grounds stay open all night! That's how you know this village means business!
Somebody stole my drum for the festival! I'll find them! Probably! Help me look, would you?
The old boat by the river's got a hole in it, and I promised to row the kids across at the festival! It's in three days!
My sandal flew off during a kick and landed on the Academy roof! I'm not climbing it in front of the teachers!
Great! Fantastic! Let's do something!
Good! Could be better! Let's make it better!
I fixed the leak in my roof in the pouring rain! Soaked to the bone! The roof's dry! I'm not!
I entered the shrine's bell-ringing for the New Year! Loudest ring in years! The priest flinched!
Someone said my pickles were too sour! Too sour! I made them sourer! They came back for more!
I lost my temper at a stubborn jar lid. Then I won. Then I ate the whole jar! Glorious!
My neighbour planted their pumpkins right by my fence! Now we're competing for the biggest! Mine's winning!
A soft one. I found a baby sparrow under the eaves and put it back in the nest. The mother came back. I was so relieved.
I spent the morning brushing the old dog at the clinic. It falls asleep halfway through. Every time.
The little ones on my street brought me dandelions. I put them in a cup on the windowsill. They'll wilt. I don't mind.
I've been reading to my grandmother. She falls asleep in the middle of a chapter, and I just keep going softly.
The shrine's moss garden needed watering. You have to do it gently, or the moss gets upset. That's what I think, anyway.
A butterfly landed on my sleeve at the market and stayed for a whole street. I walked very slowly.
My daughter's learning to braid. She practises on my hair every evening. I look very strange. I love it.
I helped a child who was crying by the river. They'd lost a sandal. We found it together. Small things matter.
I made rice porridge for my husband. He's not ill, I just thought he looked tired. He ate two bowls.
There's a little dish of water by my door for the stray cats. Four come by now. They take turns, very politely.
I spent the afternoon pressing flowers for a friend who's moving away. Each one's from somewhere we went together.
I've been feeding the koi in the shrine pond. There's a shy one that won't come up unless the others leave.
There's an old tortoise in the Inuzuka garden that likes strawberries. I bring one every week. It knows my steps now.
I sang the neighbour's baby to sleep. The baby's mother cried a little. Three nights without sleep, she said.
Loud days aren't for me. Today was quiet. I spent it repotting violets.
I found a worm on the path and moved it to the grass. It's silly, I know. But the path is no place for a worm.
My son brought home a frog. We named it, fed it, and let it go by the pond. He was very brave about saying goodbye.
I sat with an old woman at the hospital who had no visitors. We talked about plums for an hour.
A puppy at the clinic has a new blanket. I knitted it. Too small, too pink, and the puppy adores it.
I made tea for the builders working on our lane. They're so loud, but they're nice. They said thank you three times.
There's a crow that brings me shiny things in exchange for bread. Today, a button. I'm keeping them all.
Evenings, I walk under the cherry trees. Even when they're not blooming, they're good company.
I spent the day helping my aunt make bean paste. My arms are tired. My heart is full.
A little girl asked me if flowers feel cold. I told her they wear their petals like blankets. She looked so satisfied.
The children in the hospital get letters from me. Little stories about animals. One wrote back with a drawing of a rabbit.
I don't cook much. But I make good tea. People come by just for the tea. I think. Or maybe the cat.
I cried at the fishmonger's today. A crab escaped and I cheered for it. It was caught again. I paid for it and let it go.
I work at the Inuzuka clinic, cleaning the kennels. The puppies are all teeth. I don't mind. I come home very happy.
I look after the little ones at the day house while their parents work. Today we drew clouds. Eleven clouds. All lovely.
I'm a medic. Today I set a broken arm and held a scared child's hand. I like the second part better.
On my last mission I found an injured fox in a trap. My squad waited while I freed it. They're good people.
I trained with the ninken today. I'm not good at the fighting part, but the dogs like me. That counts for something.
The shrine lets anyone leave a small bowl of rice for the birds on the first day of each month. It's lovely to see.
The Inuzuka clinic treats any animal, not just ninken. I've seen them bandage a duck.
On graduation day, the parents tie paper cranes to the tree by the Academy swing. For luck. It looks so pretty.
There's a kitten stuck under the bridge on the river side. It's too scared to come out to me. Maybe it'd come to you.
My grandmother's hairpin fell between the floorboards at the tea house. It's very old. I'm afraid to ask them to lift the floor.
The baby birds under the shrine eaves keep falling out. I've been putting them back, but I'm not tall enough for the last one.
Gentle, thank you. I hope yours is too.
It's been nice. Quiet and nice.
I mended the torn page of a child's picture book today. The story's about a bear who's afraid of snow.
The old horse at the farm gate likes having its ears scratched. I stop every morning. I'm late most days now.
I left a cup of warm tea for the night guard on my street. The cup came back washed, with a little flower in it.
My husband's hands are rough from work, so I made a salve with beeswax and chamomile. He pretends not to use it.
Swallows nesting under the bridge: nine nests. I hope they all come back next spring.
Dreamy. The morning fog made the whole village look like it was still being drawn. I didn't want it to finish.
I'm writing a story about a teapot that wants to be a kettle. It's going badly. The teapot is very stubborn.
I watched the lanterns float on the river and imagined each was a little boat carrying a wish to sea.
Today the clouds looked like a fleet of dumplings. I got hungry looking at the sky. Is that strange?
I painted the Hokage Rock at sunset. It came out purple. My teacher said it's wrong. I think it's honest.
My son says the shadows under the bridge are trolls. I've been making up their names. The big one's called Pebble.
I'm sure the old willow by the river is listening when you walk under it. I always say hello. Just in case.
The rain this morning sounded like a hundred tiny drummers on my roof. I lay in bed and conducted them.
I made up a song for the crows on my roof. They didn't join in. They're not ready.
I keep a box of buttons. Every one is a person I've imagined. That green one's a retired pirate.
I dreamt the Academy was made of rice crackers and the teachers were trying to eat their way out. I woke up hungry.
I've been sketching people's shoes at the market. Shoes tell you everything. Those sandals there are very tired.
The smell of the bakery at dawn is the colour orange. I can't explain it. It just is.
I've been building a tiny village out of pebbles in my garden. It has a mayor. It's a snail.
I wrote a poem about my cat. Seven verses. The cat was asleep for all of them.
The wind today kept trying to tell me something. I think it was "close the window". I did.
I imagine the river is a long silver cat that never sleeps. It purrs under the bridges at night.
I sewed stars onto my curtains so the night comes in even at noon. My husband says it's like living in a lantern.
I was supposed to buy carrots, but a sunset happened. I came home with no carrots and a very good mood.
I tell my children the stars are the windows of a village in the sky. Now they want to visit. I need a better ending.
My tea went cold while I watched a spider build a web. It looked like a tiny map of the whole village.
I've decided the fishmonger is secretly a retired sea captain. I'm building the whole story. Don't ruin it.
Today I found a stone shaped like a heart, a leaf shaped like a hand, and a cloud shaped like my aunt.
I hum while I work. The bread rises better. That's my theory, and I'm keeping it.
I painted a door on my bedroom wall. Sometimes, before sleep, I imagine where it goes. Last night: a library of the sea.
I've been inventing festivals nobody holds. The Festival of Lost Socks is my favourite. Very solemn.
The first snow of last year looked like the sky was shaking out a pillow. I think about that every autumn.
I made my daughter a kite with a dragon's face. Every time it dives, she screams. It's the happiest sound I know.
I paint shop signs. Today's was a fish wearing a hat for the fishmonger. Didn't ask for the hat. Loves the hat.
I make paper lanterns. Every one I fold, I imagine whose window it'll hang in. It makes the work go quick.
I've been designing a genjutsu that only makes you smell bread. Useless in a fight. Wonderful on a cold morning.
On missions I imagine the trees are old giants watching us pass. Keeps me alert. And company, too.
My summons would be a moth if I had one. Quiet, soft, drawn to lights. I've thought about this a great deal.
The Kurama lane has paintings on every wall. Some look like they move if you don't stare. I love that street.
On the night of the moon viewing, people float paper boats on the river. Each one has a wish written on the sail.
Children here say the Hokage faces turn their heads at night to watch over the village. I half think so myself.
I lost my sketchbook somewhere on the market street. It's full of people's shoes. I'd die if anyone read it.
A painting of mine went missing from the tea house wall. A purple Hokage Rock. Someone must love it. Or hate it.
There's a door painted on the wall behind the dango shop that wasn't there last week. I'd love to know who's done it.
Like a cup of tea with a cloud in it. Soft. Warm. A little foggy.
Blue, with a bit of yellow coming in. That's how today feels.
I've been naming the steam clouds over the bathhouse. That one's a whale. That one's my landlord, as a whale.
I wove a bit of red thread into every basket I sold today. Like a secret all my baskets share.
I tried to paint the sound of the shrine bell. It came out as a gold spiral. Close enough.
Productive. I relabelled every jar in my kitchen. Then I relabelled the labels. The first set was crooked.
I wake at 5:40 exactly. Not 5:30, that's too early, and not 6:00, that's lazy. 5:40 is correct.
I've finally finished alphabetising my spices. Cinnamon was in the "S" section. I don't know how long that went on.
My neighbour borrowed my broom and returned it facing the wrong way. I'm choosing to say nothing. I'm saying it to you.
I've written tomorrow's schedule on a card. Nine items. There's a slot for "unexpected things". It's eleven minutes long.
This morning I ironed my handkerchiefs. All of them. Even the ones I don't use. Especially those.
Three grams short! I measured my rice this morning, and the bag was light. I'll be having a word with the grocer.
I keep a ledger of every ryo I spend. Today: tea, two ryo. Bread, four. A sweet I didn't need, one. I've noted the sweet.
Sock drawer: reorganised by colour, then by thickness. The thickness system won.
My husband stacks the bowls largest at the top. Twelve years married, and I still restack them every night.
I spent the morning re-rolling my scrolls so all the seals face the same way. You don't know how satisfying that is.
There are four hundred and twelve tiles on my roof. I counted after the storm. Four hundred and eleven now. I'll fix it.
I don't like surprises. I like plans. A surprise is just a plan that someone forgot to tell you about.
Every pencil in the house is sharpened. Then I lined them up by length. Now I'm afraid to use them.
I sorted my letters by date received, then by sender. I've received a lot of letters from my mother.
Today's tea steeped three minutes, twenty seconds. Perfect. Yesterday's was three-forty. I don't talk about yesterday.
Laundry goes in thirds. Halves leave a crease down the middle, and I won't have that.
I swept the street in front of my house. Then the street in front of my neighbour's, so mine would look right.
Ask me any date. My calendar has every festival, birthday and holiday for the next two years.
I made a chart of when the shops open and close. The dango shop never matches it. I suspect the owner of whims.
I spent an hour straightening the picture frames in the tea house. The owner didn't ask. The owner didn't stop me.
My handwriting has been the same since I was nine. I practised until it couldn't change. Some things should stay put.
That clock in the square runs four minutes fast. I've told three people. Nobody's done anything.
I wrote a list of my favourite things. Then I ranked it. Number one is a well-made list.
It's three hundred and sixty steps to the market. If it's more, I've taken a wrong turn or I'm tired.
I repainted the trim on my door. The colour's called "pine shade". It's one shade lighter than before. Nobody noticed.
Receipts. I keep all of them. In boxes, by season. My daughter says I could build a second house out of them.
My garden rows are exactly a forearm apart. The carrots are thriving. I credit the forearm.
I spent my day off reorganising the drawers at my sister's place. She was out. She's back now. She is not pleased.
I keep the books for three shops on the market street. Today the numbers matched to the last ryo. I nearly wept.
I tailor uniforms. A Chunin vest needs fourteen pockets, and every one must sit level. I check them with a ruler.
I check my pouch three times before every mission: kunai, wire, tags, bandages, in that order. My squad calls it the ritual.
I write mission reports the evening I get back. My squad hands theirs in three days late. I've stopped commenting. Mostly.
I keep my kunai sharpened to the same angle. My sensei said it doesn't matter. It matters to me.
Did you know the Mission Desk files every report by rank, then by date, then by squad number? Beautiful system.
The library shelves its scrolls by the colour of the cord: red for history, blue for jutsu theory, green for herbs.
The market's weights are checked by an inspector every season. A stamped weight means you can trust the scale.
Someone's been moving the stones in the shrine garden. One a day. I've noticed. I'd like to know who.
I'm missing one teacup from a set of six. Blue glaze, a crane on the side. It's ruining the set.
The sign at the ramen stand is spelled wrong. I've drafted a correction. I just need someone to give it to them.
I lost my ledger somewhere between the bank and the tea house. Small, black, very neat. Very, very neat.
On schedule. Which is all I ask of a day.
Orderly. Thank you for asking.
I re-spaced the pegs on my washing line. Seven fingers apart. The laundry dries evenly now. You can see the difference.
I wrote the neighbour a note about their gutter. A polite note. Two drafts. Both polite.
Great! I swapped all the sandals at the bathhouse door. Not mine, everyone else's. I'm hiding from about nine people.
I bet my brother I could eat ten dango in one breath. I lost. I'm still a winner in my heart.
I've been practising a face that makes cats sit down. It works on two cats. And one very confused gate guard.
Today I taught a parrot at the market to say "ramen". Now it won't stop. The owner is not pleased.
I spent the morning racing a duck along the river. The duck cheated. It used wings.
I've invented a game called "don't touch the street". Roofs, fences, carts only. I've fallen in a flowerbed twice.
My sister dared me to wear my clothes inside out to the market. Nobody noticed. I'm a little hurt, honestly.
I found the perfect hiding spot for hide-and-seek. So perfect nobody found me. For three hours. I won, though!
I drew a moustache on my reflection in the pond. Didn't work. I'll try a smaller pond.
I balanced a teacup on my head all the way from the tea house. Paid for the cup, kept the glory.
I hid a toy frog in my husband's lunchbox. He hid it back in my sandal. This war has gone on for a year.
The old cook at the barbecue house and I have a riddle trade. Every visit, one riddle. I'm losing badly.
I keep a jar of excuses by my door. "A cat sat on my sandals" got me out of three chores this month.
I learned to whistle with two fingers! Very loud. My whole street knows I learned to whistle with two fingers.
I lost a game of stone-paper-scissors to a five-year-old, then lost a rematch. The child is unbeatable.
Every morning I say good morning to the Hokage faces. One of them winks back. Probably the sun. Probably.
I tried to juggle eggs. Two went fine. The third has a new home on the ceiling.
I made a paper crown for the fishmonger. Wore it all day, didn't notice. Wonderful fishmonger.
Today's plan was to nap. I napped. A complete success. I'm thinking of making it a tradition.
I hid my own birthday present so well I can't find it. Now I'm excited and annoyed at the same time.
I've been teaching the neighbour's dog to bow. It bows, then sneezes. We're calling it a style.
I've got a bet going that I can make the stern shopkeeper on the corner laugh before the festival. Two weeks left.
I counted how many steps it takes to cross the village while hopping. Seven hundred and forty, and one bruise.
I wrote a song about my landlord. The landlord heard it and asked for a second verse. I wasn't ready for that.
I challenged a crow to a staring contest. It won and then took my rice ball. Rude bird. Great bird.
My kids think I can talk to frogs. I've been practising the croak. I'm very convincing now.
I keep losing at cards to my grandfather. He says it's skill. I say he's hiding a whole deck in his sleeves.
I slid down the shrine banister. The priest saw. I'm sweeping the shrine steps for a week. Worth it.
I run the ring-toss stall at festivals. The secret? The rings are fine. People just throw like they're angry.
Somebody bought a fish from me and I sold it with a song. They came back for another fish just for the song.
On my last D-rank I had to catch a runaway goat. We became friends. I let it win a few races.
I put a transformation on my teammate's lunch so it looked like a frog. They ate it anyway. Hungry squad.
My sensei banned pranks during missions. Didn't say anything about the walk home, though.
Every summer the kids hold a secret frog race under the second bridge. The adults all know. We all bet.
There's a game here called kunai-and-crane: you toss a paper crane, and someone hits it with a stick. Old Leaf fun.
The fishmongers hold a shouting contest on Market Day. Loudest call wins a free lunch. I'm training my lungs.
The tea house keeps a slate behind the counter of everyone who's ever beaten the owner at shogi. It's very short.
My lucky marble rolled down a drain by the market. It's blue with a little bubble in it. I'll never find another.
I dared someone to climb the water tower, and now their hat's up there and they're blaming me. Fair, actually.
Somebody keeps stealing my wind chimes. I think it's a monkey. Or a very tall neighbour.
Pretty good! I've got a joke, but I'm saving it for a better day.
Fantastic, terrible, I can't decide. Ask me again in a minute!
Day's not over. Still time for something silly.
I hid a hundred paper frogs around the tea house. The owner found ninety-nine. The last one's my masterpiece.
I've been walking backwards to the market all week. It's research. For what, I'll decide later.
Profitable. Sold the last of the winter radishes before they went soft. Timing is everything.
I fixed the roof myself. A carpenter wanted forty ryo. Two hours and a ladder, and I've saved enough for a month of tea.
Rice, I buy in fifty-pound sacks. Cheaper by the sack. My wife says the pantry looks like a fortress. Good. It is one.
I spent the morning comparing tea prices on the market street. Third stall from the bridge is two ryo cheaper. Same leaves.
Sandals, I mend myself. Leather, needle, wax. Why would I pay someone for something I can do in ten minutes?
My son wants a kunai set for his birthday. I said: earn half, I'll pay half. He's been weeding gardens for a week.
I grow my own green onions in a pot on the windowsill. Cut them, they grow back. Best value in the Leaf.
I sold my old cart and bought a better one with the money and a bit more. Now I carry twice the load. Simple maths.
The festival's coming. Everyone's buying new yukata. I'm wearing last year's. It still fits and nobody remembers.
There's a shortcut through the alley behind the bathhouse. Saves four minutes a day. That's a day a year.
Never buy fish in the afternoon. The good ones go by eight. That's the rule I live by.
A merchant tried to sell me a "lucky" teapot today for triple the price. Luck isn't a glaze.
I reuse the water from washing rice on the garden. The plants don't care. The water bill does.
I lent my ladder to three neighbours this week. Next time, I'm charging in vegetables.
I learned to sharpen my own knives. The smith charges three ryo a blade. That's a dango every time.
Every coin under ten ryo goes in a jar. At the end of the season, it pays for a festival evening. Small change adds up.
I don't buy things I can borrow, and I don't borrow things I'll need twice.
My father taught me: if it's broken, fix it; if it can't be fixed, sell the parts. He sold a lot of parts.
I spent the day planning next month's meals. Saves time and ryo and arguments.
Same coat every season. Layers underneath. One coat, four seasons. Practical.
I patched my roof with tiles from the old shed. They don't match. They don't leak, either.
My house is four streets from the market and two from the river. That's why I chose it. Location, location, fish.
The new tea house charges eight ryo a cup. The old one charges five and it's closer. I'm loyal to my wallet.
I've started drying my own herbs on the porch. Saves money, and the house smells like a forest.
I go to the bathhouse at the end of the day when it's half price. Same water. Fewer people.
I'm teaching my daughter to haggle. She got a ryo off a bag of peaches today. I've never been prouder.
Two lists: things I want, things I need. The second list gets bought. The first gets slept on.
I run a stall on the market street. Shinobi pay well, but they're never home. Civilians pay less, but they come back.
I sell firewood. Winter's my season. I spend all summer chopping and all winter counting.
A D-rank pays eighty ryo if you're quick. Two in a morning, and the rent's paid. Weeding's not glamorous. Rent isn't either.
I buy my kunai in bulk from the smith. Discount for twenty. Sharp is sharp.
I take the missions nobody wants. Fewer squads competing, and the clients are grateful. Grateful clients tip.
Soldier pills cost sixty ryo. I carry one, never use it, and sell it back if it's close to expiry. Don't tell the Desk.
Market Day once a week is when the farmers bring their best. Prices drop by noon. That's when I buy.
The pawn shop gives half the price of anything new. Half's better than a cupboard full of junk.
The Leaf charges no gate tax on food coming in. That's why the farmers come here instead of the towns.
Shops close by evening. Ichiraku stays open later. That's why it's always busy. Smart business.
My scale at the stall's been weighing heavy. I need it checked before the inspector comes, and I can't leave the stall.
Someone's been taking firewood from my stack at night. Not much. Enough that I've noticed. I'd like that stopped.
I need a crate of nails from the Hagane shop. Twenty minutes there and back, and I can't spare twenty minutes.
Fine. Busy. Busy is good.
Not bad. Could be cheaper.
A new cart axle costs thirty ryo. I greased the old one instead. Squeaks less than my knees.
My wife wanted new curtains. I traded a week of firewood for them. Nobody spent a ryo. Everyone's happy.
Busy keeping an eye on things. The children on my street were playing too near the river again. I moved them to the yard.
I stayed up until my daughter got home from training. She's sixteen and says I fuss. I do. I'll keep doing it.
Every lock on my street: checked last night. Twice. Habit. Nobody complains when the thieves go elsewhere.
I walked the old man from the tea house home. The lane's dark past the bend. It's ten minutes. Why wouldn't I?
I put a railing on our steps after my wife slipped last winter. Now I'm wondering about the neighbours' steps.
My little brother's on his first long mission. I've been to the gate three times today to see if the squad's back.
There's a first-aid kit in every room of my house. My husband says three is enough. Five is enough. I'm at six.
The ice on the pond looks solid but it isn't yet. I've told every child on the lane. Some of them twice.
That stray dog by the market has a sore paw. I wrapped it. Now it follows me home. That's fine.
I don't sleep well when the weather turns. I lie there listening for the wind on my neighbours' roofs.
I taught my son to whistle for help. Three short, one long. Every child on my street knows it now.
I walked my sister to the hospital for her check-up. She's fine. I'm still worried. That's my job.
A cart nearly hit a kid on the main street this morning. I had a word with the driver. A long word.
There's a lantern lit in my window at night so anyone walking home can see the corner. It's a small thing.
Every time there's thunder, I go round to the widow next door and sit with her. She hates storms.
I made the kids on my street promise to walk to the Academy in pairs. They roll their eyes. They do it.
I patched a hole in the fence by the river. Someone's toddler would've been through it in a week.
I've learned the name of every child on my street, just in case. I'd want someone to know mine.
My mother lives alone now. I visit before work and after work. She says I hover. She also leaves the door open.
I chased off a fox that was eyeing my neighbour's chickens. It came back. I'll be up tonight again.
A spare scarf goes with me everywhere. It's never for me.
I asked the gate guards how many came in today. They told me. It's not my job. I just like to know.
After every rain, I check the river level. If it's up past the second post, I warn the houses on the bank.
I followed a lost child around the market for half an hour until the parents turned up. Wasn't going to leave the poor thing.
My son's sensei sends a note after every mission now. I may have asked for that. Politely. Loudly.
That old bridge in the dark worries me. Half the boards are loose. I walk across it first and test them.
My sandals sleep by the bed. If anyone shouts, I'm out the door. My wife thinks I'm ridiculous.
I'm no shinobi, but I know every alley on this side of the river. If anyone's in trouble, I can get them out.
I run the corner shop, so I see everyone go by. If a child's out too late, I send them home with a rice ball.
I always take rear guard on missions. If something comes, I want it to come through me first.
I'm back from escort duty. Three days, a merchant with five crates, no trouble. No trouble is the goal.
I checked my squad's gear before we left this morning. One had a dull kunai. You fix that before, not during.
When the gate opens at dawn, I count my squad back in. Every time. Even when we came in together.
The Leaf has watch posts along the wall, manned day and night. You'll see the lamps if you look up at night.
Every street has a fire bucket line. If the bell rings twice, everyone grabs a bucket. We practise it every spring.
The hospital rings a bell when someone comes in hurt from a mission. People stop and look toward the gate.
The Military Police walk the main street twice a night. Some think it's too much. I sleep better for it.
There's a gap in the fence behind the Academy yard. Kids slip through it to the river. Somebody should report it.
The old man on my lane hasn't been seen since the storm. His door's closed, and I've got a pot of soup on.
A dog's been howling near the forest edge all night. Might be hurt. Might be stuck. I'm on shift and can't check.
Good, so far. Everyone's accounted for.
Fine. You got here all right? Good.
I spent the morning showing the children on my lane where to go if the fire bell rings. They thought it was a game. Good.
I carried an umbrella to the Academy at noon. Rain was coming. My nephew pretended not to know me. Took the umbrella though.
I warned the fisherfolk the bank by the willows is crumbling. They nodded. I'll check tomorrow anyway.
Excellent, naturally. My persimmons took first prize at the market again. Third year running. Not that I'm counting.
My family has made tea bowls for five generations. I glazed one this morning that my grandfather would have signed.
I was second in the river race this morning. Second. I'll be training until it's first.
The neighbours have a new garden lantern. Stone, very nice. Mine's bigger. Older, too. I just thought you should know.
My son brought home top marks in calligraphy. Of course he did. I taught him to hold a brush before he could walk.
I don't do anything halfway. If I sweep the step, I sweep it so well people stop and look.
I've been told my grilled eel is the best on the street. I've also been told by people who haven't tried it. Same result.
I wore my grandmother's festival yukata to the shrine. It still fits perfectly. Some things are made to last.
I beat the tea house owner at shogi today. Two moves before the owner saw it coming. I'll remember that for weeks.
My sister thinks her dumplings are better than mine. Hers are fine. Mine are a tradition.
Someone said my garden was "nice". Nice! It took me nine years. Nice is a word for weather.
My family's name is carved on the old bridge. We helped build it. I polish the letters every spring.
I don't accept help with my roof. I've done it myself since I was fifteen. It hasn't leaked once. Not once.
I wrote a poem for the shrine contest. It's very good. I'm only saying so because it's true.
My husband says I'm too competitive. I'm not. I'm simply better at being competitive than he is.
I repainted the family crest on our gate. Took all morning. The gold has to be exactly right, or it looks cheap.
I never wear the same outfit twice in a week. People notice these things. I notice them, at least.
I was asked to judge the dango contest. I accepted, obviously. My standards are the reason they asked.
I'm teaching my nephew to fish. He caught one today. Small. I told him it was enormous. Don't repeat that.
I lost at cards to my brother. He cheated. I'm almost certain he cheated. We play again tomorrow.
My great-grandfather planted the cherry tree by the river. Everyone sits under it. Nobody knows. I know.
I made a kimono from scratch. Every stitch mine. If you see it at the festival, you'll know it's mine. It's the best one.
I don't brag. But my rice is the whitest on the lane, and people should know how much work that takes.
I've never been late in my life. I was early to my own birth, according to my mother.
The new family down the road asked me for gardening advice. Of course they did. I gave them a full list.
I keep my grandfather's medal in a frame by the door. I'm not showing off. It's simply where the light is best.
I won't say I'm the best cook on this street. I'll let the empty bowls say it.
My shop has the best tea on the market street. The other shops sell leaves. I sell a reputation.
I'm a civilian, and proud of it. Somebody has to bake the bread the shinobi eat before they go out heroing.
I finished the D-rank in half the time the client expected. I'd like that written down somewhere.
My squad placed first in the sensei's tracking drill. My idea, my plan. I'm just stating facts.
My family has served the Leaf for four generations. I'd be ashamed to be the one who did it badly.
My throwing's improved. Nine targets out of ten. The tenth was windy. The wind will regret it.
The founding families of the Leaf still have their names on the old bridge stones. Some of us still polish them.
Every year the Academy hangs the best calligraphy in the front hall. The names under them stay for a whole season.
The market street has a prize for the best stall sign each spring. Winning means something on that street. Trust me.
Someone scratched the paint on my gate. My family crest! I want to know who. And I want an apology.
My prize persimmons are being picked at night. One or two at a time. Whoever it is has excellent taste, and must stop.
I've challenged the potter across the lane to a bowl contest, but I need someone fair to judge. Everyone's taken sides.
Very good. As usual.
Better than most, I'd imagine.
My calligraphy hangs at the tea house now. Above the good table. Where it belongs.
My mother's pickle recipe won a ribbon forty years ago. I won the same ribbon with it today. Two ribbons. One jar.
My lantern was the brightest at the last festival. Somebody asked who made it. I said nothing. I simply stood next to it.
I spent the whole morning polishing my grandfather's armour. It doesn't fit anyone now. It still shines.
Quiet. I fixed a shelf. It's level now.
Read a book. Drank tea. Nobody knocked. Ideal.
I went to the festival meeting. Said nothing. Volunteered for lanterns. Lanterns don't talk.
My sister visited. Talked for four hours. I said "mm" eleven times. She thinks it went well.
Fine. I found a bench by the river nobody else uses. I'm not telling you which.
I grow bonsai. One tree, nine years. It's nearly the shape I want.
I don't like crowds. Market Day is a test of character. I passed. Barely.
I fed the koi at the shrine pond. They don't ask questions. Good company.
I painted my door. Same colour as before. Nobody noticed. That was the point.
My neighbour waves every morning. I've started waving back. Took me two years.
I play the flute at night, quietly. If you've heard it, you haven't. Understood?
I went to the tea house and sat at the corner table. Someone else was in it. I went home.
I keep a diary. Three lines a day. Today's: rain, rice, shelf.
My wife does the talking for both of us. It's a good arrangement. I do the dishes.
I like the hour before dawn. The village is mine then. Briefly.
Somebody asked me to a party. I said I had plans. My plans were a book.
I repaired a clock today. It ticks now. Satisfying, in a small way.
I carve small animals from offcuts. A fox today. Gave it to a child who was crying. Don't spread that around.
I walked the long way home to avoid a conversation. It started raining. Worth it.
I sat on the roof and watched the clouds. The Nara do it too. They have the right idea.
My brother's always telling me to "open up". I opened a window. It's a start.
Not much. I like it that way.
I learned to make one dish properly. Grilled mackerel. I make it every night. I'm not bored.
I bought a new teacup. Plain grey. I like it more than I should.
I sweep the shrine steps at dawn. Nobody's ever seen me do it. Keep it that way.
I've been asked to give a speech at my cousin's wedding. I'm considering moving villages.
A stray cat sleeps on my windowsill. We have an understanding. Neither of us mentions it.
I tried the new tea house. Too loud. Good tea, though. I'll go when it rains.
I keep pressed flowers in my books. Each one's a day I liked. There aren't many. They're good ones.
I bind books for the library. Silent work. Paste, thread, cloth. Best job in the Leaf.
I run the night stall at the bathhouse. People come in tired and leave quiet. Suits me.
Back from a mission. It went as planned. That's all you'll get from me.
My squad talks the whole walk out. I take rear guard. Further from the talking.
I trained alone at Ground 3 at dawn. Just me and the stumps. They don't chatter either.
The library has a reading room on the top floor. No talking allowed. It's the best room in the village.
The Aburame don't make small talk. I've always respected that.
There's a stone bench at the back of the shrine where people go to be left alone. Everyone knows. Nobody says.
Someone left a crate outside my door. No note. I haven't opened it. I'd like it gone.
My flute's missing a cap. Small brass thing. Probably fell by the river. I won't ask twice.
A lantern on my lane keeps going out. I'd fix it, but the lantern-keeper is chatty. You go.
Fine.
Adequate.
Mm. Good enough.
Made soup. Ate soup. Good soup.
I mended my socks. Somebody saw. Now they want me to mend theirs. I said no. Probably I'll do it.
It's... fine. I said good morning to the baker today. Out loud. First time.
I tried to order at the new tea house, but I pointed instead. They understood. I think. I got something.
I've been... drawing. Just small things. Teacups, mostly. You don't have to look. It's fine.
My sister made me go to the festival meeting. I sat in the corner. Someone asked my opinion. I said "yes". To what, I'm not sure.
One tomato. That's what I grew. It's very red. I haven't told anyone. Except you now. Um.
Someone smiled at me at the market and I walked into a pole. It's fine. The pole's fine.
I wrote a letter to the shrine priest asking to help with the festival. I haven't sent it. Maybe tomorrow.
The library's nice. It's quiet, and nobody expects you to talk. I read about birds today.
I baked cookies for my neighbour, but I left them on the step and ran. I hope they knew they were from me. Or didn't. Either.
I have a cat. Well... the cat has me, really. It's the only one I talk to without stammering.
I sang a song in the bath. The neighbour knocked on the wall. I don't think I'll sing again for a while.
My mother says I need to speak up. I'm trying. I'm speaking up now. This is me speaking up.
I fold paper animals. Little ones. I leave them in places for people to find. It's my secret. Was. Oops.
I raised my hand at the town meeting. Then put it down. Then raised it again. Then the meeting ended.
I keep a little notebook of things I want to say to people. Mostly "thank you". I'll say them. Someday.
Mirrors are very easy to talk to. I practise conversations in mine.
Someone complimented my scarf today. I said "you too". They weren't wearing a scarf.
I made a friend at the bathhouse. We sat in silence for an hour. It was the nicest hour.
Ducks are kind. I fed them by the river. They didn't mind that I didn't say anything.
I helped carry a box for an old woman. She asked my name and I said it too quietly. She called me something else. I didn't correct her.
I've been learning the koto. Only when nobody's home. The walls are thin, so... maybe people know.
Rainy days are my favourite. Nobody expects you to go out. I can read by the window and feel... ordinary.
There's a lantern-folding group I joined. There are six of us. Five talk. I fold. It works.
My brother says I'm braver than I think. I don't know. I did ask for extra pickles at Ichiraku today.
Earlier I wanted to say hello to you, but... you were busy. Or I was. Anyway. Hello.
Sorry, I'm not good at this. My day was... nice? I watered the plants. They're doing better than me.
I found a quiet spot by the old willow. I go there to think. Sometimes I just sit. Is that weird?
I work in the back of the bakery. Kneading's nice. Dough doesn't look at you.
I sort letters at the courier's office. I know everyone's name and nobody knows mine. It's... comfortable.
My squad's very loud. I like them, though. They ask what I think. Sometimes I even tell them.
I gave the mission report myself today. My voice shook. The desk clerk said "good work". I've been smiling all afternoon.
I'm good at hiding. On missions it's useful. At parties it's... also useful.
The library has little desks by the windows that face the Rock. People mostly leave you alone there. It's nice.
At the festival, the shrine hangs wish slips on a rope. You don't have to sign them. I write one every year.
The bathhouse has a quiet hour in the morning. You're not meant to talk. I... look forward to it.
