I dropped my notebook somewhere in the market. It's... private. Blue cover. Please don't read it if you find it.
There's a cat stuck in the tree by my window. It's been crying all morning. I'm too scared of heights, and of asking.
I'm meant to bring tea to the shrine priest every morning, but I'm sick and... could someone? No. Never mind. Unless...
Um. Good. You?
Okay. It's been okay. Thank you for asking. Really.
I waved at someone today. They waved back. Then I realised they were waving at someone behind me. Still... nice.
I made onigiri for the lantern group... and left them by the door. Nobody knew who made them. They ate them all, so...
I sat at the front of the shrine talk today. Not the very front. Second row. That's... very front for me.
I bought a bell for my cat so I'd always know where it is. Now it knows where I am too. We're even.
I was asked to read a poem at the shrine. I said maybe. Maybe means no. Maybe means yes? I don't know yet.
Steady. Fixed my neighbour's gate, like I said I would. Took me a week to get to it, but it's done.
I promised my mother I'd visit every Sunday. Twelve years now. I haven't missed one.
Up at dawn, chores done, nothing broken. That's a good day in my book.
I've had the same pair of boots for nine years. Resoled them four times. Good boots don't quit, so I don't either.
Carried water for the old couple up the hill again. They try to pay me. I just keep coming back.
I don't say much at the meetings on my street. But when there's a roof to fix, people know who'll show up.
My son asked me what I'm good at. I said, "showing up." He looked disappointed. He'll understand later.
Same as yesterday. Up early, worked hard, ate rice. I don't need more than that.
I've walked the same route to work for fifteen years. The cobbler on the corner sets the shop clock by me.
I keep my word. Even when it's small. Especially when it's small. Small promises are where people learn to trust you.
My father built this house with his hands. I patch the roof every spring the way he showed me.
I helped dig out the drain on our lane after the rain. Nobody asked. Someone had to.
I'm not clever, but I'm reliable. My wife says that's rarer.
Finished my shift, walked the dog, fixed a chair. Tomorrow I'll do the same, and that suits me.
I lent a friend money years ago. They paid it back today, every ryo. I never doubted they would.
I've kept the same hours at my job since my first day. Some people think that's dull. I call it dependable.
I learned a long time ago that you don't wait for the right mood to do the work. You do the work and the mood follows.
The well at the end of my street gets stuck every winter. Every winter, I free it. It's become a kind of friendship.
I've been training the young ones on my street to split wood properly. Back straight, let the axe fall. No shortcuts.
I said I'd paint the fence at the shrine before the festival. Two coats done. One to go.
My daughter forgot her lunch, so I walked it to the Academy. Then went back to work. That's how the day went.
I keep a spare key for half the doors on my street. People trust me with them. I don't take that lightly.
I sat with my brother at the hospital last night. Didn't say much. Didn't need to. He's better today.
I don't like to complain. Rain is rain. Work is work. You put your coat on and get on with it.
Every morning I check the old woman next door has lit her stove. If there's no smoke, I knock.
My grandfather's motto was "one more bucket". I think about that whenever I want to stop early.
I've stood in the same spot at every Leaf Festival for twenty years, by the third lantern post. People find me there.
Not much to tell. I did my part. That's enough.
I've delivered the morning rice to the Akimichi kitchen for eleven years. Never missed a day. Not even in the snowstorm.
I run the night lamps on the main street. Every lamp lit by dusk, every one out by dawn. It matters to people.
I've never left a squadmate behind on a mission. I never will. That's not a boast, it's just how it is.
I stood gate duty in the rain for six hours today. Nobody came. That's what a good shift looks like.
My sensei told me the best shinobi are the ones who come back and do it again tomorrow. I try to be that.
I've taken every D-rank the Mission Desk offered me this week. Somebody has to weed the farms. Might as well be me.
On our street, whoever finds a fallen tree after a storm clears it. You don't wait for the village to send someone.
When a house burns in the Leaf, the neighbours rebuild it in a week. It's been that way since the founders.
The gate guards change shift at six and six. Rain or snow. In all my years I've never seen it late.
The handrail on the river steps is loose. I told the builders a month ago. I'll fix it myself if no one does.
My wheelbarrow went missing from outside the shrine. It's got my initials burned in the handle. Someone just borrowed it, I'm sure.
The old woman on my lane needs her firewood split before the cold comes. I'm on a double shift all week. I can't do it in time.
I promised to deliver a parcel to the farms by tonight, and my knee's acting up. Never broken a promise yet.
Good. No complaints.
Fine. Busy. The usual.
I've rung the shrine's evening bell every day since the old ringer's hands gave out. Nobody asked me to keep doing it.
I sharpened every hoe at the farm co-op. Took all day. They'll last the season. That's what counts.
Adequate. I rose at five, trained, worked, and ate plainly. That is how a day should be spent.
My son left his sandals in the hallway. Again. He will be cleaning every sandal in the house tomorrow.
I corrected the tea house menu. "Their" was wrong. Nobody else would have done it.
The children on my lane were throwing stones in the river. I made them pick up every stone and put it back. All of them.
I don't celebrate birthdays. A day is a day. My family celebrates mine anyway. I allow it. Once a year.
Sloppy footwork everywhere at the training grounds today. I said nothing. Today.
I sweep my step every morning. If you sweep only when it's dirty, you'll never notice when it starts.
I reprimanded a merchant for short-changing an old woman. The merchant paid her back, double. Good.
My father taught me to stand straight. I teach my children the same. They complain. Their backs will thank me.
Naps? No. Naps are for those who did not sleep properly. Sleep properly.
A Genin skipped warm-ups in front of me today. Pulled a muscle within five minutes. The lesson taught itself.
I finished my chores before dawn. The rest of the day is for work, and the evening is for reflection. Nothing else.
My wife says I could smile more. I smiled at the festival last year. Once is sufficient.
The neighbour's fence joints: I re-did them. They were wrong. Now they are not.
I do one hundred push-ups each morning. At my age, it's ninety. Next year, eighty. Never zero.
I keep my house the way my mother kept hers. Spotless. You can tell everything about a person from their kitchen.
My daughter came home with a scraped knee and a good mark. I asked about the mark first. Then I cleaned the knee.
Strong, bitter tea. That's how I make it. Sweet tea makes people soft.
I do not gossip. But I heard the bridge repairs are behind schedule, and someone should be held to account.
No alarm. I wake on my own. The body learns if you're strict with it.
I told my nephew his calligraphy was poor. He rewrote it thirty times. Now it's acceptable. He's proud. As he should be.
The neighbour's children now bow correctly. I taught them. They were doing it like ducks.
Some people waste the morning. I am not some people.
Finished a book on discipline. Mostly correct. The final chapter was soft.
My grandmother lived to ninety-seven on rice, pickles and no complaining. I intend to follow her example.
Sandals in a line by the door. Toes forward. You leave a house ready to return to it.
I don't like waste. Food, time, words. You'll notice I'm not wasting many now.
I helped the old woman on my lane with her roof. She thanked me. I told her not to climb up there again. She won't.
I run the bathhouse. Wash before you soak. Every time. I don't care whose child you are.
I teach the abacus to merchants' children. If they can't add, they'll be cheated. I won't allow that.
My squad ran drills until sunset. They hate me today. They'll thank me on a mission.
I've seen what carelessness costs out there. That's why I check every knot twice. You should too.
I gave the Mission Desk a report so thorough they asked me to shorten it. I declined.
The Leaf forbids fighting in the streets. Disputes go to the training grounds or the police. That rule keeps us standing.
Every Genin learns the founders' rules at the Academy. Most forget them by Chunin. I recite them every morning.
The Military Police keep order inside the walls. Respect them. They earned it.
Someone's been dumping rubbish behind the shrine. I want it found and stopped. I have my suspicions.
The lantern on the corner's been out three nights. The lamp keeper's lazy. Someone needs to light a fire under them.
The steps up to the Rock are cracked on the fourth landing. Report it, if you pass the builders. I've told them twice.
Acceptable.
Productive. As it should be.
I timed my morning run. Thirty seconds slower than last year. Unacceptable. I'll run twice tomorrow.
I made my nephew rewrite his thank-you letter to his aunt. Twice. A thank-you is not a shopping list.
I told the dango seller the skewers were overcooked. The next batch was perfect. Standards are a gift you give others.
I don't hold grudges. I simply remember. Clearly.
I've been rereading a book of travel letters. The writer complains about inns for forty pages. Strangely comforting.
Slow, in a good way. I watched the river for an hour and decided not to decide anything today.
I've been wondering why we bow lower to the Hokage Rock in the morning than in the evening. Nobody I've asked knows.
I wrote a letter to an old friend and then didn't send it. Writing it was the point, I think.
I keep a notebook of things children ask me. Today's entry: "Does the moon get tired?" I still don't have an answer.
My father used to say a question is a door you leave open. I've been leaving a lot of doors open lately.
I finished a book this morning and felt that small grief you feel when a good book ends. Do you know it?
I tried to count the stone steps up to the shrine. I lost count twice, so I've decided there are "enough".
A quiet day. I sat in the library and read the same page three times. The page was fine. My mind wasn't.
I've been thinking about how the Leaf smells different in every street. Bread here, ink there, wet dog by the gate.
Someone asked me what I'd do with a free afternoon, and I couldn't answer. So I took one to find out.
I learned that the old bridge was built without a single nail. I've walked over it for years and never once wondered.
I like to sit at the back of the tea house and guess what people are talking about. I'm almost always wrong.
My wife says I think too slowly to win an argument. I say I'm still thinking. We've been married twenty years.
I planted a tree this spring knowing I'd likely never sit in its shade. That felt right, somehow.
There's a line in an old poem: "the frog jumps; the water remembers." I've been chewing on it all week.
I spent the morning sorting my books by how they made me feel. It was a terrible system. I loved it.
I've decided patience is mostly just curiosity that's learned to sit still.
Today I watched an old man teach a child to skip stones. Neither of them was good at it. Both were very happy.
I keep meaning to learn calligraphy properly. Every brush I buy ends up holding a bookmark.
It rained on my walk and I didn't hurry. There's a kind of freedom in being already wet.
I read that the first Academy had only one classroom. I wonder what the teachers argued about.
I've been trying to remember my grandmother's voice. I can remember her laugh, but not her speaking. Odd, isn't it?
My son asked why the sky is blue. I gave him three answers and he found a flaw in each. Proud of him, honestly.
I spent an hour choosing a tea and then forgot to drink it. Typical.
I think the best conversations happen while doing something else. Shelling peas, walking, mending a net.
I've noticed the cicadas start their song at the same minute each evening. I timed it. My neighbours think I'm odd.
I've been keeping a list of words that have no good translation. "The smell after rain" is my favourite so far.
A strange thing: every time I'm sure I'm right, I learn something that makes me less sure. It's getting tiring.
I spent the evening watching the lanterns go on, one window at a time. Every light is somebody's whole life.
I lent a book to someone two winters ago. I don't want it back. I just hope they read it.
I copy old scrolls for the archive. Today's was a grocery list from sixty years ago. Eggs were cheaper. Everything was.
On watch last night I counted the stars I could name. Eleven. On a long mission you learn which ones keep you company.
My sensei told me a jutsu learned too fast is forgotten just as fast. I didn't believe that at twelve. I do now.
The Leaf's library lends scrolls for a season at a time. People say it's so you finish them. I think it's so you miss them.
Old residents still call the main street "the long road", from before the shops. Words outlive the things they name.
The shrine keeps a book where anyone may write a wish. I read the old pages sometimes. People wished for rain a great deal.
They say each Hokage's face on the Rock was carved by a different hand. You can see it in the eyebrows, if you look.
I left my reading glasses somewhere along the river this morning. I've been squinting at everything since.
There's a word carved on the bridge railing I can't read. Old script. I'd love to know what it says.
I lost a bookmark from my late father. Plain wood, a pressed maple leaf. Probably in the library, somewhere.
Hm. Let me think. Decent, I'd say. Yes. Decent.
Good, I think. I'll know for certain tonight, when I look back on it.
I've been asking myself whether the river is the same river every day. The water's new. The name's old. Hm.
I watched the potter break a bowl that had a flaw only the potter could see. I keep thinking about that.
I made too much miso soup again. I always cook for six, and there are three of us.
Busy! I've been knitting scarves for the gate guards. They stand out there in all weathers, poor things.
The neighbour's cat has decided my porch is home. I've started buying it fish, so that's my fault now.
I spent the morning pressing rice balls for my sister's shop. My thumbs smell of salt and seaweed.
My husband caught a cold, so I've been making ginger tea by the potful. He pretends to hate the fussing.
Good, thank you. I taught the little one next door to fold paper cranes. We have forty now and nowhere to put them.
Someone left a basket of plums on my step with no note. I've been guessing all day who to thank.
I always keep a spare umbrella by the door. Somebody always needs one, and they never bring it back. I don't mind.
I tried a new pickle recipe. The jar is either delicious or dangerous. Too early to say.
A tired day, but a nice one. I sat with the old man across the lane while he told me about his fishing years.
My mother used to say a full pot is a full house. I still cook as if the whole street might drop in.
I've been airing out the futons. Nothing beats a bed that smells of sunshine.
Lovely, actually. My daughter wrote home from her mission, three whole pages. Mostly about the food, but still!
I mended a hole in my son's flak vest and stitched a little leaf inside where nobody will see it.
The bakery gave me yesterday's sweet buns for nearly nothing. I've been handing them out down the lane.
I burnt the rice. First time in years. I'm blaming the gossip at my door, not my cooking.
I keep a list of everyone's birthdays on my kitchen wall. It's getting long. I need a bigger wall.
Today I finally learned to make a proper omelette roll. Twelve tries. The neighbours ate the eleven failures.
My grandmother's teapot cracked this morning. I glued it. It leaks a little, but I can't throw it out.
I've been sewing festival yukata for the twins down the road. Their mother works nights at the hospital.
A happy day! The stray dog I've been feeding let me pat it at last. Took three months and a lot of chicken.
I always walk the long way past the hospital. Sometimes a nurse needs a hot drink more than anyone.
I'm drying persimmons on the balcony. The crows think I'm doing it for them.
I've been teaching my husband to cook. He makes very confident, very salty soup.
The tea house lady was feeling low, so I sat and drank three cups to keep her company. I'll be up all night.
I planted beans by the fence so the children on the way to the Academy can pick a snack.
There's nothing I like more than a crowded table. Elbows everywhere, someone always spills the soy sauce.
I keep a jar of honey sweets in my apron. You never know who's having a hard day.
I gave my good shawl to someone shivering by the river. I'll knit another. I like knitting anyway.
My sister says I mother everyone. Someone has to. Half this village forgets to eat.
Quiet. I spent it cleaning out my brother's old room. He's on a long mission and I wanted it nice for him.
I think the secret to a good stew is cooking it for someone. Stew for one never tastes right.
I run the noodle cart's night shift on weekends. Tired shinobi coming off duty are the best customers. Always grateful.
My stall's been slow, so I gave away the bruised peaches. Better in a child's hand than the compost.
I came back from a mission with sore feet and a bag of mountain mushrooms for the whole floor of my building.
On long missions I cook for my squad. My sensei called me the team's secret weapon. It was the dumplings.
On cold nights the families on my street take turns heating one big bath and sharing it. Saves firewood and gossip flows.
When a shinobi on my street goes on a long mission, we take turns watering their plants. Nobody has to ask.
There's an old Leaf habit: you return a borrowed dish with something in it. My cupboards are full of other people's bowls.
The widow at the end of my lane hasn't opened her shutters in two days. I'd knock, but I don't want to intrude.
I baked a cake for the gate guards, but it's too heavy for my back to carry all that way.
My kite's stuck on the bathhouse roof again. The children made it for me, so I can't just leave it there.
I lent my good cooking pot to someone at the last festival and can't remember who. It had a dent shaped like a heart.
Can't complain. Have you eaten? You look like you haven't eaten.
Fine, fine. Better now someone's asked.
The swing on the big tree out front has been there longer than any of the instructors. Every child in the Leaf has fought over it.
The Academy yard is all target posts and dust. On a still afternoon you can hear shuriken thunking into wood from the main street.
The big fire sign over the entrance is repainted every spring by the senior class. It's a privilege, and they still spill the paint.
Classes run nine to noon on weekdays. By half past twelve the yard's empty and the dango stall down the road is full.
The janitor's been here forty years and knows every loose floorboard. That's how the late pupils get caught.
Graduation photos line the corridor by the staff room. Look closely and you'll find Jonin who used to have terrible haircuts.
The library is through the main hall on the left. The workshop's behind it, with the Academy workbench, if you need to make something.
The training posts behind the building are free after lessons. Mind the third one; it leans.
The Hokage Residence is just over there, the round building with the fire sign on its roof. Don't mix them up; plenty do.
If you're looking for an instructor after hours, try the staff room window. There's always a lantern lit over the marking.
The Umino houses on the streets around here belong to the teachers' family. Knock if you're lost; somebody will be marking.
The Academy kitchen sells rice balls to pupils at two ryo. They're small, but they're the cheapest lunch in the village.
Exam week, the whole street goes quiet. Even the dango stall turns its brazier down so the pupils can think.
The yard's back fence has a gap the size of an eleven-year-old. Officially, nobody knows about it.
The market street wakes at seven when the shutters go up, and by eight you can't hear yourself think for the haggling.
Market Day is once a week. The farmers come in from outside the wall, and the whole street smells of fresh radish and grilled squid.
The two tea houses on the corner have been undercutting each other for a month. The regulars are thrilled; the owners aren't.
Every stall has a cat. Nobody knows whose cats they are, and they all seem to know exactly when the fish stall restocks.
The Akimichi compound is right off the market street. You can smell their kitchen from the fishmonger's.
Lanterns go up over the street every evening. By dusk the market looks like a festival even on a Second Day.
The grocer is halfway down on the left, under the green awning. Onigiri are three ryo, and the shop takes part-time help in the mornings.
The weapon shop and forge are at the far end, past the scroll shop. Follow the sound of hammering.
The barbecue house is round the corner by the Akimichi gate. Look for the smoke and the queue.
The pawn shop is in the alley behind the tea houses. It buys what bandits drop, and it never asks where you found it.
The furniture shop's showroom is at the top of the street, with everything it sells laid out as display pieces.
Prices on the market street climb three days before a festival. Buy your lanterns early, or pay double.
The fish stall sells sardines for a ryo each. Cheapest protein in the Leaf, if you can stand the smell on your hands.
The haggling rule here is: first price is a joke, second price is an insult, third price is the price.
The main street runs from the gate straight to the Hokage Residence. Stand in the middle and the faces on the Rock look right at you.
Ichiraku's lanterns are the first thing you see coming in from the gate. Half of the Leaf's homecomings end on those stools.
The Yamanaka flower shop is on the main street, so the whole street smells of lilies by noon in summer.
Processions use this street: the police parade, the Leaf Festival, the lantern walk. The cobbles have heard a lot of drums.
The utility poles along the main street are the only ones in the village with paper lanterns. Genin use them for jumping practice. They're not supposed to.
Shop signs up and down the street are painted by the same family on the artists' lane. You can tell by the curl on every last stroke.
Ichiraku's on the left before the crossroads. A bowl's six ryo, and they take on help at the counter.
The Hokage Residence is at the end of the street, under the Rock. The Mission Desk is on its ground floor.
The main gate is the other way, back down the street. Big doors, painted characters, guards who'll ask your business.
The tailor is by the crossroads, three doors along. Outfit variants start at a hundred ryo; mending is cheaper.
The bath house is off the main street down the lane with the blue curtain. Look for the steam.
Every new arrival in the Leaf walks this street first. Every squad home from a mission walks it last.
Market Day overflows from the market street onto this one, and the cart traffic stops dead at the crossroads for an hour.
The noticeboard outside the Residence lists the week's events and lost pets. The lost pets column is always longer.
The residential streets are mostly civilian families. Laundry on every balcony, shoes on every step and a cat on every wall.
Every house on this street has a round water tank on the roof. On a hot day, the children climb up and dangle their feet in them.
The old grandmother at the end of the lane sits out on her step at four every afternoon. Nothing happens on this street she doesn't see.
These streets are quiet at night apart from the occasional shinobi landing on a roof. The residents just turn over in bed.
Somebody on this street is always cooking. Grilled fish at six, miso at noon, and at midnight, someone's mother frying tempura.
The street shrine on the corner has a fresh rice ball every morning. Nobody admits to leaving it.
The Haruno family lives on the street with the cherry tree in the front garden. Their shop's on the market street, though.
The garden district past the bend is where the Yuhi grove is. The old trees are lovely, but don't wander in uninvited.
Cut through the alley by the bathhouse and you'll come out on the main street. It saves a good five minutes.
The Aburame house is at the wooded edge of the district. Walk slowly past their garden and don't swat anything.
Children play kick-the-can in these lanes until the dinner bells. If one comes flying your way, kick it back.
The house plaques by every door show who lives there. Newcomers' plaques are always the shiniest.
The neighbourhood bath on Third Lane is cheaper than the big one off the main street. Smaller tubs, louder gossip.
Moving day on this street is a festival of its own. The whole lane turns out to carry boxes and judge the furniture.
The main gate's doors are each painted with a single character. Together they spell out what the Leaf is for, if you think about it.
The guard booth by the gate has two chairs, one kettle and a logbook that's filled every month.
Carts come through at dawn, squads go out after eight, and travellers trickle in all afternoon. You could tell the time by the gate.
The Inuzuka compound is just inside the wall here. You'll hear the kennels long before you see them.
The gate barracks house the guard and the Shiranui family, whose wall of senbon targets is something to see.
Squads coming home stop under the gate and look up at the Rock. Every one of them, every time. I don't think they know they do it.
Outside the gate is the outer road and the training fields. Beyond the hills, you need a mission scroll and a stamp.
The Inuzuka clinic is just inside the wall to the right. That's where to go if you want to adopt a ninken pup.
Get your mission paperwork stamped at the Mission Desk before you come here. The guards won't let a squad out without it.
The Tobari lanes are just behind the wall here, dark and quiet. Mind your voice if you cut through after sundown.
The gate's busiest day is Market Day. Carts back up halfway to the far fields, and the guards get very little tea.
The wall walk is open to anyone with a reason to be up there. Ask the guards; on a clear day you can see three valleys.
The waystation on the east road is a morning's walk past the gate. Merchants rest there before the last stretch.
Travellers sign the book in the booth. The book from fifty years ago is still in the archive, if you ask nicely.
Four faces, each one taller than a house. On a clear evening the sunset catches the left side of every nose.
The stone at the top of the Rock is forest. Nobody built up there, and the deer from somewhere seem to like it.
Children climb the stairs beside the Rock on dares. The real dare is touching the eyebrow of the second face, and nobody ever has.
Every Hokage's face was carved by hand over a whole season. The stoneworkers' scaffolds stayed up for months.
There's room on the cliff for more faces. Everyone in the village has opinions about who should go up next.
The view from the top takes in the whole village and the wall all round. It's the only place where the Leaf looks small.
The stairs up the Rock start behind the Residence. It's a long climb, so take water, and maybe a dango.
The Shimura house is just under the Rock. It's very quiet, and they prefer it that way. Walk past it softly.
At the top, follow the path to the left for the best view of the main street. The right path goes nowhere but trees.
In the mornings the Rock's shadow covers half the village. By noon it's pulled back to the Residence's doorstep.
Pigeons nest in the ears of the third face. The cleaners go up once a year, and the pigeons come back the next week.
Sit on the bench at the base and watch who walks past. Everyone in the Leaf crosses this square eventually.
New Genin climb to the top on their first free day. It's not a tradition anyone made; it just keeps happening.
The Senju compound sits at the foot of the Rock, beside the Residence. You can see their great tree from the stairs.
The Residence is round, with a fire sign painted on the roof. From the Rock you can see it like a target.
The ground floor is all corridors and queues: the Mission Desk, the clan registry and a bench nobody ever gets to sit on.
The Hokage's office is upstairs. The window faces the village, and the lamp in it is usually lit long after dark.
Squads waiting for a mission brief trade gossip in the hall. Half the village's rumours start on that bench.
The hawk loft is on the roof. The courier birds go out at dawn and sit on the railing in a row at dusk.
The clan registry keeps every family's records. Its clerk can tell you which clan built which house, if you've got an afternoon.
The Mission Desk is on the ground floor, open eight till six. It takes Genin and up; Academy pupils get turned away politely.
The clan registry is the door past the Mission Desk. That's where clan matters are filed and family names recorded.
The Academy is just next door. People mix the two buildings up all the time; this one is round.
Don't go upstairs unless you're called. The guards on the landing are very polite about it, twice.
At eight in the morning the Mission Desk queue reaches the front steps. By ten it's mostly Chunin grumbling about D-ranks.
Notices for the week are pinned by the front door: festivals, curfews and requests for help.
The Residence garden has one plum tree, planted by the first Hokage. Nobody's allowed to pick from it, so the birds do.
The hall bench has a carved fire sign on the armrest. Rubbing it before a mission brief is supposed to bring luck.
Training Ground Three has three stumps in a row and a memorial stone shaped like a kunai. Every squad in the Leaf has stood there.
The lake on the far grounds is for water-walking. On a calm morning you'll see Genin falling in one after another like frogs.
The climbing cliff has scuff marks halfway up and very few above. That's where most people's chakra runs out.
The groundskeeper rakes the clearings every evening. By morning there are footprints all over them, and the raking starts again.
Logs, target posts and dummies line the edges of every ground. Most of them have more kunai holes than wood.
The Gekko dojo is by the grounds, with the moon platform on its roof. On full moons you'll hear swords from there till late.
Ground Three is past the stream, through the trees. Follow the sound of shuriken.
The lake for water-walking is on the eastern grounds. Sneak to sink if you need a rest; just don't do it in the deep middle.
Sparring partners hang about the posts after noon. Ask a ranked resident for a round; it ends at thirty percent, nobody dies.
The Namiashi dojo is just past the training grounds. You'll know it by the polished floor and the very quiet people.
There's an unbeatable post on the far ground. Nobody's ever knocked it over, and everyone has tried.
Mornings are for squads with a sensei; afternoons are for anyone. Night is for people who can't sleep.
The water barrel by the stumps is refilled every morning. Drink from it; the groundskeeper won't mind as long as you put the ladle back.
The trees around the grounds have scuff marks on every trunk at the height of a jumping Genin. That's how you find the tree-walking route.
The hospital is the tallest building after the Residence. The top floor windows face the Rock, so patients wake up to the Hokage.
Anyone who falls in a fight wakes up here the next morning, patched up and rested. Nobody sends a bill.
The Suzuran herb gardens are just behind, with the drying racks along the fence. The whole ward smells faintly of mint.
Visiting hours are ten to six, but the window ledges on the second floor have sandal prints from midnight visitors.
The children's ward has painted walls: frogs, Hokage and a very wobbly deer. The painters' lane did it as a gift.
The medics take tea on the roof at three. If you hear laughing from up there, the morning went well.
The front desk is through the main doors. Tell them who you're visiting and they'll point you to a floor.
The hospital stall by the entrance sells soldier pills, sixty ryo each. They taste dreadful and they work.
The herb gardens are round the back. Don't pick anything; half of it's medicine and the other half is the opposite.
The night shift is always short of hands. If you ever want to help, ask at the front desk after dark.
The bench outside the front door is where families wait. Sit with them sometimes. It helps more than you'd think.
The hospital kitchen makes rice porridge for every patient whatever's wrong with them. Even a broken ankle.
The bell on the roof only rings when a big group comes in from the gate. When it rings, the whole street makes room.
Your bed here clears your fatigue like your own does, but you won't wake well rested. Hospital pillows are a mission of their own.
Two hundred steps up to the shrine, and the priest sweeps every one of them each morning.
The wish plaques hang by the gate in rows. Some are about exams, some are about pets, and a lot are about ramen.
The rope over the main hall is renewed every autumn. Eight people, a ladder and a lot of opinions about knots.
New Year's Eve, the queue for the bell reaches the bottom step. Everyone gets one ring, and the shinobi get told to stop showing off.
The stone fox statues by the gate wear knitted caps in winter. Somebody steals one every year.
The big cedar behind the hall is older than the village. Nobody ties fortunes to it; those go on the little pine.
The wish plaques are five ryo at the little hut. Write yours and hang it on the left wall; the right one's full.
Fortunes are two ryo. Bad ones get tied to the pine by the gate and left behind.
The path behind the hall leads down to the spring, where the tea houses get their water. Don't drink from the top basin; that's for washing hands.
Weddings are held here in spring. The whole stair turns into a procession and the dango sellers set up at the bottom.
The shrine bell rings at dawn and dusk. If you hear it at another hour, somebody's been dared.
Shinobi come here the night before long missions. They don't say much, just stand under the cedar for a while.
The view from the top step takes in the whole east side of the village. It's the best place to watch a festival's fireworks.
The river runs right through the south of the village. Anglers on the banks, laundry on the stones, children in the shallows.
The ferry crosses where the river's too wide for stepping stones. They're building a new bridge downstream, and the ferryman is not pleased.
The washing stones by the second bridge have been used so long they're worn smooth as soap.
Herons stand in the reeds at dawn like little guards. The fishermen say a heron on the left bank means a good day.
The river families mend nets on the far bank every morning. They know more about the village than the gate does.
The Namiashi children practise on the stepping stones before breakfast. You'll hear them falling in.
The ferry landing is downstream from the second bridge. A crossing is one ryo; dogs ride free if they sit.
The best fishing spot is upstream of the mill, where the water slows down. Bring a lunch; the fish take their time.
The fish stall's supplier lands the catch at the jetty below the bridge at sunrise. That's where to buy if you want it fresh.
Summer evenings, the riverside families have a rowing race. No jutsu allowed, and the shinobi bet on it anyway.
The lanterns floated on the river at the end of summer drift all the way to the wall grate. The Tobari fish them out by dawn.
The water's warm enough for paddling by midsummer. The deep pool under the mill is cold enough to make you yell in any season.
Eel man by the second bridge sells grilled skewers at dusk. When the sauce runs out, he closes, so go early.
The apartment blocks near the Residence are mostly shinobi: Genin, clanless Chunin, a few old Jonin who never wanted a house.
Every landing has a shoe rack and a notice board. The board is mostly rules about noise and complaints about the noise rules.
The roof is where everyone hangs laundry, watches fireworks and practises jutsu they've been told not to practise indoors.
The landlady lives on the ground floor and hears every door. Whatever time you came in, the ground floor knows, and has opinions.
Water tanks on the roof feed every flat. In summer the morning shower is warm and the evening one is warmer.
The furniture shop is a short walk up the main street. Your flat looks better with more than a futon in it.
The bath house is two streets over if your flat's tub is too small, which it is.
Ichiraku's the closest dinner to the blocks. Most of the building eats there twice a week, some of us more.
The child upstairs practises jutsu at midnight. Thumps, shouts, the occasional smell of smoke. You get used to it.
Furnish your flat however you like; the walls are yours. Just don't put a forge where the landlady can see it.
Moving into the blocks, you get a futon, a key and a stern look from the landlady. Everything else you earn.
The block's notice board lists part-time shifts around the neighbourhood. That's where most Genin find their rent.
Every great clan has a gate, a main hall and a few houses behind its wall. The crest on the gate tells you whose ground you're on.
The clan quarters are quieter than the rest of the village. Fewer shops, more gardens and a lot of watching from windows.
Clan days change the whole quarter. Lanterns on the gate, food in the hall and cousins visiting from every corner of the Leaf.
Some quarters stand side by side: the Senju and the Uzumaki memorial, the three-clan alliance by the market. Others keep their distance.
Every clan's gate is guarded by somebody, but most of them are grandparents on a bench with a pot of tea.
The walls of the quarters are low enough to see over. They're for saying whose house it is, not for keeping anyone out.
The Uchiha quarter is out at the edge of the village, walled, with the police station in the far corner.
The Hyuga estate is a short walk from the Residence. The koi pond is just inside the gate; bow before you look at it.
The Nara house backs onto their deer forest at the village edge. The deer are protected; don't chase them.
The Inuzuka compound is by the main gate. Follow the barking.
Visitors bow at a clan gate before stepping through. Not deeply; just enough to say you know whose ground it is.
Clan members who make Chunin often move back behind their family's gate. Plenty stay in the apartment blocks for the noodles.
The clan registry at the Residence keeps the records of every quarter. If you want to know who lives behind a gate, start there.
Clan quarters host clan days on different weeks, so somewhere in the Leaf there's nearly always a lantern on a gate.
Shop opened at seven, closed at six, and in between I sold forty bowls of rice. Not a single jutsu involved.
I watch the squads leave through the gate every morning on my way to the stall. I always wonder which ones I'll see come back tired.
People think civilians just sit about while the shinobi work. You try hauling fish crates at dawn.
My stall is right by the Mission Desk road. I can tell how a mission went by how fast a squad walks home.
I'm the third generation of my family to run this shop. None of us could mould chakra. All of us could make change.
My son wants to join the Academy. I'm proud. I'm terrified. Mostly I'm buying him a lot of rice.
I tried to throw a kunai once at the festival stall. Hit the stall owner's hat. They gave me a prize just to make me stop.
My neighbour's a Jonin. Lovely person, never home. I water the plants and they bring me odd fruit from far places.
I do the books for the hardware shop. Shinobi buy wire by the mile. I've stopped asking what for.
The best thing about being a civilian? When the alarm bell rings, my job is to go home and lock the door. Simple.
I launder Chunin vests for half the shinobi on this street. You'd never believe what ends up in those pockets.
I've lived in the Leaf my whole life and never once climbed a wall without a ladder. I'm very proud of my ladder.
When I was young I wanted to be a shinobi. Now I bake. Some mornings, shaping dough feels like a kind of jutsu.
My daughter's a Genin now. She tells me nothing about her missions. I find out from the laundry.
I sell sandals. Shinobi wear through three pairs a season. Bless them, they pay my rent.
Some shinobi come in and pay with odd coins from far villages. I keep a jar of them. It's like having a little map.
I sweep the street outside my shop and find shuriken in the gutter. I keep a box for them. Someone always comes back.
Running a tea house means hearing everything and repeating nothing. That's the civilian's code, more or less.
I don't have a headband, but I've got a good knife and the sharpest tongue on the market street.
My husband's a carpenter. He fixes what the training grounds break. There's always a lot to fix.
The farmers outside the wall are civilians too. They grow every grain of rice this village eats. Never forget that.
I deliver letters. On a good day I can walk the whole village twice. Shinobi do it in ten minutes, over the roofs. Show-offs.
Every time a squad brings a merchant back safe, the merchant comes to my inn. I hear the story twice: once scared, once brave.
I don't understand half of what the shinobi say. "C-rank", "B-rank". I just know an A means they'll be gone a while.
I had a ninja come in to buy flour, and they paid by walking up the wall to get the top sack. Very helpful.
I can't make a clone, but I can make three dinners at once. I think that's a fair trade.
I grow vegetables for the Akimichi kitchen. They say my carrots taste of sunshine. They're being polite. They're right.
I'm a civilian born to shinobi parents. Couldn't mould a scrap of chakra. My mother said I'd have a longer life. She was right so far.
I sit on the market council. Mostly we argue about where carts may stop. It's very important. To us.
My fishing boat's older than most of the Jonin. Still floats. Still catches more than they do.
My job is to keep the bath hot and the gossip cold. I'm good at the first one.
Civilians run the Leaf's daily life: the shops, the farms, the baths. The shinobi protect it. That's the deal.
Shinobi pay the same prices as everyone. No discount for a headband. Some of them still try.
The market council is all civilians. Even the Hokage has to ask us before moving a stall.
On festival nights the civilians run everything: the stalls, the music, the lanterns. The shinobi just eat.
Civilian children can enrol in the Academy like anyone else. Most come out with nothing but good manners and strong legs.
When a squad doesn't come home, the whole street knows within the hour. The shops close early. Nobody says why.
Civilian families keep shrines for their shinobi neighbours too. We light a candle when they leave on a long mission.
Most of the shops in the Leaf are civilian-run, even the weapon shop's front. The forge is the only shinobi-run part.
The Leaf pays farmers in good times and bad. In return, the farms feed the village through any winter.
Some civilian families have run the same shop since the founding. The noodle stalls have the longest memory of all.
If a shop's shutter is half down, the owner will still sell to you. All the way down means go home and come back at seven.
Market Day is once a week. Farmers come in from outside the wall with the freshest produce. Prices drop by noon.
If you want work without a headband, ask the shops. Ichiraku, the grocer, the flower shop and the forge all take part-timers.
The pawn shop will take what you don't need for half its price. Don't expect more. They've heard every story.
A Genin squad was meant to deliver my flour this morning. They never came. I'd ask the Desk, but I can't leave the shop.
My grandson's training sword snapped. Shinobi gear's beyond me. Maybe someone knows a smith who'd look at it.
Somebody's chickens keep getting into my lettuce. I suspect a ninken's been chasing them out of their coop.
My mother's shrine charm was lost at the last festival. Small red bag. She's convinced it's what keeps the roof up.
A squad walked through my garden on a roof run and squashed half my melons. I'd like them to know.
Shop's open, bills are paid, no shinobi crashed through my roof. A good day.
Busy, busy. Not as busy as the Mission Desk, thank goodness.
Weeded three gardens today. Three. My sensei says it builds character. My back says it builds blisters.
We spent the morning chasing a lost cat. Third time this month. Same cat. I think it enjoys the attention.
My squad almost finished a D-rank without arguing. Almost. We argued about the last bucket.
I got my first proper mission pay today. Ninety ryo. I bought ramen for the whole squad. Now I have six ryo.
My sensei made us carry logs up and down the training ground for two hours. I can't feel my arms. Worth it, apparently.
Painting a fence is a D-rank. Who knew? We did the whole thing in an hour. Our sensei did a different one in five minutes.
My teammate's always late. Every single morning. We started meeting fifteen minutes earlier, and they're still late.
I tried to impress my sensei with a new jutsu. It fizzled. My sensei laughed and showed me where I was wrong.
We escorted an old merchant to the farms and back. Long walk. The merchant told us the same joke four times.
I fell in the river during a fishing D-rank. My squad laughed. I caught the biggest fish anyway. Ha.
My sensei says teamwork matters more than talent. I'm talented and terrible at teamwork. I'm working on it.
My squad has a code word for "the sensei's watching". We use it so much now it doesn't mean anything.
I wear my headband to bed sometimes. Don't tell anyone. I'm still not used to having one.
The Mission Desk gave us a babysitting job. Three toddlers. Hardest mission of my life. I'm not joking.
I've been practising tree walking. I can get halfway up now before I slip. Yesterday it was a third.
My squad got our first C-rank and the whole thing was carrying boxes. Still. A C! I'm putting it on my wall.
Some days I feel like a real shinobi. Today I picked up rubbish by the river for four hours. Not one of those days.
We trained until sunset. My sensei bought us dango. I think that's the reward system. I'm learning.
My teammates and I have a bet on who'll make Chunin first. The loser buys ramen for a month.
I learned to tell how heavy a crate is by looking. That's from D-ranks, not training. Very useful skill, honestly.
I spent all morning trying to catch a bird that escaped from the tea house. It sat on my head when I gave up.
Got a scolding from my sensei for showing off a trick during a mission. Fair. I still think it was a good trick.
I helped rebuild a farmer's fence. The farmer gave us a sack of potatoes. Best pay I've had.
I can throw four shuriken at once now. Two hit. One got stuck in a tree. One's missing. We're looking.
My parents still treat me like a child even with the headband. I'm a shinobi! Who also has to be home by dinner.
My sensei can tell when I've skipped warm-ups just by watching me walk. It's very annoying.
Our squad's first mission outside the wall was a delivery to the waystation. I've never been so far. Didn't see a single bandit.
I thought Genin life would be all battles. It's mostly gardens, cats and helping people move furniture.
My squad finally learned to read each other's hand signals. Took months. Now we can be rude to each other silently.
We had a squad sleepover at our sensei's after a late mission. Our sensei snores. Loudly. Like a bear.
My teammate's mother makes the best rice balls. We always take that teammate's lunch. Team effort.
I'm saving for a better kunai pouch. Eight more D-ranks. Maybe nine if I buy dango.
I asked my sensei why we do D-ranks. The answer: "So the village knows your face before it needs your fists."
Every Genin squad is three students and a Jonin sensei. You do everything together. Everything.
D-ranks are the village's chores: weeding, deliveries, lost pets, fence painting. The Leaf runs on them.
Genin get their missions from the Mission Desk on the Residence's ground floor. You line up with your squad.
The Chunin Exams happen in spring and autumn. Squads enter together or not at all.
A sensei can refuse to put a squad forward for the exams. Mine says we'll go when we're ready. I'm ready now!
The headband's metal plate is pressed with the Leaf's symbol at the smithy. They're all the same. Feels special anyway.
There's an unspoken rule that the newest Genin squad gets the muddiest D-rank. It's a kind of welcome.
Genin squads keep a log of every mission. Ours has eighty-three entries. Fifty are about weeds.
Senseis can train their students at any ground they like. Ground 3 is the most popular. The stumps are famous.
The Mission Desk is open from eight till six. Come early. The good D-ranks go first.
Training before a mission helps, but not too much. Exhausted Genin make mistakes.
A D-rank pays sixty to a hundred and fifty ryo. Enough to eat well and save a little.
If a mission's going badly, you go back and report. Pride doesn't count as a reason to keep going.
We were supposed to find a client's lost ring at the farms. We didn't. It's still out there somewhere.
I left my training weights at Ground 3. They're heavy, so probably nobody took them. Probably.
My squad's been asked to paint the Academy fence, but we're one short this week. If you know a pair of hands...
Long day. Good day. I'm a Genin. Every day's both.
Missions done, sensei satisfied, ramen next. Life's good.
Desk duty all morning. I stamped two hundred mission forms. My hand has become a stamp.
I lead my first squad of Genin next week. I'm more nervous than I was in my own exams.
I spent the day teaching a squad how to set a camp. One of them set their tent on fire. Learning.
I took the Chunin Exams twice before passing. I tell every Genin that. It helps more than any advice.
The vest is warm in winter and terrible in summer. Fourteen pockets and I still can't find my keys.
I'm on the Mission Desk rotation this month. You learn a lot about a village from what it asks for help with.
I escorted a merchant caravan to the border village and back. Six days, no trouble. That's the best kind.
I proctored a written exam at the Academy. Saw two cheating attempts and one very creative sandwich.
Some days I'm a leader, some days I'm a clerk. Today I was both before lunch.
I make the Genin squads I lead do warm-ups whether they like it or not. They do not like it.
I got my first B-rank. I'm not allowed to talk about it. I'm allowed to say I'm very tired.
My younger brother's a Genin now. He's on a squad I trained with once. It's strange watching from the other side.
Sometimes I miss D-ranks. You weed a garden, the garden's weeded. Simple. Leading a squad is never that simple.
I filled in for a sick Jonin sensei for a week. The squad asked when their sensei was coming back. Every hour.
I keep a little book of every mistake I've made on a mission. It's thick. I read it before every new one.
I spent the night on wall watch. The stars are beautiful from the top. The cold isn't.
I was given a squad of three loud Genin. I have learned to speak in a whisper so they have to stop and listen.
I was sent to teach a class at the Academy on wire traps. The children wanted to know if I'd ever fought a bear.
The hardest part of being a Chunin is deciding. On a mission, someone has to choose, and now that's me.
I wrote my first report as a squad leader. Eight pages. My Jonin said it should have been two.
I spent a week guarding a farm against wild boars. They came on the last night. I'll be telling that story for years.
I passed the exams last autumn. My parents still introduce me as "the Chunin". It's lovely. And a bit embarrassing.
My Jonin sensei still checks on me after every mission. I'm a Chunin! It's nice, though.
I train new Genin in chakra control twice a week. They're bad at it. I was worse.
I ran messages for the Hokage's office all day. Up and down the Residence stairs. I've decided stairs are a jutsu.
I'm saving for my own apartment. Shinobi pay's good when you get C-ranks, but rent on the main street is steep.
I volunteered to help with the next Chunin Exams. Watching from the other side is harder than taking them.
Chunin lead squads, staff the Mission Desk, teach at the Academy and watch the wall. Most of the village's work is ours.
The Chunin vest has scroll pockets on the chest. Old shinobi say that's where your life's work goes.
A Chunin can be promoted to Jonin by the Hokage. There's no exam for that, just years and a good record.
The Chunin Exams are held in spring and autumn. Squads from other villages come, and the whole Leaf turns out to watch the finals.
Chunin on wall duty take four-hour watches. You learn to love tea and hate wind.
Every Chunin in the Leaf takes a shift at the Mission Desk sooner or later. It's how you learn what the village needs.
The Mission Desk opens at eight and closes at six. Bring your squad and your report. In that order.
C-rank missions pay three to six hundred ryo, but they go beyond the wall. Prepare properly.
If a squad comes in hurt, they go straight to the hospital. The report can wait. That's a rule.
A Genin squad's been bringing back the same lost cat every week. I think someone's letting it out on purpose. For the pay.
A crate of mission scrolls went missing between the Desk and the archive. Probably misfiled. Probably.
The training post at Ground 3 has a crack straight through it. Someone ought to tell the builders before a Genin gets a splinter.
Busy. Forms, squads, more forms. You get used to it.
I came back from a month-long mission yesterday. My house plants are dead. My neighbour fed my cat. Priorities.
I'm a sensei now. My three Genin argue like a family of crows. I'm growing fond of them, which is terrifying.
I'm home for a week, then gone again. I try to eat at my favourite stall every day I'm here.
My students passed the Chunin Exams. All three. I cried in the stands. Don't tell them.
I've been a Jonin for ten years. The missions get harder. The quiet days get sweeter.
I spent the morning teaching my students to walk on water. Two did it. One swam. Honestly, the swimmer had the best form.
I write my students' parents a note after every mission. One parent sends back cake. That's my favourite student. Don't tell.
I sleep twelve hours when I get home. Then I eat everything in the house. Then I sleep again.
I carry a photo of my squad from when I was a Genin. Most of them are Jonin too. We still meet for ramen when we can.
Long missions make you miss the small things. The smell of the tea house. My own pillow. The noise of the market.
I'm teaching my squad to read terrain. They'd rather learn fireballs. Terrain keeps you alive. Fireballs don't, always.
I spent today asleep under a tree at Ground 3 while my students trained. Officially, I was "observing".
My sensei is retired now. Grows cabbages by the river. I go and help. Still learning things from that old teacher.
I keep a diary of where I've been. Seven countries. Two oceans. One very bad inn I'll never forget.
After a long mission, the first thing I do is walk the whole village. Just to see it's all still here.
I was supposed to rest today. My students found me. Now I'm training them. That's a Jonin's rest day.
Being a sensei is half teaching, half making sure they've eaten. I buy a lot of dango.
My spouse is a medic at the hospital. We see each other between shifts and missions. It works. Somehow.
I have a rule: on my first night home, I don't talk about the mission. Just food, friends, and bed.
I taught my students to set a trap. They caught me in it. I've never been prouder or more annoyed.
I've had my flak vest for nine years. It's been patched so many times it's mostly patch.
I've been offered a desk job at the Residence. I said no. Not yet. My students need me in the field.
Jonin take on the hardest missions, lead the best squads, and teach the newest Genin. Some do all three in a week.
A Jonin sensei chooses whether a new squad passes their first test. Many don't. They go back to the Academy.
Jonin meet in a hall at the Residence before big missions. Quiet room. Very good tea.
Some Jonin specialise: medics, trackers, sealing experts. The Leaf needs every kind.
A Jonin's flak vest is the same as a Chunin's. What changes is how long you've worn it.
Read a mission scroll's client line twice. The rank tells you the danger. The client tells you the trouble.
Pack light, pack smart. A kunai, a wire, a bandage, a ration. Everything else is weight.
A good shinobi eats well before a mission. Ichiraku's ramen restores a little chakra. Don't scoff at it.
My Genin left their training notes in a tree at Ground 3. All three of them. Separately. I'm not climbing three trees.
I promised my students a picnic if they passed their drill. They passed. I don't have a picnic basket.
Home. Fed. Not on a mission. That's a good day.
My day? Quiet. Let's leave it there.
I'm off duty. That's all you need to know, and most of what I can say.
I like the tea house. The corner table. People don't look twice. That's important to me.
I slept until noon. Some days that's the whole report.
I water my plants. They don't ask where I've been.
Today I bought vegetables like anyone else. I enjoyed it more than you'd think.
The Leaf has people who keep it safe in the dark. You won't see them. That's the point.
There are masks that guard this village. If you see one, you didn't. Understand?
Fine. Thank you for asking. Really.
Good enough. Keep walking.
I mend the nets for the fisherfolk. My fingers are quicker than any jutsu I've seen, and I've seen a few from my porch.
I run the bathhouse boiler. Shinobi come in after missions grey with dust and leave pink and grateful. Best part of the job.
When the squads come home at dusk, I put the kettle on. My shop's the first one past the gate. They know the smell.
I sell paper for seals and letters. I can't read a single seal, but I know which paper the Uzumaki like. Thick, cream, no dye.
My cousin's a Chunin. At family dinners everyone asks about missions. Nobody asks about my cabbages. My cabbages are excellent.
I spent today fixing the shrine roof with the carpenters. No chakra, just ladders, rope and a lot of shouting.
I keep the inn by the east road. Squads stop for one cup on the way out and three on the way back.
I watched the Genin squads racing across the rooftops this morning. My tiles were not consulted.
I spent the whole D-rank carrying bags for a lady moving house. The piano nearly beat all three of us.
Our sensei has a bell test every month. We've never taken the bell. One day. One day soon.
I wrapped my hands for training and wore the wraps to dinner without noticing. My mother noticed.
I took a mission alone for the first time. Delivering a letter across the village. I ran the whole way like it was an S-rank.
My squad got praised by the client today. The client said we were "quite tidy". Highest compliment of my career.
We had to clean the Academy's storage room. Found my old practice targets. My aim was awful. It's less awful now.
My sensei made us meditate by the river for an hour. One of us fell asleep. Two of us fell in. I was the sleeper.
I spent today learning to read a map properly. Turns out I've been holding it upside down for weeks.
The squad I'm on has a cat now. It followed us home from a lost-pet mission. The client didn't want it back.
I spent the morning sorting D-ranks into piles: easy, muddy, impossible. The impossible pile is mostly cats.
I gave a squad of Genin their first C-rank briefing. Their faces lit up like festival lanterns. I remember that feeling.
My first squad of Genin bought me a cake on my birthday. It said "Thank you, scary". I keep the card.
I took a quiet wall shift at dawn. Watched the farms wake up beyond the gate. Smoke, roosters, mist. Lovely.
The hardest part of desk duty is telling a Genin squad there are no missions left. Their faces. Every time.
I've started cooking for myself instead of eating at stalls. My first stew was a disaster. My second was fine.
I lent my vest to a Genin who was shivering on wall watch. Got it back with a kunai hole and an apology.
I run the evening sparring sessions at Ground 2. Most nights it's a mess. Sometimes, something clicks for someone.
I spent all morning writing up a mission that took twenty minutes. Paperwork's the real enemy of the Leaf.
I'm learning medical jutsu in my spare time. Can heal a paper cut now. Very slowly. With great concentration.
I came home to find my students had cleaned my house as a surprise. I can't find anything. I'm very touched.
I've been teaching for so long that my first students now have students. I feel old. I'm buying them all dinner anyway.
My students asked me what I was like as a Genin. I told the truth. Now they think I'm human. I preferred the mystery.
I spent my day off at the Academy, talking to the graduating class. Most asked about missions. One asked about my lunch.
On the long missions, I count the days by meals. Forty-two rations, then a bowl of Ichiraku at the end of it.
I keep a photo of every squad I've taught on the day they got their headbands. Every squad's grinning like they've won the world.
A good mission is one where nothing happens. The best one this year was nine days of nothing. I slept like a baby after.
Spring means graduation at the Academy. The yard fills up with families, and the new headbands catch the sun.
Spring brings the Chunin Exams. Teams from other villages start arriving, and the inns fill up overnight.
When the cherry trees bloom along the river, half the Leaf takes its lunch outside. Nobody gets any work done.
Spring is planting season at the farms. The Mission Desk fills up with D-ranks for digging and sowing.
Fawns are born in the Nara forest in spring. They wobble about the forest edge on legs like chopsticks.
In spring the market's full of bamboo shoots and wild greens. Everyone's soup tastes of the forest for a month.
Spring cleaning's serious business in the Leaf. Every futon in the village gets beaten on the balconies the same week.
High water in spring, with snowmelt from the hills. Kids are told to stay off the low bridge.
Spring rain comes soft and often. The moss on the shrine steps turns bright green overnight.
Come spring, the Yamanaka flower shop's window is all blossoms and tulips. People queue just to look.
Swallows come back to the eaves in spring. Families mark the nests and argue about whose are the same birds.
In spring the roofers are everywhere, fixing what the winter snow cracked. The village sounds like a drum.
Spring's Chunin Exam finals fill the stadium. Even the shopkeepers close up to go and watch.
I planted my beans this week. Every spring I promise myself a neat garden, and every summer it's a jungle.
Spring makes me restless. I find myself staring at the gate, wondering what the roads are like this year.
My nose hasn't stopped running since the blossoms came out. Lovely to look at. Terrible to breathe.
I always make sakura mochi in spring. Pink rice, salted leaf, sweet bean inside. My children eat them faster than I make them.
I put away the winter quilts today. Every year I'm sure I'm doing it too early, and every year I'm right.
Blossoms are out! I can't walk past the river without stopping. Even the stern folk smile under those trees.
Spring rain again. The gardens are happy. My laundry isn't.
Warm enough to leave the shutters open. Spring in the Leaf smells of wet earth and blossom.
Late snow broke a branch on the cherry tree by the bridge. If it isn't tied up, the blossoms will go to waste.
Farms are behind on planting. They're asking for anyone with a strong back and a free morning.
A swallow's nest fell off the eaves at the tea house. The chicks are in a basket on the counter. They need a new home.
Spring rain makes the training-ground logs slick. Shinobi say you learn more balance in one wet spring than in three dry summers.
Spring at last. Everything feels new.
I love this time of year. Everyone's in a good mood.
Summer's the Leaf Festival. Lanterns on every street, food stalls from the gate to the river, fireworks over the Rock.
Summer means cicadas. They start before dawn and go until dusk. You stop hearing them after a week. Mostly.
In summer the river's full of children from noon till dusk. The deep pool under the low bridge is the favourite.
Summer storms come in fast over the hills. One minute blue sky, the next the whole village is running for cover.
Ichiraku does cold noodles in summer. Same broth, chilled. People who swear by hot ramen sneak a bowl anyway.
Every rooftop water tank in the Leaf is warm by afternoon in summer. Free hot baths, if you're not fussy.
Summer at the market is watermelons stacked like cannonballs. The grocer lets the children pick the biggest.
Festival fireworks go up from the top of the Rock. You can see them from every street in the village.
Festival yukata come out in summer. The tailors are busy for weeks beforehand, and nobody gets theirs early.
Wind chimes go up on every porch in summer. On a breezy evening the whole street sings.
Summer's the time for night markets. Grilled corn, shaved ice and goldfish scooping by lantern light.
In summer the training grounds are at their hardest. Sensei love making squads run when it's hot.
Fireflies come out by the river in early summer. People walk down after dinner just to see them.
I've been sleeping with the shutters open. The cicadas wake me before dawn, but the breeze is worth it.
Shaved ice with sweet syrup is the only thing that keeps me alive in summer. Strawberry, if anyone asks.
I always buy a new fan before the Leaf Festival. I've got forty fans. I'll buy another this year.
Summer's for staying in the shade and doing as little as possible. I take that very seriously.
I won a goldfish at the festival scooping game last year. It's still alive. It's huge. I'm a little afraid of it.
Hot! Even the dogs are lying flat in the shade. The Leaf melts a little more every afternoon.
Leaf Festival's coming. I can feel it. The lantern-makers are working through the night.
Another summer storm last night. The streets are steaming already.
Someone's goldfish from the festival jumped out of its bowl into the river. The owner's been crying on the bridge all morning.
Wind chimes went missing from the tea house in the storm. The owner says the summer won't feel right without them.
Lantern-makers are short of paper for the festival. If someone could fetch a stack from the scroll shop, they'd be grateful.
Drink water in summer, especially on missions. Heat's beaten more Genin than bandits have.
Hot day, isn't it? Stay in the shade.
Summer. Long days, short nights, and too many bugs.
Autumn brings the Chunin Exams again. Foreign teams in the market, everyone guessing who'll make the finals.
Graduation comes round again in autumn. New Genin, nervous parents, lots of photos by the Academy swing.
Harvest comes in autumn. Carts of rice roll in through the gate every morning, and the farmers stay for a drink.
Maples by the training grounds go red in autumn. People walk out there just to see them.
Moon-viewing night is in autumn. People sit on their roofs with rice dumplings and tea and look up.
In autumn the market fills with chestnuts, sweet potatoes and persimmons. The whole street smells roasted.
Autumn's when the Leaf stocks up for winter. Firewood stacked by every door, pickles in every pantry.
Persimmons hang drying from every balcony in autumn. The crows think it's a feast laid out for them.
Every autumn the Akimichi hold a harvest feast. If you help carry the rice in, you're invited to eat it.
Autumn winds blow down from the hills. The kites come out again, the last good kite days of the year.
In autumn the Nara deer grow thick coats and start to look very pleased with themselves.
Leaves pile up so fast in autumn that the shrine priest gives up sweeping after noon.
Harvest jobs flood the Mission Desk in autumn. Every Genin in the Leaf learns to carry a rice sack.
I love roasting sweet potatoes in the fire pit in autumn. The smell brings the whole street out.
I make persimmon jam every autumn. My mother's recipe. I've never got it right. I'm going to try again.
Autumn makes me a bit wistful. Everything's beautiful and leaving at the same time.
I always pick the reddest maple leaf I can find in autumn and press it in a book. I've got thirty years of them.
I've been stacking firewood all week. My back aches. The pile looks magnificent.
Maples are turning. The whole training ground looks like it's on fire.
Chilly mornings, warm afternoons. Autumn can't make up its mind.
Harvest's coming in. You can hear the carts rumbling through the gate at dawn.
More rice than hands at the farms this year. They're paying anyone who'll help with the harvest.
Someone's been stealing persimmons off the drying lines on the residential street. Probably crows. Possibly not crows.
Gekko dojo's moon-viewing platform needs a new rail before moon-viewing night. They're short of carpenters.
Eat hot food when the cold comes. A good meal takes the weight off tired legs for a while, and autumn nights get long.
Autumn's my favourite. Everything smells like smoke and apples.
Getting cooler. Time to find the warm coat.
New Year comes at the end of winter. The shrine bell rings at midnight, and the line up the steps goes down the hill.
First snow is a little holiday here. Lessons go quiet, and every child in the Leaf is outside throwing snowballs.
In winter the Hokage faces wear snow caps. The children call them the Hokage's hats.
Winter means hot pots. Every home in the Leaf has one bubbling in the evening, and the windows all fog up.
Deep winter freezes the river at the edges. People skate the shallows by the reeds. Never the middle.
In winter the bathhouses are packed. The steam from them rises over the rooftops like the village is breathing.
Winter's when the Leaf mends things. Nets, sandals, roofs, coats. Every porch has someone sewing or whittling.
Rice cakes are pounded in the shrine yard for New Year. Anyone can take a turn with the big mallet.
In winter the gate guards get a brazier by the booth. Half the village stops to warm their hands on the way past.
Snow piles high on the market awnings. The stallholders knock it off with brooms every hour.
Winter nights in the Leaf are long and quiet. The lamp keepers light the street lanterns early.
New Year's first sunrise is watched from the top of the Rock. People climb up in the dark to see it.
Winter is the slow season at the Mission Desk. Mostly snow clearing and firewood runs.
I keep a kettle on the stove all winter. Anyone who knocks gets tea. That's my rule.
I knit through the whole winter. By spring, everyone I know has a new scarf whether they want one or not.
I hate the cold. I sleep in three blankets and still wake up with a frozen nose.
Winter's my favourite. Snow makes everything quiet and clean. I like the village best like this.
I make sweet red bean soup every winter. With a toasted rice cake on top. My family queues for it.
Snow again! The whole street's white. The Rock looks like it's wearing a blanket.
Cold this morning. My breath froze on my scarf. Mind the ice on the bridges.
New Year's coming. The shrine's busy hanging the straw ropes, and everyone's cleaning their house top to bottom.
The old woman on my lane can't clear her own path in the snow. Someone ought to shovel it before she slips.
More hands are wanted at the shrine for the New Year rice pounding. They're short of people who can swing a mallet.
Gate booth's brazier has gone cold. The guards' firewood store is empty, and the courier's late.
Snow on the roofs makes for bad footing. Shinobi keep to the ridges in winter, where the tiles show through.
Cold out, isn't it? Stay warm.
Winter. Good weather for tea and staying in.
In spring the Academy hangs paper carp from the roof for the new students. They flap like they're swimming upstream.
Spring is when the clans repaint their gate crests. You'll see ladders and paint pots outside every compound for a week.
First green tea of the year arrives at the tea house in spring. The old folk taste it and argue about whether it's better than last year's.
In the hottest weeks of summer the Mission Desk sends Genin to carry water to the farms. Every bucket counts.
Summer evenings in the Leaf are for sitting on the porch in a cotton robe with a fan and a cold barley tea.
Shops run the Leaf Festival games: ring toss, goldfish, target throwing. The shinobi are banned from that last one.
In autumn the sweet-potato cart comes round the residential streets at dusk. You hear the seller's song before you see the steam.
Autumn's when the Leaf's roofs are checked before the snow. The Kinoshita carpenters are booked for weeks.
Rice straw from the harvest is woven into ropes and sandals in autumn. Half of it ends up as New Year decorations.
At the end of winter every house in the Leaf is scrubbed top to bottom for New Year. Dust is not allowed into the new year.
In winter the Inuzuka ninken grow so fluffy you can barely see their eyes. The children follow them about to pat them.
Winter market sells hot ginger tea, roasted chestnuts and padded jackets. It closes early, when the cold sets in.
Stay up past one in the morning and your legs go heavy and your chakra comes back slow. Tired is the body's polite warning.
Push on to three and it stops being polite. Exhausted shinobi stumble, hit soft and miss their jumps.
If the sun comes up and you still haven't slept, you'll drop where you stand and wake in your bed at noon. Ask anyone who's tried.
Get into your own bed before midnight and you'll wake Well Rested. Your chakra comes back quicker all morning.
Your own bed is the one that does the job properly. A hospital cot or a camp bedroll will clear the tiredness, but you won't wake fresh.
Sleep at night and the hours just slip by. You lie down in the dark and open your eyes at six with the sparrows.
A hot meal won't fix a sleepless night, but it does put some spring back in tired legs for an hour or so.
Half my night patients are Genin who stayed up and then wondered why their jutsu fizzled. Sleep before midnight. Doctor's orders.
A cup of green tea pushes the tiredness back an hour. It doesn't cancel it; it just moves the bill to later.
Exhausted is no state to train in. Your strikes lose a fifth of their force and the edges of everything go dark.
Green tea in the evening buys you another hour before the tiredness catches up. A pot at ten and you'll still be sharp at two.
It's getting late. If you're out past one you'll start dragging your feet, so go home while it's still easy.
Ryo comes in notes: ones, tens, hundreds and the big thousand note nobody ever wants to break. Keep them in a pouch or a chest.
Academy pupils without family get a stipend of thirty ryo a day. It's not much, but it covers ramen and a little over.
Notes are just paper. Put the big ones in a chest at home and carry only what you mean to spend.
The cheapest meals in the village are three to ten ryo. A day's honest work covers that twice.
Furniture sells back at half what it cost. Think before you buy the expensive lamp.
The pawn shop buys bandit-camp salvage. That and selling furniture back are the only ways to turn things into ryo.
A thousand-ryo note is lovely to hold and terrible to spend. Change it at a big shop, never at a dango stall.
The stipend stops when you graduate, so save a bit now. Genin pay their own way, mostly from missions.
Your flat is yours to arrange. Inside your own walls you can set furniture down, turn it and pick it back up again.
Hold a piece of furniture at home and you'll see where it would go before you set it down. Turn it till it sits right.
Pick a chest back up and everything inside comes with it. No need to empty it first.
Step out of your own flat and you can't place furniture anymore. The landlady's hallway is not your living room.
Whatever else you move, a home always keeps one bed. That's the one that clears tiredness properly.
A chest at home is the safest place for ryo and spare kit. Nothing in a chest gets lost if you fall on a mission.
Potted plants, scroll shelves, lamps, cushions: it all counts as furniture, and it all makes a flat feel like a home.
A workbench in your flat means you can make smoke bombs and simple furniture without walking to the Academy.
Bring planks and cloth to a workbench and you can build simple furniture yourself. Cheaper than mine, though not as pretty.
A full set of furniture for a flat takes about a week of honest work to pay for. Start with a table and build from there.
You can put a pet bed by your futon. A pet that has its own spot settles at home much faster.
Shops open around seven. Come before that and you'll be knocking on shutters.
Part-time shifts at Ichiraku, the grocer, the flower shop or the forge pay forty to eighty ryo. Ask the owner; they're always short-handed.
A shift at a shop pays about as well as an easy D-rank. It's a good way to fill an afternoon between lessons.
Work the forge often enough and the smith will start teaching you. Some trades pay in knowledge as well as ryo.
Shopkeepers remember who works hard. Do a few good shifts and you'll get a friendlier price at the counter.
I'm always looking for help on busy shifts. Ask me when you've a few hours, and you'll go home with ryo in your pocket.
Market Day is when the shops need the most help. If you want a shift, today's the day to ask.
Ramen puts a little chakra back in you. That's why Genin queue at Ichiraku straight off the training ground.
Dango speed up how fast your chakra returns. A stick or two before training and you'll go longer between rests.
Barbecue puts weight in your punches. Not a lot, but enough that the taijutsu crowd swears by it.
Green tea holds the tiredness off. A cup late in the evening buys you an hour before your legs go heavy.
The good feeling from a meal doesn't last forever. Eat close to when you need it, not at breakfast for a fight at dusk.
You still need to eat ordinary food too. A buff won't fill an empty stomach.
A cooking pot at home lets you make Leaf dishes yourself. Buy the ingredients at the grocer for a fraction of a shop meal.
Every dish in this village does something for you. Ramen for chakra, dango for recovery, barbecue for strength, tea for late nights. Pick your meal for your day.
Eat something before you train, please. A full belly carries you further and you'll get less tired on the way home.
You can adopt a ninken pup at the Inuzuka clinic by the gate. Ask the vet; the pups do most of the deciding.
The shelter has cats looking for homes. They're quieter than dogs and they'll keep the mice out of your rice.
A pet follows you about and waits at home when you go somewhere it can't come. It'll be at the door when you get back.
Pets sleep at the foot of your bed. Expect a warm lump on your feet every morning.
Pets get knocked out, not killed. If yours gets hurt, it'll be back on its feet and sulking by evening.
Once you're a Genin, a ninken can follow scents on missions. A dog's nose finds what a squad's eyes miss.
