A pup wants feeding, walking and a corner of its own. Give it those and it'll give you everything else.
A ninken's partner feeds it first and eats second. That's the first thing we teach anyone who takes a pup home.
The Mission Desk is open eight till six on the Residence's ground floor. Come early; the good D-ranks go first.
D-rank missions pay sixty to a hundred and fifty ryo. A day of them covers food and leaves you half to save.
C-rank work pays three to six hundred. More ryo, more road and a lot more that can go wrong.
Fall on a mission and it fails: no pay, and the client remembers. Know when to pull back.
Missions give the most experience of anything you can do. A squad that takes them steadily levels up fastest.
The desk staff remember who finishes their work. Turn in a sloppy D-rank and you'll get the next one cleaning gutters.
The Mission Desk opens to you once you make Genin. Until then, it's lessons, part-time shifts and odd jobs for the neighbours.
After graduation, the Residence's ground floor will be your second home. The Mission Desk hands out work from eight till six.
Twelve hand signs: Rat, Ox, Tiger, Hare, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Ram, Monkey, Bird, Dog and Boar. Every jutsu is a sentence made of them.
Get one sign out of order and the jutsu fizzles. Nothing explodes; it just doesn't happen, and everyone sees.
Each sign takes a moment to form. Long jutsu are slow, so start weaving before you need it, not after.
Use a jutsu often enough and it becomes second nature. A mastered jutsu takes fewer signs and comes faster.
Your chakra comes back slowly on its own. Crouch low and keep perfectly still, and it fills much faster.
A soldier pill fills your chakra in a hurry. Sixty ryo each, and they taste like old boots.
Your chakra grows with every level. The Genin who seemed to have endless chakra just trained more.
Clone, Transformation and Substitution are the Academy's three. Learn the signs until your fingers do them in your sleep.
Meditating is just stillness. Sneak low, stop moving, breathe. The chakra comes back like a tide.
Mentors teach jutsu when they trust you. Train with them, prove your level, and they'll show you the next one.
Clone is Ram, Snake, Tiger. Say it out loud as you weave until your hands stop needing your mouth.
Transformation is Dog, Boar, Ram. Practise on a friend's face first; at least they'll tell you when the nose is wrong.
Three quick strikes make a chain, and the third knocks your opponent back. After it, give yourself a breath before the next.
Hold a strike a moment longer and it lands as a heavy blow. Slower to come, much harder to stop.
A dodge is a quick dash in any direction. For a heartbeat, nothing can touch you. It costs a little chakra and needs a moment to recover.
Block with an open hand and you'll take less than half of what's coming. Better bruised than broken.
Substitution is a dodge timed just as the hit lands, with enough chakra behind it. You're gone, and a log takes the blow.
Substitution only works once every twenty seconds or so. Use it, then fight like you don't have it.
Watch an enemy's shoulders before they swing. A long wind-up is your cue to dodge.
Keep a chain going and your opponent never gets the breath to answer. Stop halfway and they will.
Anyone can dodge. The trick is dodging toward the opening, not away from the fight.
An empty hand blocks better than a kunai. Hold it up, take the hit on the forearm and keep your feet.
A spar ends at thirty percent health, or when someone yields. Nobody gets hurt badly, and nobody loses anything but pride.
Sparring with a ranked resident at the training grounds is a good way to make a friend. Losing well counts too.
Fall in a real fight and you wake in the hospital the next morning. No bill, and your tiredness is gone.
A bad fall costs you a level's worth of progress. You never drop below your rank's floor, and you never lose the rank itself.
Any kunai and shuriken you were carrying when you fell are gone. Keep your best kit in a chest at home.
Fight experience falls off if you keep beating the same kind of opponent. Missions and training teach more.
Everyone who falls is brought here and revived. You'll wake in one of our beds at dawn, fatigue cleared, ready to go again.
Your levels are safe above your rank's floor. A fall costs some progress, not your headband.
Wake up here and the first thing you'll want to do is check your pouch. Thrown tools don't come back with you, I'm afraid.
The Academy workshop has a workbench anyone can use. Smoke bombs, wire and sealing tags start there.
Paper bombs open up at the workbench once you're a Genin. Until then, it's smoke and string.
Furniture can be made at a workbench from planks and cloth. It's slower than buying, and far cheaper.
Recipes come from your rank, from mentors and from scrolls. The scroll shop sells some; the smith teaches others.
The forge at the weapon shop makes kunai, shuriken, senbon and tanto from steel. Buy the steel from me or bring salvage from bandit camps.
A blade you forge yourself can be a grade better than my shop stock. That's the reward for sweating at the anvil.
Work a few shifts at my forge and I'll teach you what I know. Recipes are earned in this shop, not bought.
A small forge in your flat lets you make your own tools at home. Just warn the neighbours about the hammering.
A kunai is a weapon in the hand and a throw at range. Throw it, and you can pick it back up where it lands.
Shuriken stack in a pouch and fly fast. Genin learn to throw three at once.
A paper bomb sticks to a wall or a kunai. It hurts whoever's near and never so much as scratches a stone.
Smoke bombs blind the room. Anyone who was chasing you loses track of you, if you're quick.
Wire across a path makes a trip trap. Cheap, quiet and very embarrassing for whoever finds it.
A tool pouch lets you throw from your belt without fumbling. Every Genin should have one.
Practice kunai and shuriken are blunt and cheap. Learn on those before you spend forty ryo on good steel.
Tree walking is chakra in the soles of your feet. Too little and you slip, too much and you bounce off the bark.
Water walking is the same trick, steadier. When you want to sink and swim, just let the chakra go.
Running up a wall works for about three seconds. Pick where you're going before you start.
Charge your chakra into your legs and jump. You'll go three times as high, and you won't feel the landing while your chakra lasts.
The ninja run is faster than a sprint. Lean forward, arms back, and let your chakra carry you.
Hopping from tree to tree, or roof to roof, gives you a push forward every time. The trick is never stopping.
Every chakra movement costs a little chakra. Run out halfway across a lake and you'll get wet.
Tree walking and water walking come after graduation. Until then, the trees are for climbing the ordinary way.
The lake on the far training grounds is where everyone learns to water-walk. The cliff beside it is for wall-running.
Out of chakra mid-jump is the worst way to learn about falling. Watch your bar before you leap.
Levels are strength; ranks are trust. Getting stronger never makes you a Chunin by itself. The exam does.
Every level gives you a bit more chakra and a little more weight behind your strikes. Every sixth level brings another heart as well.
Every rank exam asks for a minimum level. Train for it, and the exam will be waiting.
Dawn's my favourite hour. The Rock goes pink, the river steams, and nobody's asked me for anything yet.
Bakers have been up for an hour already. You can smell the first loaves from here.
Out on the river, the fishermen are just pushing off. If you want the best catch, you'll be at the river bank in an hour.
About now the night guards are handing over at the gate. Tired faces going home, fresh ones coming out.
Up this early? Me too. The birds are louder than the whole market at this hour.
One by one, the lamp keepers are putting out the street lanterns. You can watch the dark fold up behind them.
I like walking the main street at dawn. Every shutter's closed, and the whole village feels like it's holding its breath.
Hear the shrine bell? That's dawn. Some people say a prayer. Most just roll over.
At this hour the training grounds belong to the early risers. Hear the thuds? Someone's been at it since dark.
Mist off the river at this hour makes the bridges look like they're floating.
Shops won't open until about seven. If you're hungry now, the bakery sells from its back door.
Most folk wake around six. If you slept before midnight, you'll feel it. Chakra comes easier all morning.
The Mission Desk opens at eight. Squads start queuing well before. Bring breakfast.
Morning already. The sun never asks if I'm ready.
Early, isn't it? Still, a good early.
Shutters are going up all down the market street. The grocer's already arguing with a customer about leeks.
Any moment now the Academy bell rings. Look at the children running. The late ones run the fastest.
Look at that line at the Mission Desk, out the door already. Every Genin squad in the Leaf wants the easy D-ranks.
Morning's when the market's freshest. The vegetables still have dew on them.
Squads are heading out through the gate. You can tell the C-rank ones by how heavy their packs are.
Every morning the tea house fills up with old folk. Same seats, same tea, same arguments as yesterday.
Washing's out on every balcony. On a sunny morning, the whole village looks like it's waving.
Forge's morning shift has started. Listen. That's three hammers, and one of them's out of time.
Mornings, the flower shop gets its deliveries, and the whole main street smells of lilies until ten.
Every morning the herbalists put their racks out by the hospital. By noon the air there smells like medicine and mint.
Shops open around seven and stay open until evening. Morning's the best time if you want first pick.
The Mission Desk is open from eight to six. The best D-ranks go early, so don't dawdle.
Academy lessons run from nine till noon on weekdays. After that, the yard's a madhouse.
A fresh morning. Anything could happen.
Good morning, properly. The day's still clean.
Noon already? The Academy's just let out. Listen to that racket. Like a flock of sparrows let out of a cage.
Ichiraku's busiest at noon. You'll wait for a stool, but the line moves quick.
Everyone eats at noon here. Look, even the guards on the wall have their lunch boxes open.
Sun's right over the Rock. No shade anywhere. The cats have all gone under the porches.
Noon is when the market gets loud. Every stall's shouting its best price before the afternoon slump.
Quietest hour at the shrine is noon. Everyone's eating. Good time to sit up there and think.
Hear the forge stop? That's the smiths at lunch. The silence is almost odd.
At noon the tea house does a cheap lunch set. Rice, soup, pickles and a fish. Best bargain in the Leaf.
Squads that left at dawn on short D-ranks start coming back about now, muddy and starving.
At noon the river's full of children cooling off. The water's cold enough to shout about.
If you slept well last night, that extra spring in your chakra's about to wear off. It lasts until noon.
Academy lessons end at noon. If you want the library quiet, go before then. After lunch it's full.
Lunch time. That's the best time.
Half the day gone. Not bad, so far.
Afternoons are for training. Hear the training grounds? Kunai thunking into posts from here to the river.
Market's slowed right down. The stallholders are fanning themselves and playing cards.
Afternoon sun makes the Rock look carved out of honey. Painters love this hour.
After lunch, everyone gets a little slow. Even the dogs.
Nobody's at the bathhouse in the afternoon. Best time to go, if you want the hot water to yourself.
Squads with long D-ranks are still out in the farms. You'll see them stagger home near dusk.
In the afternoon the kites come out. Children fly them off the bridges. Some of them even come back down.
Every afternoon the old shogi players set up their boards on the benches by the river. Nobody's allowed to watch silently.
The tea house is full of people pretending they're not napping. The owner pretends not to notice.
Afternoon is when the part-time shifts start. Ichiraku needs onion choppers, the forge needs coal haulers.
The Mission Desk is open until six. If you want a mission today, now's the time.
Shops close in the evening, so if you need supplies, don't leave it much later.
Plenty of folk take part-time jobs in the afternoon. Ask at Ichiraku, the grocer, the flower shop or the forge.
A slow afternoon. I don't mind them.
Long day yet. Plenty of time.
Lanterns are going up along the main street. Evening in the Leaf always smells of grilling fish.
Evening's when Ichiraku really comes alive. Shinobi coming off missions, families out for dinner.
One by one, the shops are shuttering. That clatter's the sound of the Leaf saying "enough work for today".
Look at the sky behind the Rock. Orange, then purple. The faces look like they're glowing.
Squads are back from the day's missions. Listen to them bragging on the bridge.
At dusk the river fills with lantern reflections. Some people sit on the banks and do nothing else.
Evening's when the barbecue house fills up. The smoke over the Akimichi roofs is a kind of dinner bell.
Mothers are calling children home all over the residential streets. Some of the names get shouted three times.
There goes the dusk bell from the shrine. Half the village stops for a breath. The other half doesn't hear it over dinner.
Cicadas start up at dusk. In summer, they're louder than the market at noon.
The Mission Desk closes at six. If you've a report to hand in, you'll have to wait for morning now.
Most shops close in the evening. Ichiraku's still open. So are the bathhouses, for an hour or two.
Festivals and events go on in the evening, but they're done by midnight. The Leaf goes to bed on time.
Evening already. Where did the day go?
Nice evening. The kind you want to keep.
How fast the village goes quiet at night. One minute the main street's full, the next it's just lanterns and cats.
At night you can see the lanterns on the wall from anywhere in the Leaf. A ring of little fires.
Every night the watch walks past my window at the same time. I've started waving. They wave back.
At night the Rock's just a shadow. You can only see the faces when the moon's out.
Bathhouse steam rises white in the dark. It's nice to walk past on a cold night.
I like the sound of the river at night. You can't hear it during the day over all the noise.
Police are out on the main street at this hour. Strict, but they'll walk you home if you ask.
So many stars over the Leaf tonight. Less light from the shops, more from the sky.
Owls are out. One's been sitting on the Academy swing all night. Thinks it's a student.
Last of the ramen customers are leaving Ichiraku now. Sleepy faces, full bellies.
Sleep before midnight and you'll wake Well Rested. Your chakra comes back quicker all morning.
If you can't sleep, a cup of green tea will keep the tiredness off for an hour. Don't make a habit of it.
Your own bed's the best place to sleep. You'll wake at six, fresh, and ready.
Getting late. Time to think about bed.
Quiet night. I like them.
Still up? The whole village is asleep. Even the dogs.
This late, it's just the night watch and the owls. And us, apparently.
I can't sleep. I've been sitting on my step listening to the wind in the training ground trees.
Main street lanterns have burned low. Some have gone out altogether.
In a few hours the bakers'll be up. That's how late it is. Nearly early.
Past midnight. The Leaf belongs to the cats now.
At this hour, even the river sounds sleepy.
I heard the night watch change on the wall a while ago. That's how I know it's very late.
Past one, and you'll start to feel it. Heavy legs, slow chakra. Bed's the only cure.
Stay up past three and you'll be stumbling. Chakra jumps go short, kunai fly wide. Get some sleep.
If you're still awake at six, you'll drop where you stand and wake at noon. Ask me how I know.
Any bed will clear your tiredness, but only your own bed before midnight leaves you Well Rested. Too late for that now.
A hot meal helps when you've been up too long. Takes the weight off your legs for an hour.
It's very late. Go to bed. I'm going to.
Late, late, late. What are we doing up?
You can see the Hokage Rock from every street in the Leaf. People say that's on purpose: nobody's ever out of sight of the faces.
Four faces on the Rock, and plenty of bare stone beside them. The carvers say they left room on purpose.
Every spring the stonemasons climb the Rock to clear the moss from the faces. They hang off ropes like spiders. Brave folk.
When the morning sun hits the Hokage Rock, the faces go gold for about a minute. Early risers stop in the street to watch.
Up on top of the Rock it's all forest. Kids say you can see the whole village from there like a map. They're right.
The Hokage Residence is the big round building right under the faces. Fire painted on the roof. You can't miss it.
Mission Desk on the ground floor, the Hokage's office at the top. Everything in between the Residence holds is paperwork.
Walking the whole wall round the Leaf takes half a morning. Guards walk it every night.
Two characters are painted on the main gate's doors, one on each. Every child learns what they mean in their first week.
Even the Hokage signs the gate guards' ledger. Everyone who comes and goes goes in that book.
Travellers coming in through the gate always stop and stare at the Rock first. You can tell the newcomers that way.
The Academy sits at the foot of the Rock. Big fire sign out front, and that old swing hanging from the tree.
That swing in front of the Academy has been there longer than most teachers. Generations of children have sat on it.
Inside the Academy there's a library, a workshop and a yard full of target posts. The posts are older than they look and very scarred.
On graduation days the Academy yard is full of parents. Spring and autumn, every year. The whole street smells of celebration rice.
Ichiraku's been serving ramen since before I was born. A few stools at a counter, and the best broth in the Leaf.
Ichiraku's counter seats only a handful. Everyone ends up elbow to elbow, Genin, Jonin and grandmothers alike.
Right through the middle of the Leaf runs the river. Most bridges are wood. The old stone one near the market is the oldest.
In summer the children jump off the low bridge into the deep pool. The adults pretend not to notice. Some join in.
Fishermen line the river at dawn. You can buy their catch right off the bank, if you're quick.
From the main street to the river, the market street sells fish, vegetables, tea, weapons. Everything on one long walk.
Market Day comes once a week. Farmers bring their carts in through the gate at dawn. It's the busiest morning of the week.
The hospital's the tall white building near the herb gardens. Medics and nurses work day and night there.
If you collapse or get hurt on a mission, you'll wake up in the hospital. The beds are hard but the nurses are kind.
Mint and something bitter: that's the smell of the Suzuran drying racks in the gardens by the hospital.
The shrine's up the long stone steps. People go there at New Year, for weddings, and when they need to think.
At dawn and dusk the shrine bell rings. If you hear it, you know the time without looking at the sun.
Twenty-five clans live in the Leaf, from the great compounds to the small trade families. Most folk belong to none.
The Senju compound is beside the Residence. Their hall is grown around a living tree. Leaves come through the roof in spring.
Next to the Senju stands the Uzumaki memorial shrine. The spiral crest is carved on every lantern there.
Close to the centre is the Hyuga estate. Two halves, a dojo and a koi pond people say is older than the wall.
Out at the edge of the village, by their deer forest, live the Nara. The deer wander out sometimes and eat people's flowers.
The Akimichi compound is by the market street. Their kitchen hall smokes from dawn till night. The barbecue house is theirs too.
Every wedding and every funeral in the Leaf has flowers from the Yamanaka shop on the main street.
You'll hear the Inuzuka ninken before you see them. Their kennels and the vet clinic are right by the main gate.
The Uchiha compound is on the outskirts, walled, with their fan crest on every wall. The police headquarters is theirs.
At the wooded edge of a residential street sits the Aburame clan home. Their garden hums. Not unpleasantly.
Near the Residence there's the Sarutobi house, with a monkey crest over the door and a yard for fire training.
On the old artists' lane live the Kurama. Their walls are painted inside and out. Some of the paintings look back at you.
The Gekko keep a sword dojo by the training grounds with a platform for watching the moon. Very quiet place.
Minor clans live among everyone else. The Hagane forge on the market street, the Kinoshita in the carpenters' lane.
Half the teachers in the Leaf are related to the other half. Most are Umino, living in the streets near the Academy.
Every sensei has a story about Ground 3. Three stumps in a row, a river nearby. The training grounds are all numbered.
Outside the wall there's a fenced forest with forty-four gates. Training Ground 44. The trees there are as wide as houses.
When the stadium's full for the Chunin Exam finals, you can hear the crowd from the market.
Nearly every big street has a bathhouse. The oldest has a painted mountain on the wall behind the water.
Six generations of one family have run the tea house by the bridge. The cups are older than the furniture.
On festival nights the barbecue house is full to the door. You order by the plate, and they never stop coming.
Every season the flower shop changes its window. People walk past just to see what's in it.
Blank scrolls, ink, sealing paper: the scroll shop's owner can tell how many sheets you need just by looking at you.
People go into the furniture shop just to sit on the chairs. Every piece they make is in the showroom.
Out back of the weapon shop is the forge. You can hear the hammers from the market street all day.
Onigiri wrapped and ready by the grocer's door every morning. Shinobi grab them on the way out.
Old armour, odd swords, other villages' coins: the pawn shop on the corner takes anything. Pays half, never more.
Pink, white and green. People argue about the right order to eat the dango from the shop by the river.
Round water tanks sit on the Leaf's roofs. On hot days, kids climb up and dip their feet in them. Not allowed. Very common.
Most of the Leaf's homes are plaster, in cream and terracotta. When the sun's low, the whole village looks warm.
Lanterns hang along the main street. The lamp keepers light them at dusk and put them out at dawn.
You can follow your nose from the main gate to the carpenters' lane. Fresh cedar, always.
The Uchiha police walk the main street at night. They're strict, but they'll walk you home if you're lost.
Shinobi apartment blocks are stacked and plain. Nobody needs fancy rooms when half the tenants are never home.
Our water comes from springs up behind the Rock. That's why it's so cold and sweet.
There's a memorial stone at one of the training grounds. People leave flowers and stand there quietly. You'll see it.
All the main streets point at the faces, like spokes of a wheel. The founders built the Leaf in a fan around the Rock.
Shinobi in the Leaf travel by rooftop as often as by street. The tiles on the market street get replaced every year because of it.
Every shinobi in the Leaf wears the headband somewhere. Forehead, arm, belt. The way you wear it says something about you.
Village rule: no fighting in the streets. Disputes go to the training grounds or the police. That's been the law since the founding.
Jutsu aren't allowed in the market. A fire jutsu near paper lanterns? You can imagine the trouble.
Roof-running is allowed, but not on the shrine or the Residence. People who forget get a visit from the police.
In the Leaf, you take your sandals off before stepping onto someone's tatami. Even in a hurry. Even on a mission.
It's custom to bow to the Hokage Rock when you come back from far away. Some do it, some just look up and smile.
You don't whistle at night near the shrine. Old superstition. Most people still won't do it.
When someone new moves onto a street, the neighbours bring rice. It's how you say welcome in the Leaf.
When a squad leaves on a long mission, families tie a strip of cloth to the gate post. It comes down when they're home.
In the Leaf you never pour your own tea when someone else is at the table. You pour theirs, and they pour yours.
No curfew for grown folk here, but the shops close by evening and the streets get quiet fast.
Everyone stops working when the shrine bell rings at New Year. Even the forge goes silent.
Clans of every kind live side by side here. The Inuzuka's dogs sleep on the Hyuga steps. Nobody minds. Mostly.
In the Leaf, the Hokage's name is on every mission scroll. It's a reminder that each job is for the whole village.
Farmers, traders, orphans: the Leaf takes in people from everywhere. If you live here, you're Leaf.
There's an old saying here: "the leaves grow from one tree". It means we all share the same roots.
A bowl of ramen at Ichiraku runs about eight ryo. More if you want extra pork. Worth every coin.
Onigiri from the grocer cost three ryo. A cup of tea's about five. Cheapest meal in the village.
Kunai at the weapon shop run five to forty ryo, depending on the steel. Shuriken are cheaper. Smoke bombs are a fortune.
Soldier pills cost sixty ryo each. Most shinobi carry one and pray they never need it.
Furniture's dear. A good table costs more than a month of ramen. People save for years for a proper chest of drawers.
Festival games cost a ryo or two. The prizes are mostly paper fans and bags of sweets. People play anyway.
A new outfit from the tailor costs a few hundred ryo. Most people wear the same three until they fall apart.
Dango's two ryo a skewer at the stand by the river. Three if you want the sweet sauce.
Prices go up before festivals. The grocer says it's demand. Everyone else says it's the grocer.
Two ryo for the bathhouse, or one if you bring your own towel. Children go free with a parent.
Rice is cheapest in autumn after the harvest. In late winter, everybody's counting grains.
A part-time shift at Ichiraku or the grocer pays forty to eighty ryo. Not bad for a few hours of chopping onions.
A single stem at the flower shop is a ryo, a whole bouquet ten. Lots of people buy one stem every week.
Steel for a smith costs a few ryo a bar. Good steel costs more. Cheap steel costs more in the end.
The Mission Desk is on the Residence's ground floor. Eight in the morning till six in the evening.
Ichiraku's on the main street. Follow your nose. If you smell pork broth, you're there.
Near the herb gardens, white walls, big doors: that's the hospital. You'll see medics going in and out.
Up the long stone steps at the end of the lane is the shrine. Count the steps if you like. Nobody agrees on the number.
Want to see the whole village? Climb the stairs to the top of the Hokage Rock. The view's worth the legs.
Off the main street, running down to the river, is the market street. You can buy nearly anything there.
Anyone can walk round the furniture shop's showroom. You can see every piece they sell before you buy.
Want a ninken pup? Ask at the Inuzuka clinic by the main gate.
Anyone can read in the Academy library, but keep quiet. The librarian is very fast.
Look for the smoke and listen for the hammers. That's the weapon shop and forge, on the market street.
Blue curtains, by the bridge: the tea house. Best place to sit and watch the river.
Next to the Akimichi compound is the barbecue house. Go hungry. Leave happy.
On the corner of the market street is the pawn shop. Bring things you don't need. Leave with ryo.
Training grounds are past the edge of the houses. Ground 3 is the one with the three stumps.
Sealing paper? Try the scroll shop on the market street, near the forge.
Look for the red umbrella by the second bridge. That's the dango stand.
The flower shop is on the main street, at the front of the Yamanaka compound. Can't miss the colours.
For hot water and a lot of chatter, go to the oldest bathhouse, the one with the mountain painting.
At the end of the main street is the main gate. That's where the squads leave and the travellers come in.
Look for the swing in front and the big fire sign. That's the Academy, at the foot of the Rock.
Every festival has a committee of shopkeepers who argue for a month and then make it perfect in one night.
The shrine keeps a great drum that's only played at New Year and weddings. You feel it in your chest from the market.
Visiting teams for the Chunin Exams lodge at the inns near the gate. The innkeepers learn a dozen new accents a season.
New Genin always buy their first proper kunai pouch the week after graduation. The weapon shop does a roaring trade.
On festival nights the bridges are closed to carts. Too many people, too many lanterns, and far too much dancing.
Festival stall spots are handed out by the market council. Families keep the same spot for generations and guard it fiercely.
The fireworks for every festival are made by one family outside the wall. Nobody's allowed to watch them work.
Each clan has its own clan day. The Akimichi feast is the one everyone hopes to be invited to.
Weddings at the shrine are open to the whole street. You don't need to know the couple to throw rice.
Market Day turns into a kind of fair when the weather's good. Music, jugglers, and the fishmongers' shouting contest.
Someone's been leaving paper cranes on the Academy swing every morning. Nobody knows who. It's been weeks now.
The second bridge has a loose plank that's been loose for a month. Someone's going to go through it into the river.
There's a stray dog by the main gate that follows anyone with food. The guards have been feeding it. It's getting very round.
Half the lanterns on the market street haven't been lit in days. The lamp keeper fell ill. It's dark down there at night.
The notice board by the Residence is overflowing. Lost pets, sales, someone wanting a cart pushed. Anyone could help.
Anyone who can carry trays without spilling is wanted at the tea house for the festival. They're short a pair of hands.
A family's moving house on the residential street and they've far more boxes than arms. They're asking around for help.
After the storm, the shrine steps need sweeping. The priest is getting on and can't manage it all.
The flower shop's lost a delivery crate somewhere between the gate and the main street. Full of lilies. They're wilting fast.
There's something nesting in the water tank on the apartment block roof. The tenants are hearing scratching at night.
A merchant at the market lost a purse full of foreign coins. Says it'll pay a good reward if it's returned. No questions asked.
Kids say there's a frog as big as a cat in the Academy pond. The teachers are pretending not to hear about it.
Somebody keeps knocking the stones off the shrine's lantern posts. The priest is quietly furious about it.
The Nara deer got into the market again and ate a whole stall of cabbages. The grocer wants someone to walk them back.
The bathhouse boiler's been making a noise like a dying goose. If it breaks before festival week, half the village goes unwashed.
The farm road outside the gate washed out in the last rain. The farmers' carts are getting stuck. They need a few strong backs.
Everyone's turning up late for everything. The old clock by the market's stopped again. Someone should tell the clockmaker.
The swing at the Academy needs a new rope. It's fraying. Someone's going to have a very short flight.
A ninken pup's gone missing from the Inuzuka kennels. It's small and brown and likes to chew sandals.
Overdue scrolls are piling up at the library. The librarian's started writing the borrowers' names on a board.
A good place to live, the Leaf. Busy, noisy, a little nosy. Home.
Nice to walk around the village on a day like this.
Every street in the Leaf has something going on. That's what I like about it.
Half the steps in the Leaf were cut by the Tsuchigumo families. They live in stone houses by the quarry.
The Shiranui house near the gate barracks has a wall bristling with senbon. Target practice, decades of it.
Near the training grounds the Namiashi run a little footwork dojo. You can hear the tapping from the street, like rain.
The Haruno family's garden on the residential street is the neatest in the Leaf. Not a weed dares.
In a grove of old trees sits the Yuhi house. People say the paths there are never quite where you left them.
On a quiet lane is the Hatake house, a lone old place with a small yard. Most people walk past without noticing it.
The Tobari live behind the wall in shuttered houses. Their lane is the quietest place in the village. Even footsteps go soft.
Barred windows on the Morino house near the police headquarters. The family's perfectly polite. The house just looks grim.
Look under your table. Most of the furniture in the Leaf was made in the Kinoshita yard, and their mark's there.
Every hinge in the Leaf still swings thanks to the Hagane metalworkers. Their shop's beside the forge.
On harvest day the Akimichi feed anyone who helps carry the rice sacks into their storehouse. The line is very long.
Feed the Nara deer if you like, but you can't chase them. They're protected. They know it, too. Bold creatures.
The Inuzuka ninken have the run of the gate district. If a big dog sits in your path, you wait. That's just manners.
For a ryo, the ferryman at the wide bend takes you across. There's a bridge further down, but the ferry's more fun.
Each district has a well with a little roof over it. People meet at the wells in the morning. That's where news starts.
Letters to the farms and the border villages go from the courier office near the Residence. Couriers run the roads every day.
The Leaf's oldest residents sit on the benches by the main street every afternoon and rate everyone's walk. Be warned.
At night the lanterns on the wall's watchtowers look like a ring of stars around the village.
There's a sound the Leaf makes at dusk: shutters closing, pots on stoves, dogs being called home. You'll learn it.
No two bridges over the river are quite alike. The Kinoshita built the newest, the founders built the oldest.
Each stone lantern along the shrine path was donated by a family. Their crests are carved on the bases.
The Leaf has gardens tucked everywhere: on roofs, in alleys, on balconies. If there's sun, somebody's growing something.
Most houses in the Leaf keep a lantern by the door. It's lit when someone's out late, so they can find their way home.
Before dawn the bakery on the main street opens. The smell reaches the gate. The night guards call it their alarm.
Behind the market street there's a maze of alleys with tiny workshops: lacquer, paper, combs, kites. Worth getting lost in.
For hard winters there's a village storehouse, run by the Akimichi and the council. Rice for everyone, if the snow comes.
Every year on the founding day, the oldest residents tell stories in the square. The stories get bigger every year.
There's a little island in the river with one pine and a great many ducks. Children swim out to it every summer.
Herons stand by the fishmongers' stalls by the river like customers. The fishmongers throw them scraps.
Each of the big compounds has a gate with its crest. Strangers aren't to go in uninvited, but most clans are friendly.
Need a letter taken to the farms? The courier office is near the Residence.
Ring the bell on the post at the wide bend of the river and the ferryman comes.
Past the stone houses at the edge of the village is the quarry. Mind the carts. They don't stop quickly.
If you need furniture mended, ask in the Kinoshita yard. Carpenters' lane, off the market street.
The herb gardens are next to the hospital. The Suzuran will sell you a bundle of medicine herbs if you ask nicely.
Requests go up on the notice board outside the Residence every morning. Some pay. Some just say thank you.
Lost something important? The police keep a lost-and-found at their headquarters, in a corner of the Uchiha compound.
You'll know the Gekko dojo by the moon-viewing platform on its roof. It's by the training grounds.
Stand by a well for ten minutes in the morning and you'll know everything. That's where the gossip happens.
Walk the Kurama lane in the evening when the light's golden. It's the one with paintings on the walls.
The ferry bell's gone missing from its post. The ferryman's been shouting across the river all week. Voice is nearly gone.
Someone's been drawing chalk faces on the bridge railings. Funny faces. The builders don't find them funny.
Muddy water's coming up from the well on the residential street. Someone should tell the builders before it gets worse.
There's a crate of festival lanterns sitting in the rain behind the shrine. Somebody forgot them. They'll be ruined soon.
The herons at the fish stalls have started stealing straight off the counters. The fishmongers want a scarecrow, or a hero.
A cart lost a wheel on the main street this morning. The owner's been sitting next to it all day looking for help.
A kite from the workshop in the alleys is stuck on the Residence roof. Nobody wants to be the one to fetch it.
Anyone with fast legs is wanted at the courier office. They're behind on letters to the farms.
Something's been digging up the flower beds by the Yamanaka shop at night. The Yamanaka suspect the Nara deer. The Nara deny it.
The founding-day storyteller lost the old picture scroll they use every year. Without it, the story falls apart.
Toppled in the storm: the stone lantern by the shrine path. It's too heavy for the priest to set right.
The fisherfolk keep finding someone's sandals in their nets. Same sandals, always one at a time. Someone upstream is very careless.
Rain like this and the Ichiraku queue doubles. Everybody wants something hot, and nobody wants to cook it.
The gutters on the market street can't take more than an hour of this. By noon the fish stall will be selling from a puddle.
The training grounds turn to porridge in the rain. Good for practising your footing, terrible for your sandals.
The stone steps up to the shrine get slick as river rocks. Take the handrail, whatever your pride says.
The frogs in the Academy pond are singing like they've been paid. You can hear them from the main street.
Rain on the Hokage Rock runs down the faces in streaks. The children say the Hokage are crying, and the grown-ups say they're washing.
The bath house will be full by four today. Wet people want warm water; it's simple arithmetic.
Every paper umbrella in the Leaf is open at once. From the Rock, the main street must look like a row of mushrooms.
The river's up to the second step at the ferry landing. Another day of this and the ferryman will be poling over the washing stones.
Laundry day ruined again. Every balcony on this street has the same sad row of damp shirts.
The drying racks behind the fish stall are all under tarps. Rain is bad news for anyone selling dried mackerel.
A good soaking rain is what the farmers outside the wall have been praying for. The cabbages will be the size of heads.
Rain makes the dogs at the kennels sulk. Forty damp ninken, all piled together and smelling exactly like you'd expect.
The roofs are too slippery for jumping today. You'll see a lot of shinobi walking the streets like ordinary people.
Mission scrolls go out in oiled pouches on days like this. A wet briefing is no briefing at all.
The tea houses close their garden doors in the rain and light the braziers. The best seats are by the window, watching it come down.
The water tanks on the roofs are filling nicely. That's a warm bath for the whole block for a week.
My sandals squeak in this weather. I can't sneak up on anyone, which my family is very grateful for.
The Academy moved yard practice into the hall today. Thirty children throwing practice shuriken indoors: the janitor is not happy.
Rain stops the market haggling dead. Nobody wants to stand in it arguing over two ryo; the prices fall all morning.
I like the rain, honestly. The village goes quiet and soft, like somebody turned the noise down.
I left my umbrella at the tea house again. That's three this month. The owner's started a collection.
Rain makes my old knee ache. That's how I know it's coming before the clouds do.
I always mean to stay home on rainy days, and I always end up out in it. Something about puddles.
Race you to the end of the street without an umbrella! Loser buys the hot tea.
Puddles this deep are basically a training exercise. Jump them all and you've done your footwork for the day!
Are you dry enough? Stand under the awning a minute. A cold now and you'll be sniffling all week.
The stray cats have all found doorways to sit in. I put out a dish under the eaves for them.
Rain means indoor work: mending, inventory, sharpening. I've had my whole list ready since yesterday's clouds.
Rain or no rain, the Mission Desk opens at eight. A D-rank doesn't care that you're wet.
This rain is worth a hundred ryo a day to the fields. I'd dance in it, if my knees would let me.
Wet days, the river carries mud down from the hills. The fish go deep and sulk, and so does my trade.
Rain is good for business. A bowl of something hot never sells better than when the street's a river.
I put an extra pot on this morning. The clouds were too grey to waste.
Tracking's useless in this. Every scent washed off and every footprint a puddle. Ask any Inuzuka how they feel about it.
Rain hides sound well. Good for scouting, terrible for hearing who's scouting you.
Paper bombs and wet days don't mix. Keep your tags wrapped, or you'll be throwing very expensive confetti.
Spring rain knocks the cherry blossoms off in a single night. Tomorrow every street will be pink and soggy.
Summer rain is warm enough to stand in. The children are out in it already, catching it in their mouths.
Autumn rain strips the maples. By tomorrow the training grounds will be a red carpet with mud underneath.
Every dog in the Inuzuka kennels is under a blanket right now. Even the war-trained ones hate thunder.
The Mission Desk sometimes holds outgoing squads in weather like this. Lightning picks the tallest thing on a ridge, and that's usually a Genin.
The tea houses shutter their windows at the first crack. Nobody wants to drop a cup when the sky bangs.
That one rattled the bowls on the shelf. My grandmother says it's the sky clapping for somebody.
The shrine keeps a lightning rod on the cedar. The tree has been hit three times in a hundred years, and it's still standing.
Thunder echoes off the Hokage Rock like a drum. It sounds twice as loud by the Residence.
Storms like this blow the lanterns off the market street. The stallholders will be picking paper out of the gutters tomorrow.
The bath house never closes for a storm. The keeper says no lightning has ever got through all that steam.
Thunder at night and the whole apartment block wakes. You can hear every flat's kettle go on at once.
The river turns brown and fast in a storm. The ferry's tied up and the ferryman is sitting under the landing roof, glaring at the sky.
Children at the Academy count between the flash and the bang. The instructors pretend it's an arithmetic lesson.
The farmers will be out with tarps over the seed beds the moment this passes. One big storm can flatten a month of growing.
Lightning lit the whole village white for a moment just then. I could see every roof tile down to the wall.
The gate guards bring the booth's kettle inside in a storm. Someone learned that the hard way.
The roof-runners are all on the ground today. Running across tiles in a thunderstorm is how you meet the hospital staff.
A storm this size usually clears overnight. Tomorrow will be rinsed clean and smell like cut grass.
The Tobari night watch calls a storm a blind night. You can't hear anything on the wall, so you have to watch twice as hard.
That was close. The air smells like a forge right after a strike, burnt and sharp.
Thunderstorms send the herons up off the river in a cloud. They'll be back on their stones by morning, as if nothing happened.
My cat is under the bed and won't come out until the sky apologises.
I love a good storm. I sit on the porch with the shutters half open and count the strikes. Twenty-three last time.
I'm not scared of thunder. I just happen to be standing very close to this doorway, that's all.
When I was small, my father told me thunder was the Hokage moving furniture upstairs. I believed him for years.
Storms make me restless. I'd rather be out in it doing something than inside listening to it.
Is it... is it getting closer? I'll just stay under this roof a bit longer, if that's all right.
The baby birds under the eaves are all huddled up. I hope the nest holds.
Listen to that sky! That's what a lightning jutsu ought to sound like.
Storms are the best time to train your nerve. Anyone can concentrate when it's quiet!
Stay off the roofs and away from the training ground trees. I won't say it twice.
Go home if you've nowhere you need to be. There's nothing out here worth a lightning strike.
A lightning-natured shinobi feels a storm in their teeth. I know three who can't sleep through one.
Thunder covers footsteps. On a mission, a storm is a friend for about an hour, and then it's an enemy.
Missions don't stop for weather, but smart squads do. Shelter, wait it out and move when it passes.
Damp in the air and my glue won't set. Today's a day for sharpening, not building.
A storm's no time for the forge. Lightning likes metal, and I like having eyebrows.
Every pup in the clinic is pressed against my legs. I've been standing in the same spot for an hour.
Summer storms come up over the hills in the afternoon and blow out by supper. Like a bad temper.
Storms between seasons are the worst. Warm wind, cold rain and thunder that can't make up its mind.
The Hokage faces have snowy eyebrows this morning. The second one looks like a very stern grandparent.
Snow on the training grounds means footprints for everyone to read. A sneaking exercise in this is a lesson in humility.
The bath house will be packed by sunset. In this weather, a hot soak is worth more than ryo.
The market street shovels a path down the middle at dawn. By noon it's packed ice, and somebody's always sliding.
Every roof in the Leaf has a white cap. The round water tanks look like giant rice cakes.
The Akimichi kitchen hall has a pot of hot soup going all day when it snows. Their doors are open to anyone cold.
Snow muffles the whole village. Even the kennels are quiet, and that never happens.
The children have built a snow Hokage outside the Academy. It looks nothing like any of them and it's perfect.
The river's freezing at the edges. The ferryman says another cold week and you'll be able to walk across without chakra.
The shrine priest knits caps for the fox statues when it snows. They've all got new ones on today.
The gate guards drink their tea standing in a snowfall. They say sitting makes your bottom freeze to the bench.
Fresh snow at dawn is the best time to see who's been out at night. Every alley has its own story in footprints.
The tea house has put out its winter cushions, thick and heavy. You sink into them like a bowl of rice.
Snow makes the main street look twice as wide. All those dark roofs turned to white, and the lanterns glowing through it.
The deer in the Nara forest come right up to the house when it snows. The clan feeds them on the porch.
Grocers sell more sweet potatoes on a snowy day than in a month of sun. There's a man with a roasting cart on every corner.
The ice on the Academy pond is thick enough to skate on. The instructors have forbidden it, which means everyone is skating on it.
Wet snow sticks to the training dummies. They look like snowmen in sparring stances.
The Uchiha police walk their rounds in black coats in the snow. You can see them from the Rock, dark spots moving along every street.
A snowy village sounds like a held breath. Even the shinobi landing on rooftops make a soft little thump.
I've never been able to resist the first footprint in fresh snow. It's like signing your name on the day.
Snow makes me want to stay home under the kotatsu with a book and a bowl of oranges. I'm fighting it.
I grew up in a village where it never snowed. My first winter here, I thought the sky was falling.
I'm terrible on ice. Two winters ago I slid the length of the market street on my back. Nobody let me forget it.
Snowball war at the Academy yard, this afternoon! Clan against clan, and the clanless get to pick sides.
Bet you can't walk up that drift without sinking. Chakra or no chakra!
You're not dressed for this. Wrap a scarf round your face at least; your nose is going red.
Make sure you've got something hot for dinner tonight. Cold days creep into your bones if you skip a meal.
Snow makes the village look like a painting someone hasn't finished. All the colours waiting under the white.
Every snowflake is different, they say. I wonder who checked.
Snow hides sound and shows tracks. A squad that walks in single file and steps in the same prints is a squad that knows its trade.
Cold slows chakra in the hands. Warm your fingers before you weave signs, or you'll fumble the Tiger.
Water-walking on a half-frozen lake is a lesson you only need once. Ask me how I know.
Carts can't get through the east road in this. Everything in the market today is whatever was already in the village.
Deliveries take twice as long in the snow. I've had to swap my sandals for straw boots, and they're terrible for running.
Snow days are my best days. The steam off my counter brings people in from all the way down the street.
Deep winter now. The shops open late and close early, and everyone carries a little charcoal warmer in their sleeve.
Snow this early? The farmers will be rushing to get the last of the radishes in before the ground freezes.
This heat would melt a kunai. The children have taken over the river shallows and the dogs have taken over every shadow.
Ichiraku sells cold noodles on days like this, and the queue still goes round the corner.
The cicadas are so loud by the training grounds you can't hear yourself throw. Everyone's chakra feels like it's boiling.
The bath house keeper says nobody comes on a day this hot. Then the cold box of milk sells out by noon.
The stone of the Hokage Rock holds the heat until midnight. Sit against it after dark and it's like a warm stove.
The tea houses are serving barley tea over ice. It's the only thing anyone wants in this weather.
Shinobi in full gear on a day like this are made of sweat and determination. Mostly sweat.
Not a cloud from the Rock to the wall. You can see all four faces sharp as if they were carved this morning.
That's a perfect sky. The kind of blue you only get after a week of rain.
Wind's up from the east today. All the laundry on the residential streets is trying to fly away.
The wind's strong enough today that the Academy cancelled shuriken practice. Half of yesterday's throws ended up on the main street.
Sky this clear and the hawks from the Residence loft are flying high. You can see them circling over the Rock.
On a day this clear you can see the far hills past the wall, blue in the distance, like a painting of somewhere else.
Clear night ahead. If you stay up, the stars over the training grounds are better than any festival.
Bright sun on yesterday's snow. Everyone's squinting and the icicles are dripping from every roof.
A clear winter morning is the coldest kind. Frost on every railing and your breath hanging in front of you like a cloud.
Clear autumn air and the maples on the Rock look like they're on fire. Best week of the year to climb the stairs.
Crisp and windy. The kites are out over the Academy yard, and three of them are already stuck in the big tree.
Clear spring day and a warm wind. The cherry petals are blowing down the main street like pink snow.
The awnings on this street are flapping like sails. Half the stallholders have given up and gone to the tea house.
Every shop on the street has pulled its shutters halfway down. You can still buy things, you just have to duck.
The target posts are wearing snow hats. Hit one and it drops the whole lot on your head; the Genin call it the second lesson.
The yard's under a foot of snow, so practice today is clearing it. The instructor calls that taijutsu.
The moon's so bright tonight you could read a mission scroll by it. The Gekko will be up on their platform.
My family always makes red bean rice on birthdays. It's not a birthday without it.
I went up to the Hokage Rock at dawn to start my birthday with the view. A little tradition of mine.
I don't need presents. Well. A small one wouldn't hurt.
Every birthday I visit the shrine and thank the year for being kind to me.
My friends are taking me for barbecue tonight. I've been hungry since breakfast thinking about it.
On my birthday I always buy myself one thing I don't need. This year it's a little paper lantern.
Birthdays make me think back. A year ago today I'd never have guessed where I'd be now.
My neighbour left a bundle of dango on my doorstep this morning. The whole street knows, apparently.
I baked buns for everyone I'll see today. It's my birthday, so I get to give the presents.
I've planned the whole day: tea at ten, a walk at noon, supper at six. Don't let me be late.
For my birthday, I'm going to walk somewhere in the village I've never been. There must be a lane left.
I'm having a party! There'll be games and sweets and my cousin's going to juggle.
I made a wish on my candle. I can't tell you, or it won't happen. It's about a dog.
The visiting teams stay in the guest lodging by the stadium. Lights on all night over there.
Every tea house has a betting board up. Half the village has a few ryo on some team or other.
I put five ryo on a team from a village I'd never heard of. Don't ask me why, I liked their hats.
The stadium seats sell out for the finals the same day they go on sale.
The bakers make special exam buns. Sweet bean inside, a little headband drawn in sesame on top.
Merchants follow the visiting teams. There are stalls in the market street I've never seen before.
The guards at the gate are checking travel papers twice over this week.
The noise from the stadium on finals day carries all the way to the river.
The visitors stare at the Hokage Rock like they've never seen a carved mountain before. They haven't.
Exam weeks are good for business and bad for sleep. My inn hasn't had a quiet night since the fourteenth.
Some of the visiting shinobi bought out the whole dango stall. Twice.
The written test is on the first day, they say. After that, nobody outside knows much until the finals.
The betting boards are for fun. Lose a few ryo, not your rent.
The finals are open to anyone with a seat. The stalls outside sell cushions, bring one.
I keep a ledger of every team's odds. Not to bet. Just to see who's right.
Exam weeks, the grocer orders triple. Visitors eat like they've never seen a vegetable.
Every visiting team wears its headbands differently. One ties them round the arm, another round the waist.
I wonder what the visitors think of us. Our food, our streets, our stone faces.
I remember my first exam. My hands shook so hard I could barely hold the pencil.
Every young shinobi in the Leaf is watching the visitors and sizing them up. Me included.
I don't follow the matches, I just like the crowds. The whole village feels bigger for a week.
I'm going to be in the Chunin Exams one day. I'll win it in a single day.
My dad put a ryo on a team for me. If they win, I get two ryo!
We sneaked to the stadium wall to listen. You can hear the crowd roar from outside.
I've sold more in exam week than in the whole season before it. My feet are begging for the finals.
Some of the visiting Genin look so young. I gave a few of them rice balls. They're far from home.
I've got two ryo on the team with the loudest captain. If they're loud, they're winning. That's my system.
The stadium's been swept top to bottom for the finals. Even the seat cushions have been beaten.
Every clan has a day of its own, spread through the year so no two fall in the same week.
Clan days are when the clans open their gates. Even civilians get a peek inside.
The minor clans share a day of their own, out in the neighbourhoods. Tables in the street, everyone's invited.
On a clan day, the clan's elders sit in the gateway and greet everyone who passes.
The {clan} clan's day is a good one to visit. They feed anyone who turns up polite.
I keep a list of the clan days on my wall. My calendar is nothing but feasts and ceremonies.
I'm not from any clan, but I go to every clan day. It's like visiting a different village for an afternoon.
The harvest feast runs from noon until the last pot is scraped. Some years that's midnight.
On feast day the Akimichi kitchen cooks for the whole village. We set out more bowls than we have family.
Every family brings one dish to the harvest feast. My grandmother's pickled radish is the first thing gone.
We say a thank you to the fields before we eat. Then we eat a lot.
On pairing day, our children meet their first pups. The pup chooses, never the child.
The kennels are scrubbed for a week before pairing day. You could eat off the floor. Don't.
My partner chose me on pairing day when we were both tiny. We've not been apart a day since.
Pairing day ends with a run round the outer fields, every child and every pup together.
Once a year we count the deer in the clan forest. Every fawn gets a name in the book.
The deer count is slow. You sit, you wait, they come to you. Rushing only scares them off.
We bring the deer a little rice cake on count day. They know the date better than we do.
The antlers the stags shed are gathered on count day, for the clan's medicine work.
For the flower festival we fill the main street with pots from the greenhouse. It takes all night.
Every guest at the flower festival leaves with one stem. We choose it for them by how they look.
The greenhouse opens to the public only once a year, on our festival day.
My first arrangement was in the flower festival when I was six. Lopsided. My father kept it anyway.
The Military Police parade from the compound to the Residence once a year. The children line the street.
The parade is mostly marching, then the captains bow to the Hokage. It's very solemn, then we eat.
Every officer polishes the fan crest on their jacket the night before. We inspect each other.
The parade goes past the market, and the stallkeepers throw paper flowers. It's a nice custom.
On insect night the fireflies rise over our gardens. Thousands. We have tended them for a year.
Guests are asked not to carry lanterns on insect night. The fireflies give all the light anyone needs.
Children always try to catch the fireflies. We let them, gently, then they let them go.
Insect night is very quiet. Perhaps that is why so few come. Those who come, come back.
Our grove is the oldest stand of trees in the village. On viewing day, people sit under them and say nothing.
We sweep the grove paths at dawn and lay mats under the blossoms. Bring tea, if you come.
The grove looks different every hour of viewing day. At dusk, everyone stays to watch the light change.
The duels are fought on the moon-viewing platform, by moonlight only. No lanterns.
A moon duel ends at the first touch. It's about grace, not winning. Though winning is nice.
Guests sit on the slope below the dojo and watch. The swords flash silver in the moonlight.
We drink one cup of tea to the moon before the first duel. Then the dojo goes silent.
We walk from our house to the Hokage Rock with lit lanterns. Anyone can join behind us.
The lantern walk is about passing the flame along. Each lantern is lit from the one before it.
By the time the walk reaches the Rock, there are hundreds of lanterns. You can see them from the wall.
At the founders' memorial we lay a branch from the living tree on the shrine altar.
The memorial is short. A few words, a bow, and the whole village remembers who built it.
At the memorial we read the names aloud, every one. It takes a long time. Nobody minds.
We stand beside the Senju at the memorial. Old allies, old friends. That has never changed.
Our studio opens for the exhibition today. Every painting on the walls was finished this year.
Visitors always ask how long a painting takes. The honest answer is: longer than you think.
On our shared day the minor clans set tables down the neighbourhood streets. Anyone can sit anywhere.
Each family brings out its trade on the shared day. Herbs, carpentry, metalwork. It's half fair, half feast.
On the shared day we open the forge doors and let children try a hammer on cold iron. Gently.
For the shared day our yard builds one new bench for the street. We've done it so long the street is all benches.
On the shared day we give away little bags of dried herbs. For sleep, for colds, for tea.
On the shared day the teachers' houses on the Academy streets open their doors for anyone with questions.
Every exam week, the parents line up outside the Academy gate. As if they're the ones being tested.
The teachers set the target posts out in the yard for the throwing test. Same posts as thirty years ago.
The Academy library stays open late during exam week. The librarian brings tea for the stragglers.
The written test is the one everyone fears. The clone test is the one everyone fails.
Ichiraku gives a free egg to any Academy student during exam week. Bless that stand.
You can hear the students reciting hand signs through the Academy windows.
Sleep before midnight in exam week. Waking well rested gives you more chakra for the morning.
A full stomach and a good night's sleep do more for a test than another hour of reading.
I make onigiri for every child on my street during exam week. Somebody has to.
Exam week always makes me nervous for the little ones, even though it's not my exam.
I passed by reviewing every hand sign every morning for a month. There's no trick but repetition.
I wrote all the hand signs on my arm. Then I washed my arm. So that's gone.
My big sister says the clone test is easy if you don't think about it. How do you not think about it?
I studied so much I dreamed in hand signs. Tiger, boar, ox, dog...
If I pass, I'm getting the large bowl at Ichiraku. With two eggs.
The Hokage comes to the yard and every new Genin is called by name. It takes all morning.
The families sit on benches along the yard wall. The front row is fought over like a market stall.
After the ceremony, the new Genin all go for ramen. Ichiraku's queue goes round the corner.
The headbands are blessed at the shrine the night before. That's an old Leaf custom.
I still have my headband from my own graduation. The cloth's faded, but the plate still shines.
The teachers pretend not to cry. They do every time.
The Academy holds graduation twice a year, spring and autumn. Two chances, for those who need a second.
A photographer sets up by the gate. Every family wants a picture with a new headband in it.
The new Genin are put into squads right after. That's when the real nerves start.
There's always one who trips on the steps. Nobody forgets it, nobody minds.
I made a basket of sweet buns for the new Genin. They're so nervous, they forget to eat.
I always cry at graduation, even when I don't know anybody. All those proud faces.
A headband is a beginning. The hard part starts tomorrow.
In my day, the exam was harder. Still, they look a capable lot.
I threw my headband in the air at my graduation and it landed on the roof. True story.
Listen to them cheer! I want to run down there and cheer too.
My sensei found me at my graduation and said, "Well. Let's see." I've never forgotten it.
Seeing a new class graduate makes me feel old. And I'm not old.
None of my family ever went to the Academy. I still come and watch. It's the village's day, too.
I counted the graduates. Twenty-three! Last time there were nineteen.
The new Genin get to choose where they sit at ramen. That's the best part, I think.
When I graduate, I'm going to wear my headband on my arm. Or my forehead. I can't decide.
I taught most of this class to throw. Watching them cross the yard is the best day of my year.
The yard was swept and raked at dawn. By noon there'll be footprints everywhere and nobody will care.
The fireworks go up over the Hokage Rock at nine. Best view is from the bridge by the river.
Goldfish scooping is harder than it looks. The paper nets tear if you hesitate.
Target throwing is a shinobi's game, but the stallkeeper swears a civilian won it once.
The lanterns along the main street are hung by the Academy students. It's a tradition.
Every stall on the street pays a few ryo to the festival fund. That pays for the fireworks.
They say the first Leaf Festival was held the summer the village was founded.
I bought a yukata this year. Blue, with white waves. I'm very pleased with myself.
The grilled corn stall at the far end is the best one. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
If you win a goldfish, the grocer sells little bowls for them. Clever, the grocer.
The night watch still does its rounds tonight, festival or not. They get extra dango, though.
My feet hurt, my purse is empty and I'm very happy. That's a good festival.
The mask stall's selling fox and cat masks. The children are going wild for them.
Fireworks are made by a family on the east road. They come every year with the cart.
I've lost my friends in the crowd twice already. I'll meet them at the bridge for the fireworks.
Candied apples, shaved ice, grilled squid. I'll regret all three in the morning.
Festival games pay out small prizes, a few ryo or a trinket. Good fun, not a living.
The tailor sells yukata just before the festival. Buy early or they're gone.
Events end by midnight, so make the most of it. The stalls pack up after the fireworks.
I made rice balls for the stallkeepers. They never get a chance to eat on festival night.
I always buy one goldfish and set it free in the river. My mother did the same.
There's a stall from a village three days away, selling sweets I've never heard of. I've tried four.
I want to know how they make the fireworks change colour. Nobody will tell me.
I set myself a festival budget: thirty ryo. I'm at twenty-eight and it's only eight o'clock.
The goldfish stall loses money every year. The keeper does it for the children's faces.
Did you see the big gold one? It burst right over the four faces on the Rock.
The fireworks are over, but nobody wants to go home yet. Look at them all, just standing about.
I scooped three goldfish! Then the net broke. But three!
I hit the middle of the target twice! The stall gave me a paper fan.
My big brother says the fireworks are louder from the Hokage Rock. We're not allowed up there.
I'm going to stay up till the very last firework. Then I'll sleep for a week.
Shaved ice gives you a headache if you eat it fast. I found out three times.
The fox masks are best. You can sneak up on people and they don't know it's you.
This end of the street is the food stalls, the far end is the games. The middle is just people.
The lantern strings run from the Academy gate all the way to the Residence. Somebody counted once: four hundred.
I like the moment the fireworks stop. The smoke drifts over the Rock and the whole street sighs.
Hold onto your little ones tonight. Every year a child gets lost at the goldfish stall.
I'm on the stall committee. Last year we had a fire at the squid grill. This year, buckets everywhere.
I've run the target-throwing stall for eleven years. The Genin think they'll clear it. The prizes say otherwise.
My family's sold candied apples at the festival since before I was born. I could dip them in my sleep.
Shinobi aren't allowed to use chakra at the target stall. I've seen a few try. The keeper always knows.
I won a goldfish. I named it after the moon. It's very small, but so is the moon from here.
The travelling merchants set up at the far end of the street. They bring things you can't get in the Leaf.
The coast cart only comes on Market Day. Squid, clams, seaweed. Everyone fights over it.
Farmers from the outer fields sell straight from their carts. Cheapest vegetables of the week.
There's a knife grinder who comes on Market Day. Half the shinobi in the village queue at that grindstone.
The grocer shouts louder on Market Day. I think it's a competition with the fishmonger.
I always find something I didn't need. Last week it was a ceramic frog.
The guards at the gate check every cart on Market Day. It takes them all morning.
If you want a bargain, come after noon. The farmers don't like carting things home.
The noticeboards are covered in requests on Market Day. Everyone needs a hand carrying something.
A storyteller sets up by the well on Market Day. The children sit there for hours.
On Market Day half the village needs help: carrying sacks, minding stalls. Easy ryo if you ask around.
I make a list every Market Day. I stick to it. Mostly. The frog was not on the list.
Prices drop after noon by a fifth. I've timed it. Every week.
I ask every travelling merchant where they came from. One had walked from the sea.
There's a spice merchant today with a powder that turns rice yellow. I need to know how.
I've got three ryo for Market Day. I'm going to spend them very, very carefully.
The candy stall made me a sugar dragon. I can't eat it, it's too good.
My mother lets me carry the basket. It's heavy, but I'm strong.
Market Day is my whole week in one morning. I'll be asleep by sundown.
At the shrine you ring the bell, bow twice, clap twice, and make your wish. Don't tell anyone what it is.
The Hokage speaks to the village from the Residence balcony every New Year. Short, usually. Everyone's cold.
The shrine sells fortunes on paper slips. If you get a bad one, tie it to the tree and leave it there.
The first sunrise of the year is best from the Hokage Rock. The climb is worth it.
My family eats long noodles on the last night, for a long life. Then sweet rice cakes in the morning.
The bell at the shrine rings a hundred and eight times before midnight. One for every worry.
The Academy children write their resolutions on strips of paper. Mine said "stop losing kunai." It didn't work.
New Year is the one night the shops stay open late. Everyone wants hot sake and sweet soup.
The shrine steps are icy. Hold the rail, the priests don't salt them well enough.
Everyone cleans their whole house the week before. It sweeps last year out the door.
The year's first meal should be cooked by someone you love. That's what my mother said, anyway.
Tonight nobody sleeps, so the tiredness comes late. You'll be fine until two, then you'll feel it.
If you're staying up for the sunrise, eat something after midnight. A meal keeps your legs going.
Go home and sleep after the first sunrise. Tomorrow is a holiday, but your bed doesn't know that.
I like the quiet after the bell stops. The whole village holding its breath.
Every year I write down one thing I'm grateful for and burn it in the shrine fire.
What do you think the Hokage wishes for? I've always wondered.
I like to imagine the faces on the Rock watching us all celebrate. They must be bored by now.
Even on New Year someone stands at the gate. I did it last year. The guards' tea was surprisingly good.
I'm going to ring the shrine bell so hard the whole village hears it.
My fortune said "great luck"! That means I'll win at everything this year, right?
We made rice cakes this morning. You have to pound and pound and pound. My arms hurt.
I'm wishing for a dog. Don't tell anyone, or it won't come true.
The queue for the bell goes all the way down the shrine steps. It moves faster than it looks.
They burn last year's charms in the bonfire behind the shrine. Bring yours, the priests take them.
I'm making sweet bean soup for anyone who comes by tonight. Cold hands should never go home empty.
This year I'm going to climb to the very top of the Rock for the sunrise. The very top!
The shops close for the first three days of the year. I spend them doing absolutely nothing. Bliss.
On the first snow, people leave a cup of warm sake on the doorstep for the winter spirits. Old habit.
The training grounds are slippery after the first snow. Half the Genin spend the day on their backs.
The tea house brings out roasted tea on the first snow. Nobody announces it, everyone knows.
The children always build a snow Hokage by the Academy gate. It's never a good likeness.
The bath house is packed on first-snow evenings. Nothing beats hot water and cold air.
First snow means the farm carts stop coming so often. Stock up on rice and pickles now.
I like the first snow because it covers every footprint. The village looks like nobody's been anywhere.
Have you got a proper coat? First snow is the coldest one, because nobody's ready for it.
I built a snow dog. It looks more like a snow potato, but I know it's a dog.
My hands are frozen, but I'm not going inside. Not ever.
People spread mats under the trees along the river from dawn to claim the best spot.
The dango stall sells the three-colour skewers only in blossom season. They sell out by noon.
The petals fall within a week. That's what makes the viewing matter.
The Academy holds lessons outside during blossom week. Not much gets learnt.
At night they hang paper lanterns under the trees by the river. It's the prettiest walk in the Leaf.
Somebody always falls asleep under a tree and wakes up covered in petals.
The shrine has an old tree that blooms first every year. People bet on which day it opens.
Blossoms remind me that good things don't stay. You have to stop and look while they're here.
I tried to catch a falling petal for an hour. I've decided it's a training exercise now.
If you catch a falling petal before it touches the ground, you get a wish. I've had seven wishes today.
We're making petal crowns. Mine keeps falling apart, so it's a petal pile.
People set pampas grass and white dumplings on their windowsills for the moon. It's an autumn custom.
The best place to see the moon is the hill behind the shrine. Bring a blanket and something warm.
Some say there's a rabbit on the moon, pounding rice. Look closely and you'll see its ears.
On moon-viewing night the tea house serves a special roasted tea, very mellow.
They say if you see the moon reflected in the river on viewing night, you'll have a good harvest.
The old ones write short poems about the moon and pin them on the shrine gate.
I always think the moon looks a little lonely. That's why we all come out to keep it company.
A full moon means a bright night. Good for travellers, bad for anyone trying to sneak about.
I'm looking for the moon rabbit. I see its ears! I think. Maybe they're clouds.
We get to stay up late for the moon. I'm going to stare at it until I fall asleep.
The couple walk to the shrine under a red umbrella. The families follow in a long line behind.
At the shrine the couple share three cups of sake, three sips each. It's very quiet, then everyone cheers.
After the shrine, there's a party in the family's house. It goes on until someone falls asleep in the rice.
Wedding guests bring ryo in a folded envelope. Odd numbers only, for luck.
The two families sit across from each other at the wedding meal. By the end, you can't tell them apart.
I was at a wedding where the dog walked the whole procession. Nobody minded. It looked very proud.
The shrine priests go through the wedding blessing slow. It's one of the longest prayers they know.
A wedding between two clans means two crests on the lanterns. People count how many of each.
The couple gives every guest a little box of sweets to take home. I keep the boxes.
My spouse and I married at that same shrine. The cedar by the steps was just a sapling then.
If you're invited to a wedding, wear your best and bring a gift. A small one is fine, a thoughtful one is better.
I'm going to dance at the party until my feet fall off. Then I'll dance sitting down.
I'm in charge of the seating plan. Two families, forty people, three old grudges. Pray for me.
A wedding is two families agreeing to share their worries. That's a braver thing than people think.
At an Akimichi wedding, the meal lasts longer than the ceremony. By about six hours.
In our clan the ninken walk in the wedding procession. A wedding without a howl isn't a proper one.
Weddings have the best food. I ate four sweet rice cakes and nobody stopped me.
The grown-ups danced. It was very embarrassing. I loved it.
My aunt visits from the market every Metalday and brings melon. I love Metaldays.
My friend moved to the other side of the village. Now we meet at the Hokage Rock steps every Sunday.
Our neighbourhood association meets at the tea house every Sunday. We argue about drains for an hour and then eat cake.
Patience isn't a gift. It's a muscle, and mine is very tired on Metaldays.
The history shelf is the dustiest and the most important. I give it a wipe every Metalday and nobody notices.
The tea house was out of my favourite dumplings. Out! On a Fireday! I'll be there at opening tomorrow.
I spent the afternoon deciding what colour Firedays are. I've settled on a soft green, like moss after rain.
Cook once, eat three times. Moonday stew is Fireday soup and Waterday rice topping. Waste nothing.
The stairwell smells of whatever the third floor is cooking. Firedays it's curry, and nobody knows who's making it.
